title: P01.38.B PROTEOMIC ANALYSIS OF EXTRACELLULAR VESICLES DERIVED FROM GLIOBLASTOMA STEM-LIKE CELLS TO CHARACTERIZE CELL HETEROGENEITY AND DIFFERENTIATION POTENTIAL
authors: H Kupcova Skalnikova; J Cervenka; H Ananbeh; E Garcia Borja; P Busek; A Sedo
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs) represent a distinct cellular population within the glioblastoma microenvironment, contributing significantly to intratumoral heterogeneity, therapy resistance, and disease recurrence. GSCs possess the capacity for self-renewal and can differentiate into more specialized cell types, including those expressing neuronal and/or astrocytic markers. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane enveloped particles that carry molecular cargo, such as proteins, RNAs and other molecules, which can be transferred to recipient cells and modify their phenotype. In glioblastoma, EVs are predominantly associated with pro-oncogenic signaling and angiogenesis. Given that GSCs comprise heterogeneous populations with distinct differentiation potentials, we aim to characterize the proteome of EVs secreted by several patient-derived GSC lines (n>10) to better understand the GSCs heterogeneity and differentiation capacity.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We have established a biobank of 24 patient-derived GSC cultures, characterized for tumorigenicity in immunodeficient mice and evaluated for differentiation potential by immunocytochemistry. Initial experiments were conducted using the NCH644 GSCs, which were grown in serum-free medium. EVs were isolated from conditioned medium via ultracentrifugation and characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting for exosomal markers. EV proteins were extracted using RIPA buffer and processed with a modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol. Proteomic analysis was performed using a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer coupled with a NanoElute2 HPLC system, followed by data analysis in Spectronaut software.
RESULTS
We successfully isolated EVs with diameters ranging from 30 to 200 nm, consistent with the size range of exosomes. Western blot analysis confirmed the enrichment of exosomal markers CD63, CD9, Alix, and TSG101 in EV preparations compared to parental GSCs. Proteomic profiling quantified 7,665 proteins in EV samples. Notably, all proteins from the Top 100 most commonly reported EV-associated proteins in the Vesiclepedia database were detected.
CONCLUSION
We have established a robust workflow for proteomic profiling of EVs released by patient-derived GSCs. This platform will be used to analyze EVs secreted during both proliferative and differentiated states of GSCs, with the goal of identifying protein signatures indicative of astrocytic, neuronal, or mixed differentiation potentials. These findings will advance our understanding of GSC heterogeneity and differentiation dynamics in glioblastoma.
SUPPORT/DISCLOSURE
This study was supported by National institute for cancer research (Project no.: LX22NPO5102) financed by the European Union - Next Generation EU. The authors declare no conflicts of interests.

title: P01.39.A CHARACTERIZATION OF AN IDH1-MUTANT ASTROCYTOMA CELL BIOBANK REVEALS A QUIESCENT STATE OF ASTROCYTE-LIKE CELLS WHICH DRIVES CELLULAR HETEROGENEITY UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF NOTCH PATHWAY
authors: L Garcia; D Pineau; D Sika; S Hideg; C Labadie; C Granotier; F Boussin; L Gauthier; M Mouthon; L Stuani; S Urbach; K El koulali; M Seveno; K Daddi; M Verreault; A Ibdaih; C Gozé; H Duffau; J Hugnot
abstract:
BACKGROUND
IDH1-mutant diffuse low-grade gliomas—oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas—are slow-growing brain tumors that can progress to higher grades and exhibit significant intratumoral cellular heterogeneity. Previous studies identified three populations in these tumors: astrocyte-like, oligodendrocyte-like, and stem-like cells. Some cells appear to be in a quiescent-like state, while others are actively dividing. However, the link between glioma cell phenotype and quiescence—and its contribution to heterogeneity—remains poorly understood, largely due to the lack of appropriate experimental models.
METHODS
In this study, we established a biobank of four patient-derived astrocytoma cell lines of varying grades and mutations, characterized using multi-omics. We then used CD44 and GLAST to isolate astrocyte-like and oligodendrocyte-like populations to investigate their properties and roles in tumor heterogeneity.
RESULTS
One specific cell line, LGG275, derived from a grade 2 astrocytoma, was identified as the relevant in vitro model for studying cellular heterogeneity. This slow-growing cell line harbors an IDH1 mutation, as well as TP53 and ATRX mutations, and CDKN2A loss, resulting in D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D2-HG) production and an alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) phenotype. It exhibits cellular heterogeneity, including astrocyte-like, oligodendrocyte-like, and stem-like populations. We have found that the astrocyte-like population corresponds to a quiescent state, resembling quiescent neural stem cells (qNSC). The oligodendrocyte-like population, on the other hand, reflects an active NSC state. Astrocyte-like cells are also plastic and can switch to an oligodendrocyte-like phenotype to restore cellular heterogeneity. This plasticity is regulated by the Notch pathway. In contrast, other established astrocytoma cell lines from our panel, particularly those derived from higher-grade tumors, display more complex subclonal architectures and a greater proportion of cancer stem-like cells, highlighting LGG275 as a simplified and tractable model to dissect the mechanisms underlying glioma plasticity.
CONCLUSION
We developed and annotated four new astrocytoma cell lines that recapitulate patient tumor features. LGG275 stands out as a simplified yet informative model to study glioma heterogeneity and plasticity, uncovering a notch-dependent transition from quiescence to activity in glioma cells.

title: P01.40.B СONDITION MEDIUM OF GLIOBLASTOMA CELLS INDUCES THE EXPRESSION OF A MEMBRANE-BOUND HEAT SHOCK PROTEIN MHSP70 IN MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS
authors: A Shapovalova; R Likhomanova; E Oganesyan; N Aksenov; A Nechaeva; M Shevtsov; N Yudintceva
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive form of gliomas and is characterized by increased levels of heat-shock proteins (HSPs) expression (including membrane-bound forms of HSP70, HSP90), which play a pivotal role in tumor progression. The aim of this work was to evaluate the effect of cell-conditioned medium of primary cultures of GBM on the transformation of normal mesenchymal cells which do present in the GBM microenvironment.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The experiments were performed using a three-dimensional model of cell culture in a spheroidal state, since this is considered the closest approximation to the in vivo environment. FetMSC (human embryonic bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell line) and primary culture GBM cells isolated from adult patients (n = 4) with newly diagnosed GBM without treatment were employed. The effect of three days of GBM cell-conditioned medium on changes in mHsp70 expression levels was evaluated. GBM cell culture medium and standard culture conditions for the FetMSC cell line were used as controls. The obtained data were analyzed using ImageJ software. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software Inc., USA).
RESULTS
The expression of mHsp70 on FetMSCs as detected using confocal microscopy (Olympus FV3000 system, Japan) and CytoFLEX flow cytofluorometry (CytoFLEX, Beckman Coulter, USA) revealed a more than 50% increase of mHsp70 expression by normal FetMSC cells exposed to GBM cell conditioning medium compared to the control. On stem cells the mHsp70 was located on the surface of plasma membrane in dotted patterns indicating its localization in lipid rafts (which was further proved by co-staining with anti-CD77 antibodies).
CONCLUSION
The obtained results demonstrate the influence of the secretome of primary GBM cell culture on the change in the level of mHsp70 expression by the normal mesenchymal cell line FetMSC, which may indicate their acquisition of a pro-tumorigenic phenotype.

BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive form of gliomas and is characterized by increased levels of heat-shock proteins (HSPs) expression (including membrane-bound forms of HSP70, HSP90), which play a pivotal role in tumor progression. The aim of this work was to evaluate the effect of cell-conditioned medium of primary cultures of GBM on the transformation of normal mesenchymal cells which do present in the GBM microenvironment.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The experiments were performed using a three-dimensional model of cell culture in a spheroidal state, since this is considered the closest approximation to the in vivo environment. FetMSC (human embryonic bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell line) and primary culture GBM cells isolated from adult patients (n = 4) with newly diagnosed GBM without treatment were employed. The effect of three days of GBM cell-conditioned medium on changes in mHsp70 expression levels was evaluated. GBM cell culture medium and standard culture conditions for the FetMSC cell line were used as controls. The obtained data were analyzed using ImageJ software. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software Inc., USA).
RESULTS
The expression of mHsp70 on FetMSCs as detected using confocal microscopy (Olympus FV3000 system, Japan) and CytoFLEX flow cytofluorometry (CytoFLEX, Beckman Coulter, USA) revealed a more than 50% increase of mHsp70 expression by normal FetMSC cells exposed to GBM cell conditioning medium compared to the control. On stem cells the mHsp70 was located on the surface of plasma membrane in dotted patterns indicating its localization in lipid rafts (which was further proved by co-staining with anti-CD77 antibodies).
CONCLUSION
The obtained results demonstrate the influence of the secretome of primary GBM cell culture on the change in the level of mHsp70 expression by the normal mesenchymal cell line FetMSC, which may indicate their acquisition of a pro-tumorigenic phenotype.

title: P01.41.A MASS SPECTROMETRY-BASED PROTEOMIC ASSESSMENT OF GLIOBLASTOMA STEM-LIKE CELL DIFFERENTIATION
authors: J Cervenka; E Garcia Borja; H Kupcova Skalnikova; P Busek; A Sedo
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs) represent a tumor-initiating subpopulation that plays a central role in driving glioblastoma heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, and recurrence. Characterized by their capacity for self-renewal and multipotent differentiation, GSCs can give rise to cell types expressing neuronal and glial markers. To investigate the proteomic landscape underlying these properties, we performed mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling of seven patient-derived GSC lines. Our analysis focused on identifying proteins associated with stemness and differentiation potential, offering insights into the molecular mechanisms that sustain GSC function and plasticity.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patient-derived GSCs were cultured in the presence of EGF and bFGF to maintain stem-like conditions, followed by induction of differentiation through growth factor withdrawal and exposure to fetal calf serum for ten days. Cells were lysed using RIPA buffer, and protein samples were prepared using our modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol. Proteomic analyses were performed using both data-dependent acquisition (DDA) and data-independent acquisition (DIA) modes on a timsTOF HT mass spectrometer coupled to a nanoElute 2 HPLC system. Raw data were processed using Spectronaut software with the directDIA workflow and a hybrid spectral library for protein identification and quantification.
RESULTS
We analyzed the cellular proteomes of seven patient-derived GSC lines and their differentiated counterparts. By combining DDA for spectral library generation with DIA for quantification, we identified and quantified over 11,500 proteins. These included key markers of stemness (e.g., Nestin and SOX-2), neuronal differentiation (e.g., Microtubule-associated protein 2 and Tubulin beta-III), and glial identity (e.g., Glial fibrillary acidic protein and Oligodendrocyte transcription factors 1 and 2). We observed a decrease of stemness markers and variable changes of neural markers during differentiation.
CONCLUSION
We performed proteomic analyses to investigate the serum induced differentiation of patient-derived GSCs and found evidence of limited differentiation under these conditions. While stemness markers showed a decreasing trend in differentiating cells, changes in neuronal and glial markers displayed high variability across cell lines. Our proteomic workflow enables the characterization of GSC heterogeneity and differentiation responses, supporting its utility for studying GSC plasticity.
SUPPORT/DISCLOSURE
This study was supported by National institute for cancer research (Project no.: LX22NPO5102) financed by the European Union - Next Generation EU as part of the Czech Recovery Plan. The authors declare no conflicts of interests.

title: P01.42.B CHANGES OF MAJOR GENES RELATED TO CELLULAR SENESCENCE IN GLIOMA
authors: N Pećina-Šlaus; J Težak; A Kafka; A Bukovac; N Njirić; F Dumančić; K Babić; R Hrašćan
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Cellular senescence is a process in which cells permanently cease to divide, playing a key role in controlling tumor growth and response to therapy. Increasing research indicates the significance of senescent glioma cells in shaping the clinical profile of glioma tumors. Gliomas are the most common primary tumors of the central nervous system, often with a poor prognosis due to aggressive clinical behavior and frequent recurrence after therapy. The aim of this study was to analyze the frequency and type of alterations in genes involved in cellular senescence in different types of gliomas.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
We analyzed 3425 glioma samples using data from the cBioPortal for Cancer Genomics. After querying 88 genes involved in senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), we selected and studied in more detail the 10 most frequently altered ones: TP53, CDKN2A, EGFR, ATM, TNFRSF1A, IGFBP7, TNFRSF11B, TP53BP1, HGF and SERPINE1. Data analysis included determining the frequency of mutations, amplifications, deletions, and multiple alterations in each type of glioma.
RESULTS
The results showed that TP53, CDKN2A, and EGFR were the most frequently altered genes. CDKN2A, EGFR, ATM, IGFBP7, TP53BP1, and HGF had a higher percentage of alterations in high-grade gliomas (HGG), while TP53, TNFRSF1A, TNFRSF11B and SERPINE1 were more frequently altered in low-grade gliomas (LGG). A statistically significant difference in alterations between the HGG and LGG groups was found for TP53, CDKN2A, EGFR, IGFBP7 and TNFRSF11B.
CONCLUSION
We have shown that the studied genes are more frequently altered in high-grade gliomas. The results highlight the importance of specific gene changes in cellular senescence and their association to glioma grade. Further research is needed to better understand the mechanisms by which these genes influence senescence and the clinical course of gliomas.

title: P01.43.A PD-L1 AND B7-H3 CHECKPOINT INHIBITOR BLOCKADE IN GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: A Knight; V Vybihal; V Juran; T Kazda; M Tomandlova; M Sova; P Fadrus; M Smrcka; M Piskacek
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with a short patient survival and is often associated with highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. The B7 family of immune checkpoint receptors are valuable targets for anti-tumour immunity and their blockades have revolutionized the field of cancer immunotherapy.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Glioblastoma tumors in newly diagnosed patients (n=80) were processed using enzymatic kits and gentleMACSTM Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec Inc.) and tumor cells phenotyped for the immune checkpoint inhibitor ligands B7-H1 (CD274) and B7-H3 (CD276) by multicolor flow cytometry. Glioblastoma cells were cultured in presence of PD-L1 inhibitor (atezolizumab, avelumab and durvalumab) or B7-H3 inhibitor (omburtamab) and subsequently used in killing assays with magnetically sorted innate immunity effector lymphocytes NK and γδ T cells, both with known prominent reactivity against GBM. The B7-H3 blocking studies were also performed using the CRISPR/Cas9. Next, we used Luminex xMAP technology to quantify plasma levels of PD-L1 and B7-H3 in patient samples at diagnosis (n=48), prior chemo/radio therapy (n=23), post therapy (n=22) and during disease progression (n=13).
RESULTS
We showed that B7-H1 and B7-H3 i) were highly expressed on primary GBM tumor cells at diagnosis and expression correlated with patient survival, ii) blockades modulated NK and γδ T cell cytotoxic activity against glioblastoma cell lines and primary tumor cells, iii) are directly involved in GBM-mediated suppression of tumor control, and iv) were significantly elevated levels in patients at diagnosis compared to age-matched healthy controls (HD, n=15) and remained significantly increased throughout the therapy.
CONCLUSION
Our study highlights the specific blockades of B7-H1 and B7-H3 immune checkpoint inhibitor ligands resulted in significant NK cell- and γδ T cell - mediated GBM tumor cell lysis, which could be exploited in novel immunotherapeutic interventions to improve patient survival.
DISCLOSURE
This study was supported by Ministry of Health, Czech Republic (grant NV19-05-00410 to AK) by Ministry of Health, Czech Republic-Conceptual Development of Research Organization (FNBr, 65269705). All rights reserved.

title: P01.44.B AMPK INHIBITION SYNERGISTICALLY ENHANCES THE EFFECT OF FATOSTATIN-TREATMENT IN GLIOBLASTOMA CELL MODELS
authors: S Spiegl-Kreinecker; L Marosits; L Schreiner; M Laaber; R Kälin; A Gruber; W Berger
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The ability to reprogram the energy metabolism is considered a hallmark of cancer cells to meet the increased energy demands essential for proliferation and cell growth. However, little is known on the effectiveness of targeting key regulators of metabolic disorders in glioblastoma cells. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the impact of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)- and SREBP-inhibition by dorsomorphin and fatostatin on the expression of enzymes controlling de novo fatty acid synthesis (e.g.FASN) in glioblastoma (GB) cells in vitro.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patient derived cell models (n=52) established from freshly resected GB tissue were analysed for FASN expression by qRT-PCR and sensitivity against the SREBP-inhibitor fatostatin. Out of these, three cell models (T98G/BTL761/BTL53) representative for high/medium/low FASN expression were selected for further analysis. Drug-sensitivity against both, the AMPK and SREBP inhibitors dorsomorphin and fatostatin was tested using an MTT-based approach. The effect of lipogenesis inhibition on the expression of AMPK, phospho-AMPK and SREBP effector proteins (e.g. FASN, ACC) was investigated following drug treatment by Western blot.
RESULTS
In our GB cell models FASN mRNA was found to be expressed at varying levels, but was significantly higher as compared to human normal astrocytes. Additionally, high FASN mRNA expression was significantly associated with higher sensitivity against SREBP inhibition by fatostatin (p=0.0352). With respect to the selected cell models, the FASNlow expressing BTL53 cell model presented with modest response against fatostatin, but high sensitivity against the AMPK-inhibitor dorsomorphin. Interestingly, this was in contrast to the FASNhigh expressing BTL761 and T98G cells, which showed high sensitivity against fatostatin but were distinctly lower susceptible to dorsomorphin treatment. Interestingly, combined drug treatment resulted in a synergistically enhanced effect, which was irrespective of the extent of the initial FASN expression level.
CONCLUSION
GB cells presenting with high levels of FASN are susceptible to fatostatin treatment, which was indicated by IC50 levels below 20µM. Combined treatment with inhibitors directed against both, the AMPK and SREBP pathway resulted in a synergistically enhanced response. Consequently, lipogenesis inhibition by attacking different axes of metabolism regulation might be a promising novel therapeutic option in glioblastoma. The effect of drug combinations on the expression of proteins involved in de novo lipogenesis will be analysed in further studies.

title: P01.45.A FUNCTIONAL DRUG SCREENING REVEALS THE LIMITATIONS OF GENOTYPE-BASED TARGETED THERAPY IN GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: M Klein; P Achaiber Sing; J Hoogeveen; C M Dirven; A Stubbs; M L Lamfers
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive brain cancers, with standard treatment unchanged since 2005. Although targeted therapies have shown promise in other cancers, multiple clinical trials in GBM have failed to improve overall survival. This limited success may be explained by poor drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, the highly invasive growth pattern of GBM, and its inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity. Together, these factors may influence the effectiveness of traditional genotype-based targeted therapy approaches in GBM. In this study, we evaluated a genotype-driven approach by screening patient-derived glioma stem-like cells (GSCs) with targeted therapies chosen based on frequently observed gene amplifications and deletions, herinafter referred to as copy number variants (CNVs).
MATERIAL AND METHODS
CNV profiling was performed on GBM tissue samples and GSCs using whole genome sequencing, followed by CNV calling with the tool CNVkit. GSCs were only included if CNVs identified in the original tissue were retained in the corresponding GSCs, ensuring that selected models accurately reflect the genomic profile targeted for treatment. Twelve GSCs were treated with a panel of twelve drugs targeting CDKN2A, CDK4, EGFR, KIT, PIK3CA and NF1, which were selected based on six frequently occurring CNVs in the TCGA dataset. Drug responses were assessed to evaluate efficacy and correlation with the CNVs.
RESULTS
Drug screening revealed no consistent pattern in therapeutic response between samples with specific CNVs and those without, suggesting that these genomic alterations alone did not predict sensitivity to the corresponding targeted therapies. Notably, GSCs with an NF1 loss showed a trend toward increased sensitivity to MEK inhibitors compared to NF1 wildtype cultures — a difference primarily driven by response to one of the two MEK inhibitors tested. These findings emphasize the limited predictive value of common CNVs for targeted monotherapy and support the use of personalized screening approaches to identify more effective treatment options for GBM.
CONCLUSION
Our study shows that selecting targeted therapies based on frequently altered CNVs in GBM does not result in consistent or effective treatment responses, underscoring the biological complexity of the disease. While GSCs with an NF1 loss revealed a trend toward increased sensitivity to MEK inhibitors, this effect was primarily observed with one of the MEK targeted compounds, highlighting that even within genetically defined subgroups, drug response can be dependent on the specific drug applied. These results emphasize the limitations of using CNVs alone to guide personalized therapy and suggest that alternatives like functional drug screening approaches warrants further exploration.

title: P01.46.B MOLECULAR ANALYSIS OF IDH MUTATED LOW GRADE GLIOMA PROGRESSION
authors: M Trybula; M Lysiak-Lindman; M Hallbeck; C Bratthäll; M Strandéus; P Milos; A Malmström; P Söderkvist
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Isocitrate dehydrogenase-mutated (IDHmut) gliomas, frequently diagnosed at stage II, often recur at higher stages with increased aggressiveness. However, the molecular mechanisms driving these recurrences remain poorly understood, particularly given their highly variable timeline—occurring within months in some cases and years in others. This study aims to analyze the transcriptomes and methylomes of primary and recurrent tumors to identify patterns that could provide insight into the factors influencing tumor progression.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
To date, our study has included six astrocytomas (AC) and 24 oligodendrogliomas (ODG), all exhibiting at least one recurrence (19 patients). Among them, eight patients experienced two recurrences, while three had three recurrences. DNA and RNA were extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor sections marked by a pathologist to ensure a high tumor cell content (>70%). IDH status was determined using Sanger sequencing. RNA samples underwent transcriptome analysis using Clariom D microarrays, followed by processing with TAC 4.0 software for data analysis. Additionally, methylome profiling is currently being conducted using Illumina 935k methylation arrays, with findings to be presented at a later stage.
RESULTS
IDH mutation was detected in all primary tumor samples; however, in two ODG cases, the mutation was lost at the second recurrence. Differential gene expression analysis and unsupervised hierarchical clustering of all primary and recurrent samples identified four distinct clusters—two corresponding to primary tumors and two to recurrent cases. When analyzed by diagnosis, AC exhibited a clear separation between primary and recurrent tumors, with an increasing number of differentially expressed genes as recurrence progressed. Approximately 50% of differentially expressed genes were non-coding, with 3.46% belonging to miRNA precursors and 2.69% being small RNAs. In contrast, oligodendrogliomas showed no distinct differences in expression pattern when comparing primary and recurrent samples.
CONCLUSION
Transcriptome profiling revealed progressive alterations in recurrent AC cases, while ODG recurrence appears to follow a different trajectory. Further methylome analysis may offer deeper insights into the mechanisms driving glioma progression, and the inclusion of additional samples and treatment data could further enhance these findings.

title: P01.47.A IMPACT OF CHOLESTEROL SYNTHESIS INHIBITION IN G7 GLIOBLASTOMA STEM-LIKE CELLS CULTURED AS 3D SPHEROIDS
authors: S Mirza; N Gomez-Roman
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) stem-like cells (GSCs) are a treatment-resistant subpopulation of cells that underlie tumour recurrence. Emerging evidence indicates that GSCs have elevated cholesterol synthesis rates and may confer protection against standard-of-care therapies. We investigated the effects of inhibiting cholesterol synthesis at two points: upstream via simvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) inhibitor, and downstream via AY9944, which targets dehydrocholesterol 7-reductase (DHCR7).
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patient-derived G7 GSC spheroids were treated with simvastatin or AY9944 across a concentration range of 10 to 0.316 µmol/L with or without cholesterol supplementation. DMSO was used as vehicle control. Spheroids were monitored over 14 days, measured using FIJI (Image J), and statistically analysed using a two-way ANOVA. Spheroid viability was assessed using calcein-AM and propidium iodide to label live/dead cells, respectively, followed by imaging with confocal microscopy, and analysed using a one-way ANOVA. To evaluate GSC frequency, a tumoursphere formation assay using extreme limiting dilution analysis was performed after 21 days of treatment at a concentration range of 3.16 to 0.316 to µmol/L.
RESULTS
Simvastatin reduced G7 spheroid proliferation in a concentration-dependent manner, ranging from 28% (95% CI: 3.35, 53.25; p.adj < 0.05) at 0.316 µmol/L to 60% (95% CI: 34.92, 84.81; p.adj < 0.001) at 10 µmol/L, compared to vehicle-treated controls. Cholesterol supplementation partially rescued spheroid proliferation at lower concentrations (0.316 and 1 µmol/L; p.adj > 0.05), but not at 3.16 or 10 µmol/L (p.adj < 0.001). Simvastatin did not affect spheroid viability at 3.16 or 10 µmol/L at day 14, but GSC frequency was reduced compared to vehicle treated GSCs (0.194, 0.114, 0.074, 0.045 for DMSO, 0.316, 1 and 3.16 µmol/L, respectively; p < 0.001). AY9944 decreased G7 spheroid proliferation and viability but exhibited lower potency than simvastatin. While 10 µmol/L reduced spheroid fold-change by 50.66% (95% CI: 20.28, 81.03; p < 0.001), 3.16 and 10 µmol/L decreased spheroid viability by 50% (95% CI: 32.92, 69.66; p.adj < 0.05) and 62% (95% CI: 43.74, 80.47; p.adj < 0.001), respectively, at day 14. These effects were rescued by cholesterol supplementation (p.adj < 0.05). AY9944 reduced GSC frequency at all tested concentrations compared to vehicle treated GSCs (0.194, 0.124, 0.097, 0.020 for DMSO, 0.316, 1 and 3.16 µmol/L, respectively; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION
Cholesterol synthesis inhibition reduces G7 spheroid proliferation and self-renewal. Upstream inhibition exerts cytostatic, partially cholesterol-independent effects while downstream inhibition is cytotoxic and cholesterol-dependent. These findings highlight HMGCR and DHCR7 inhibition as potential treatment targets against GSC-driven GBM recurrence.

BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) stem-like cells (GSCs) are a treatment-resistant subpopulation of cells that underlie tumour recurrence. Emerging evidence indicates that GSCs have elevated cholesterol synthesis rates and may confer protection against standard-of-care therapies. We investigated the effects of inhibiting cholesterol synthesis at two points: upstream via simvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) inhibitor, and downstream via AY9944, which targets dehydrocholesterol 7-reductase (DHCR7).
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patient-derived G7 GSC spheroids were treated with simvastatin or AY9944 across a concentration range of 10 to 0.316 µmol/L with or without cholesterol supplementation. DMSO was used as vehicle control. Spheroids were monitored over 14 days, measured using FIJI (Image J), and statistically analysed using a two-way ANOVA. Spheroid viability was assessed using calcein-AM and propidium iodide to label live/dead cells, respectively, followed by imaging with confocal microscopy, and analysed using a one-way ANOVA. To evaluate GSC frequency, a tumoursphere formation assay using extreme limiting dilution analysis was performed after 21 days of treatment at a concentration range of 3.16 to 0.316 to µmol/L.
RESULTS
Simvastatin reduced G7 spheroid proliferation in a concentration-dependent manner, ranging from 28% (95% CI: 3.35, 53.25; p.adj < 0.05) at 0.316 µmol/L to 60% (95% CI: 34.92, 84.81; p.adj < 0.001) at 10 µmol/L, compared to vehicle-treated controls. Cholesterol supplementation partially rescued spheroid proliferation at lower concentrations (0.316 and 1 µmol/L; p.adj > 0.05), but not at 3.16 or 10 µmol/L (p.adj < 0.001). Simvastatin did not affect spheroid viability at 3.16 or 10 µmol/L at day 14, but GSC frequency was reduced compared to vehicle treated GSCs (0.194, 0.114, 0.074, 0.045 for DMSO, 0.316, 1 and 3.16 µmol/L, respectively; p < 0.001). AY9944 decreased G7 spheroid proliferation and viability but exhibited lower potency than simvastatin. While 10 µmol/L reduced spheroid fold-change by 50.66% (95% CI: 20.28, 81.03; p < 0.001), 3.16 and 10 µmol/L decreased spheroid viability by 50% (95% CI: 32.92, 69.66; p.adj < 0.05) and 62% (95% CI: 43.74, 80.47; p.adj < 0.001), respectively, at day 14. These effects were rescued by cholesterol supplementation (p.adj < 0.05). AY9944 reduced GSC frequency at all tested concentrations compared to vehicle treated GSCs (0.194, 0.124, 0.097, 0.020 for DMSO, 0.316, 1 and 3.16 µmol/L, respectively; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION
Cholesterol synthesis inhibition reduces G7 spheroid proliferation and self-renewal. Upstream inhibition exerts cytostatic, partially cholesterol-independent effects while downstream inhibition is cytotoxic and cholesterol-dependent. These findings highlight HMGCR and DHCR7 inhibition as potential treatment targets against GSC-driven GBM recurrence.

title: P02.01.B PERICYTES ORCHESTRATE A TUMOR-SUPPRESSIVE MICROENVIRONMENT BY IMPINGING ON THE CROSSTALK BETWEEN MACROPHAGES AND TUMOR-INITIATING CELLS IN GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: S Braun; P Bolivar; C R Oudenaarden; J Sjölund; M Bocci; K Harbst; M Safaee Talkhoncheh; B Phung; E Cordero; E Johansson; R Rosberg; G B Jönsson; A Pietras; K Pietras
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by fast progression, infiltrative growth pattern and a high rate of relapse. A defining feature of GBM is the existence of spatially and functionally distinct cellular niches, i.e. a hypoxic niche, a leading-edge niche, and a peri-vascular niche, in which malignant cells engage in paracrine crosstalk with cell types comprising the tumor microenvironment, including immune cells, astrocytes, and vascular cells.
MATERIAL AND METHODS AND RESULTS
By analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data of human GBM and transgenic mouse models of GBM, we unexpectedly identified pericytes intimately associated with the endothelium as the most active paracrine signaling hub within the tumor parenchyma. Exclusive signaling axes emanating from pericytes were received by endothelial cells, malignant cells, astrocytes, and immune cells. Depletion of pericytes through genetic engineering in several different transgenic and orthotopic mouse models of GBM demonstrated accelerated tumor progression, a disrupted blood-brain-barrier, and premature death of pericyte-poor mice. Mechanistic studies revealed that pericyte deficiency altered the cellular composition of GBM, remodeled the endothelium, and impacted on the immune cell landscape. Specifically, endothelial cells deprived of pericyte association upregulated Colony Stimulating Factor (CSF)-1, which in turn attracted peri-vascular tumor-associated macrophages polarized towards an immune-suppressive phenotype. In the absence of pericytes, the recruited macrophages expressed Hepatocyte Growth Factor (HGF), which reinforced activation of its receptor tyrosine kinase c-Met on a subset of GBM cells harboring an extreme mesenchymal-like state. Indeed, orthotopic implantation of isolated c-Met-expressing GBM cells corroborated their superior tumor-initiating capability and invasive phenotype, compared to cells negative for c-Met.
CONCLUSION
We infer that the pericyte represents a critical modulator of GBM development by orchestrating a tumor-suppressive microenvironment; our findings thus highlight the importance of pericyte preservation in the face of current and future GBM therapies.

title: P02.02.A IL6 UNDERLIES MICROENVIRONMENT IMMUNOSUPPRESSION AND RESISTANCE TO THERAPY IN GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: J S Young; N Cho; C G Lucas; K Seo; H Najem; K Mirchia; W C Chen; N Zakimi; V Daggubati; T Casey-Clyde; M P Nguyen; A Chen; J J Phillips; T Ozawa; M K Aghi; J W Taylor; J L DeRisi; A Bhaduri; A Heimberger; M S Berger; N Butowski; M H Spitzer; D R Raleigh
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The glioblastoma (GBM) tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is an immunosuppressive barrier to therapeutic innovation, and unsurprisingly GBM responses to immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) are rare. Here, we define therapeutic vulnerabilities and mechanisms underlying GBM resistance to ICI therapy.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Integration of spatial and single-cell approaches from human IDH-wildtype GBMs before and after ICI treatment with preclinical genetic, immunologic, and efficacy studies in immunocompetent mouse GBM models.
RESULTS
Human GBMs with radiographic responses to ICI had lower pre-treatment IL6 levels on spatial profiling than GBMs resistant to ICI. Multiplexed immunofluorescence revealed ICI-responders were enriched in T-cell proteins (CD3, CD4, CD8) and activation markers (CD25) at the time of salvage surgery; meanwhile, non-responders were enriched in myeloid proteins (CD68, CD163, CD11c). Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 32,877 cells from human GBMs showed IL6 is predominantly produced by radial glial like cancer stem cells. Interestingly, mice bearing intracranial SB28 GBM allografts universally suppressed intratumor IL6 levels when treated with immunostimulatory gene therapies and mouse genetic experiments confirmed prolonged survival in animals with an IL6-/- background. Mouse survival was improved by combination systemic treatment with anti-PD1 and anti-IL6 but was not improved by either antibody alone or by local anti-IL6 delivery. Mass cytometry revealed combination therapy reprogrammed the GBM TIME by increasing MHCII+ monocytes, CD103+ migratory dendritic cells (DCs), CD11b+ conventional DCs, and effector CD8+ T cells, and by decreasing immunosuppressive Tregs.
CONCLUSION
Systemic anti-IL6 in combination with systemic ICI reprograms the GBM TIME to sensitize preclinical models to ICI, shedding light on a therapeutic strategy for GBM treatment.

title: P02.03.B GLIOBLASTOMA CELL-DERIVED APLN SHOWS DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS ON MYELOID CELL MIGRATION
authors: L Pitigala-Motal; J Enders; G Mastrella; S Spiegl-Kreinecker; A Gruber; R Glass; R E Kälin
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The rapid progression of glioblastoma (GBM) is fostered by GBM-induced immunosuppression and by tumor-associated myeloid cells (TAMs), which massively accumulate in GBM and support glioma expansion. Hence, signaling-pathways controlling the tumor tropism of myeloid cells or immune-regulation of TAMs constitute a potential therapeutic target for GBM. We previously found that the angiogenic factor apelin (APLN) signals through its G-protein coupled receptor APLNR to regulate neo-vascularization and tumor cell invasion. When screening for APLNR co-regulated genes in the TCGA database they correlated best with lymphocyte-mediated immune responses.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
To study the role of APLN-APLNR-signaling in GBM-immune cell interaction we used different mouse GBM models and analyzed them for TAM by immunohistochemistry. Primary GBM and murine myeloid cells (BV2 and J774) were investigated in spheroid invasion or transwell migration assays. APLIN/APLNR expression was assessed by qPCR, immunohistochemistry and FACS and functional studies were performed using APLN knock-down (AKD) cells and APLN knock out (aplnKO) mice.
RESULTS
Analyzing xenografts of different human GBM cells we found a direct correlation of APLN with TAM cell density in the tumor area and the invasive zone. We detected APLN expression in primary GBM cells and APLNR upregulation in Iba1-postitive TAMs and murine myeloid cell cultures allowing for direct interactions. Indeed, BV2 microglia reacted chemotactic to the smallest functional APLNR-agonistic peptide apelin-13 while J774 macrophages showed no response. Interestingly, using conditioned medium of AKD GBM cells variable response to endogenous APLN were obtained with microglia showing reduced and macrophages increased mobility. In vivo, complete depletion of APLN in aplnKO mice further reduced TAM-density, while intracerebral apelin-13 infusion restored their accumulation.
CONCLUSION
Altogether, we propose that APLN-APLNR signaling is involved in the inflammatory response to tumor cells mediating the specific myeloid cell composition in GBM. We suggest that blockade of APLN-APLNR signaling mediates broad anti-tumor effects by inhibiting angiogenesis, GBM cell invasion and immune suppression.

title: P02.04.A UNCOVERING AND TARGETING METABOLIC REGULATORS OF IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE LIPID-LADEN MACROPHAGES IN GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: M Farber; T van Schaik; D Aschmann; M Boon; D J Kloosterman; J Erbani; L Akkari
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma tumors are characterized by a prominent infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), constituting up to 30-40% of the cellular make-up. These cells typically harbor immunosuppressive features which, in conjunction with T cell paucity, contribute to a tumor microenvironment (TME) uniquely refractory to immunotherapy response. Therefore, due to their critical role in tumor progression and therapy response, TAMs represent a promising therapeutic target within the brain TME.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
To address the challenge of macrophage heterogeneity in glioblastoma, we conducted comprehensive multi-omics analyses including scRNAseq, spatial transcriptomics, ATACseq and lipidomics, that identified distinct TAM subsets within tissue-resident microglia and infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophage (MDM) pools.
RESULTS
We discovered a pro-tumorigenic and immunosuppressive subset common in both cell lineages characterized by high lipid metabolic activity which we termed lipid-laden macrophages (LLMs). These cells engulf and recycle lipid-rich myelin debris to fuel cancer cell proliferation and thereby promote malignancy. Beyond these functions, LLMs also exhibit immunosuppressive features that are induced by myelin debris uptake. Next, we aim to investigate the relationship between myelin-induced metabolic pathways and the subsequent immunosuppressive phenotype of LLMs. To accomplish this, we will employ a genetic screen on primary murine macrophages using a CRISPR knockout library. This approach will target the cellular metabolome and surfaceome, with the goal of rewiring TAMs toward a more immunogenic phenotype. To enable selective targeting of LLMs, we developed lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based approaches. Our findings demonstrate that LNPs efficiently deliver cargo to macrophages in the TME, with formulations that can be tailored for enhanced cell type-specific uptake.
CONCLUSION
We identified myelin as a key molecule fostering a tumor-permissive brain TME. We are currently harnessing genetic screening together with the development of cell type-specific LNPs which will enable interventions targeting the immuno-metabolic axis, potentially advancing new treatment strategies for glioblastoma.

title: P02.05.B MAPPING MICROGLIAL DIVERSITY AND TUMOR HETEROGENEITY IN PRIMARY GLIOBLASTOMA AND PATIENT-DERIVED ORGANOIDS
authors: J Mazzoni; G Haug; E Roth; J Hiebl; J Messinger; K Mehling; E Meller; R Nickl; C Monoranu; A Appelt-Menzel; C Hagemann; F Liesche-Starnecker; V Nickl
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, marked by extensive inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity and pronounced therapy resistance. Microglia is a major contributor to this complexity and plays a pivotal role in shaping tumor behavior and modulating responses to therapy. Yet its precise phenotypic and functional states across distinct tumor regions and model systems remain poorly defined. In this study, we employ patient-derived organoids (PDOs) alongside matched primary tissue (PT) to characterize microglial diversity and investigate how microglia contributes to the cellular inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity of GBM.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Fresh tumor tissue was obtained from 13 GBM patients and sampled from six spatially distinct regions per tumor. PDOs were generated from these regions and compared to matched PT to evaluate microglial presence, distribution, and morphology. To assess intertumoral heterogeneity, we compared microglial characteristics across patients, while intratumoral heterogeneity was examined by analyzing differences between regions within individual tumors. Subsequently, PDOs were treated with temozolomide (TMZ), and microglia was visualized and quantified using Iba1 immunofluorescence to evaluate treatment-induced morphological changes and shifts in microglial abundance.
RESULTS
Microglia in PT exhibited a microglia morphology more similar to PDOs than to healthy brain tissue. Distinct microglial distribution patterns emerged across PDOs, with microglia typically arranged in one of four configurations: (1) perinuclear, (2) ring-like, (3) at the PDO margin, or (4) diffusely dispersed throughout the PDO. In 5/13 PDOs we found significantly higher microglial abundance compared to PT (PPDO 4 = 0.0013, PPDO 7 = 0.0424, PPDO 8 = 0.0153, PPDO 10 = 0.0162, PPDO 12 = 0.0083). Analysis across patients revealed significant intertumoral heterogeneity in microglial characteristics (p = 0.0405). In terms of intratumoral heterogeneity, regional differences in microglial abundance and morphology were observed within individual PDOs, with statistically significant variation only found in PDO 10 (p = 0.0211). Following TMZ treatment, 4/13 PDOs showed a significant recline in microglial abundance (PDO 2: p < 0.0001; PDO 4: p = 0.0041; PDO 7: p = 0.0015; PDO 10: p = 0.0297).
CONCLUSION
Our findings reveal significant inter- and intratumoral microglial heterogeneity in PDOs. Distinct microglial distribution patterns and variable responses to TMZ highlight the complex and patient-specific nature of microglial involvement in the GBM microenvironment. These results underscore the relevance of PDOs as a model system for studying tumor-immune interactions and therapeutic responses in a personalized context.

title: P02.06.A MASS SPECTROMETRY BASED SPATIAL PROTEOMICS REVEALS DIFFERENTIALLY EXPRESSED PROTEINS IN THE CORE AND PERIPHERY OF GLIOBLASTOMA
authors: K Saxena; R Dauke; V Petrosius; V Pedersen; X Xin; N Hammouda; D Harwood; E Schoof; B Kristensen
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma is the most frequent and malignant tumor of the brain, and due to its infiltrative behavior, tumor recurrence is inevitable. Previous studies suggest various genes and signaling pathways as regulators of glioblastoma brain infiltration but many of these use transcriptomics-based discovery approaches and only few are based on human tissue. Although multiple biomarkers have been identified at the transcript level, it has been challenging to translate these findings in a clinical setting. A significant body of research has documented the discordance between mRNA and protein levels at different scales, potentially explaining the limited success. Accordingly, here we take a protein-centric view to investigate the tumor core, transition zone, and periphery of glioblastoma in order to identify potential therapeutic targets and signaling pathways responsible for the infiltration.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Thirteen formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) glioblastoma, IDH wildtype patient tissue samples underwent Zeiss Palm MicroBeam-based laser capture microdissection (LCM) for isolation of 50.000 μm2 areas from core, transition zone, and periphery. Proteome quantifications were performed using the EvoSep One liquid chromatography platform in combination with the Orbitrap Astral Mass Spectrometer.
RESULTS
We obtained over 7500 protein groups from 50,000 μm2 sections and found 2347 spatially differentially regulated proteins, demonstrating the technological advancement in capturing regions-specific proteome profiles. We observed that the tumor core is enriched with tumor cells of mesenchymal subtype, while the periphery is enriched with tumor cells of classical, proneural, and neural-like subtype. Quantitative differential analysis revealed an increase in netrin and hedgehog signaling-related protein expression going from the tumor core to the periphery, suggesting potential signaling pathways that may play a role in the infiltration of tumor cells.
CONCLUSION
This study demonstrates our ability to perform low-input-based proteomics with high sensitivity. Our analysis identified potential therapeutic targets and their corresponding signaling pathways in the glioblastoma periphery. These targets are currently being functionally investigated and tested.

title: P02.07.B TARGETING GLIOBLASTOMA MITOCHONDRIAL METABOLISM WITH S-GBOXIN INDUCES CYTOTOXICITY UNDER CONDITIONS OF THE TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
authors: J Weinem; H Urban; T Buhlmann; A Hau; S Liebner; J P Steinbach; A Luger; M W Ronellenfitsch
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GB) is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults with a dismal prognosis. Targeted therapy approaches that exploit cancer-specific traits have yielded disappointing results in clinical trials. A novel compound targeting oxidative phosphorylation in GB via inhibition of complex V of the respiratory chain is Gboxin. S-Gboxin, a pharmacokinetically optimized version with improved in vivo stability, was efficient in a mouse GB model but has not been tested under conditions of tumor microenvironment, including hypoxia and nutrient deprivation.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Cytotoxicity and cell death under S-Gboxin treatment were analyzed in human GB cell lines and primary tumor cell cultures, as well as immortalized and primary human astrocytes. Additionally, culture conditions were modulated to induce nutrient deprivation, hypoxia, and dependency on mitochondrial fuels. As further readouts, oxygen consumption and effects of migration were measured. To analyze co-targets for a potential synergistic effect with S-Gboxin, we employed pharmacological and genetic models of inhibition of the integrated stress response (ISR) and of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
RESULTS
S-Gboxin cytotoxicity was detectable starting at concentrations of approximately 4 µM and nutrient replete conditions after 24 h in human GB cells. Nutrient starvation and mitochondrial fuels enhanced cell death. Hypoxia did not diminish the effects of S-Gboxin. Oxygen consumption was reduced under S-Gboxin. Additionally, S-Gboxin treatment led to elevated lactate production and increased glucose consumption. ATF4 as a marker of the ISR was induced in a dose dependent manner in ATF4 reporter cells, but its inhibition did not mediate resistance to S-Gboxin. In contrast, AMPK inhibition, in combination with S-Gboxin, dramatically enhanced cell death. A similar effect of increased cell death was detected under incubation with galactose, whose metabolism relies on mitochondria.
CONCLUSION
Nutrient deprivation and mitochondrial fuels, as well as AMPK inhibition, enhanced S-Gboxin dependent cell death. Hypoxia did not reduce S-Gboxin efficacy. While the ISR was induced by S-Gboxin in a dose dependent manner, this was not relevant for therapy resistance. In summary, S-Gboxin is a promising compound for targeting cancer-specific metabolic pathways in GB cells, especially in combination with AMPK-inhibition.

title: P02.08.A A SPATIALLY RESOLVED HUMAN GLIOBLASTOMA ATLAS REVEALS DISTINCT CELLULAR AND MOLECULAR PATTERNS OF ANATOMICAL NICHES
authors: H Park; P Sonpatki; C Park; W Park; N Shah
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most lethal brain tumor in adults with remarkable cellular plasticity and complex anatomical features. While single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revealed its cellular heterogeneity, the spatial cellular organization within the anatomical features remains elusive.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Here, we provide a comprehensive spatial transcriptomic dataset comprising 115,914 transcriptomes from 32 genotyped tissue sections.
RESULTS
Leveraging Xenium in situ technology, we generated spatial transcriptomic data with subcellular-resolution, significantly improving the granularity of our understanding of GBM cellular architecture. In addition, our analyses identified oligodendrocyte subtypes specifically localized to tumor cores and perivascular regions with molecular profiles associated with poor prognosis.
CONCLUSION
This publicly accessible GBM atlas provides a valuable resource for understanding the complex cellular architecture of GBM and facilitating the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

title: P02.09.B SURGICAL RESECTION OF GLIOBLASTOMA INDUCES IMMUNOSUPPRESSION
authors: J Reveilles; A Ballestin; C Pichol-Thievend; A Thomas; V Ribecco; O Anezo; G Bourmeau; B Blanchard; F M Cavalli; G R Borst; C Alanio; D Heiland; A Golebiewska; Z A Binder; J van Rheenen; F Roncaroli; K Joseph; V M Ravi; G Seano
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GB) is one of the deadliest cancers, recurring at a rate of 90%, despite a high standard of care composed of gross total surgery, fractioned and concomitant chemoradiation, and adjuvant chemotherapy. Moreover, numerous immunotherapies have not succeeded in enhancing survival rates for GB patients. GBs are known for having an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME); nonetheless, only a limited number of studies have explored the biological alterations that occur in the TME following surgical interventions.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
In this study, we established novel syngeneic mouse models for stereotaxic fluorescence-guided surgical resection of the GB. We performed multi-omics analyses (single-cell RNA-seq and bulk proteomics) combined with digital pathology to better understand the short-term molecular dynamics in the TME after surgery.
RESULTS
We discovered that surgery gave rise to ischemic and necrotic areas within the residual tumor even far from the surgical cavity. This led to remodeling of the TME with hypoxic pathways induced in all TME components. Hypoxia induced immunosuppression at multiple levels. Post-surgical immunosuppression was characterized by reshuffling of the GB immune TME. Surgery induced a decrease in the number of immunoactive cells, such as T and B cells, as well as dendritic cells, and an increase in their immunosuppressive counterparts, such as hypoxic macrophages, or Tregs. We also observed a transient increase of neutrophils. These changes were associated with an increase in immunosuppressive pathways, such as Ctla4 in T cells or Spp1 in myeloid cells, and a decrease in immune-activating pathways, such as interferon pathways. Consistent with these findings, we observed a transcriptomic reduction in antigen presentation within vascular, myeloid, and GB cells, as well as a decrease in immunoglobulins, as revealed by proteome analysis. Notably, the cell-to-cell interactions between the TME and GB cells changed radically. The hypoxic TME, such as vascular cells, hypoxic macrophages, and neutrophils, actively interacted with tumor cells, thus re-shaping the tumor towards an immunosuppressed environment.
CONCLUSION
Overall, our results showed that although surgery is a crucial procedure for improving the survival of patients with GB, it induces immunosuppression, which may lead to glioblastoma resistance to conventional therapy and immunotherapy.

title: P02.10.A CHARACTERIZATION OF THE TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT IN PERIPHERAL AREAS OF GLIOBLASTOMA USING MULTIPLEX SEQUENTIAL PROTOCOLS.
authors: M Ramírez González
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most frequent and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, with a high recurrence rate even after standard treatment, which includes surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. This recurrence is associated with the tumor’s ability to infiltrate brain tissue beyond the margins visible on neuroimaging, making complete resection nearly impossible. In a prospective study, conducted in collaboration with Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, we analyzed a cohort of radiologically-guided biopsies, including regions of tumor infiltration, vasogenic edema and even apparently normal areas. Using DAB immunohistochemistry for MIB-1, we detected proliferative tumor cells not only in the tumor core but also in the non-infiltrated peripheral zone. This finding prompted us to further characterize the tumor microenvironment in these areas.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We developed a multiplex sequential immunofluorescence (mIF) protocol based on the cyclic elimination of antibodies using 2-mercaptoethanol and SDS. Although pre-designed commercially panels exist for this type of approach, we designed custom panels focused on studying peripheral GBM regions, including specific markers for tumor, immune, glial and endothelial cells. This method enables detailed spatial characterization using confocal microscopy. In parallel, and with the aim of increasing accessibility of this technology, we developed a complementary protocol based on multiplex sequential immunohistochemistry with chromogens (mIC), compatible with conventional light microscopy. In this case, chromogen removal between rounds is performed by washing in absolute ethanol, and antibody stripping is achieved using citrate buffer pH 6. This process allows for the complete removal of previous markers and the application of new rounds of chromogenic staining on the same sample.
RESULTS
These two approaches complement each other depending on the analytical needs. While mIF enables higher multiplexing capacity and spatial resolution, its implementation requires specialized equipment. In contrast, mIC offers a simpler and more affordable solution, suitable for standard laboratory settings, though with reduced capacity for simultaneous labeling.
CONCLUSION
This combined approach allows for a more precise study of peripheral GBM areas, providing key insights into its biology and potential mechanisms of recurrence.

title: P02.11.B MODELING GLIOBLASTOMA-VASCULATURE INTERACTION ON-CHIP
authors: P O Emeh; A Fetah; J Admiraal; M Bokkers; K Jimenez-Cowell; N Wevers; M Lamfers; C M Dirven; T Burton; K Queiroz
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The tumor microenvironment (TME) of glioblastoma (GBM) is highly complex and dynamic, playing a pivotal role in tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Comprising diverse components including blood vessels, immune cells, and the blood-brain barrier, the heterogeneous TME forms distinct niches that critically shape tumor behavior. Recent TME-based classification has delineated three subtypes TMELow, TMEMed, and TMEHigh distinguished by varying vascular and immune cell compositions.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
This study focuses on elucidating the vascular interactions within the GBM-TME interface. To achieve this, we developed a brain-specific 3D vascular network by integrating primary human brain-derived endothelial and stromal cells within an extracellular matrix (ECM) on a microfluidic platform. Following the establishment of the brain vascular network model, GBM cell were incorporated to examine tumor-vasculature interactions in a 3D context. GBM integration was performed via two distinct strategies: co-seeding with vascular-forming cells within the ECM at the start of culture, or grafting GBM cells onto a pre-established vascular bed culture to facilitate invasion assays.
RESULTS
The resulting perfusable model recapitulates key features of the brain vasculature, including the expression of adherens junction markers CD31 and VE-cadherin, tight junction marker Claudin-5, and the strategic alignment of stromal cells along vascular structures. Preliminary results from the integration of GBM in the vascular network model indicate that, irrespective of the seeding method, GBM cells preferentially localize along vascular structures, suggesting an intrinsic tropism toward the vasculature. Notably, co-cultures of GBM with vascular networks exhibited significantly higher proliferative and invasive capacity compared to GBM monocultures, highlighting the pro-tumorigenic influence of the vascular microenvironment.
CONCLUSION
The brain vascular network model demonstrates physiological relevance, robustness, and scalability making it suitable for medium- to high-throughput applications. This multifaceted platform offers a unique opportunity to functionally model and stratify GBM TME subtypes in vitro, with the potential to uncover novel therapeutic targets within the vascular and immune niches of the tumor ecosystem.

title: P02.12.A DISTINCT MODULATION OF METABOLISM AND GLIOMA-ASSOCIATED MICROENVIRONMENT BY DEXAMETHASONE AND BEVACIZUMAB
authors: L Maise; F Krautwurst; S Surender; L Zizmare; D Bucci; J Trampert; M Tatagiba; C Trautwein; H Becker; G Tabatabai
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastomas are aggressive primary tumors of the central nervous system with limited registered therapeutic options. Peritumoral vasogenic or treatment-associated edema —commonly observed after radiation or immunotherapy—poses a significant clinical burden in glioblastoma patients. Dexamethasone (DEXA), a synthetic glucocorticoid, is commonly used in clinical practice in these situations, though its immunosuppressive effects may counteract immunotherapeutic strategies. Bevacizumab (BEV), an anti-VEGF antibody, is increasingly utilized in clinical practice to address therapy-induced edema. In this study, we investigated the differential effects of DEXA and BEV on tumor metabolism and the glioma-associated microenvironment in experimental models.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We performed ex vivo proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) spectroscopy-based metabolomics on glioma long-term cell lines upon treatment with DEXA or BEV to assess metabolic changes. Cytokine-release profiles were analyzed by ELISA. Microenvironmental modulation was further examined using co-culture systems and a syngeneic orthotopic glioma mouse model with immune profiling by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry.
RESULTS
Comparison of DEXA and BEV treated glioma long-term cell lines revealed changes in abundance of distinct metabolites involved in energy and amino acid metabolism (e.g. lactate, alanine). DEXA and BEV elicited distinct cytokine-release profiles in glioma long-term cell lines. In vivo, BEV treatment led to a reduced presence of regulatory T cells (CD4⁺FOXP3⁺) and an increased proportion of activated T cells (CD4⁺GzmB⁺) in the tumor microenvironment as compared to DEXA.
CONCLUSION
DEXA and BEV exert distinct effects on glioma metabolism and immune microenvironmental composition. These molecular insights could inform clinical strategies for managing treatment-associated cerebral edema in clinical trials investigating immunotherapeutic approaches.

title: P02.13.B MAGNETIC NAVIGATION OF IMMUNOBOTS TO ORTHOTOPIC EXPERIMENTAL GLIOMA MODULATES THE GLIOMA-ASSOCIATED MICROENVIRONMENT
authors: H Becker; N O Dogan; S Surender; Z I Erenoglu; J Trampert; S Erdmann; L Maise; E Yildiz; M C Ugurlu; M Tatagiba; S Beck; M Sitti; G Tabatabai
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastomas are primary tumors of the central nervous system with a poor prognosis. They are characterized by deep infiltration into the surrounding brain parenchyma and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which pose significant challenges to current therapeutic strategies. Various cellular carriers—such as neural stem cells, mesenchymal stem cells, and bone marrow-derived hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs)—have been investigated for targeted delivery, and they indeed home to intracerebral gliomas even after intravenous administration. However, their migration cannot be externally controlled. Mobile microrobots are emerging tools capable of operating at the cellular scale and being steered wirelessly, potentially enabling access to otherwise inaccessible tumor regions. In this study, we explore a novel strategy utilizing such microrobots.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We developed immunobots by loading autologous macrophages with Janus silica particles (~500 nm in diameter), which were half-coated with a 60 nm FePt nanofilm for magnetic guidance and functionalized with bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to induce an anti-tumorigenic macrophage phenotype. We evaluated their in vivo tolerability and therapeutic efficacy in the syngeneic, immunocompetent SMA560/VM/Dk glioma mouse model. Post-treatment effects were assessed by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry.
RESULTS
Direct injection of immunobots into the striatum of VM/Dk mice was well tolerated, with no signs of autoinflammation. Intratumoral administration into orthotopic SMA560 gliomas led to modulation of the tumor microenvironment, including enhanced infiltration of T cells. Furthermore, intravenous administration of immunobots followed by magnetic guidance using a permanent magnet array successfully directed them to the tumor site and induced local immunomodulatory effects.
CONCLUSION
Our study demonstrates that magnetically guided microrobots based on autologous bone-marrow-derived macrophages enable the modulation of the glioma-associated tumor microenvironment.

title: P02.14.A KDELR2 INTERACTS WITH GΑQ REGULATING VASCULOGENIC MIMICRY FORMATION OF GLIOMA VIA SRC/PI3K/MMP2/9 PATHWAY
authors: Y Chen; L He; S Li
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Gliomas are highly vascularized tumors, yet the existing anti-angiogenic therapy is not satisfactory, suggesting the deficiency of interfering classical tumor angiogenic pathways. Our previous work identified the presence of vasculogenic mimicry (VM) composed of tumor cells in glioma that plays an important role in anti-angiogenic therapy resistance. To date, the mechanism of VM is not fully elucidated. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role and mechanism of KDELR2 in VM formation in glioma, and tried to find a useful target for designing more effective approaches to overcome anti-angiogenic therapy resistance.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
In this study, IHC and transcriptome RNA sequencing of clinical specimens were used for screening out KDELR2 which was responsible for VM formation in glioma. Subsequently, three-dimensional culture, co-immunoprecipitation, immunocytochemistry and western blot were used to confirm the role and the mechanism of KDELR2 in VM formation in vitro and in vivo.
RESULTS
Our study revealed that KDELR2, a key gene mediating endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi protein transport, was highly expressed in gliomas and functioned as a crucial regulator in VM formation via Src/PI3K/MMP2/MMP9 pathway by coupling and activating Gαq in glioma.
CONCLUSION
Our results demonstrated that KDELR2 promoted VM formation in glioma by upregulating Src/PI3K/MMP2/9 pathway via activating Gαq, and KDELR2 may be a useful target for designing more effective approaches to treat glioma.

title: P02.15.B GLIOBLASTOMA IN THE CONNECTOME: NEURAL PHENOTYPES PREDICT TUMOR INTEGRATION AND CONNECTIVITY
authors: L Menzl; G Villa; Y Yabo; V Venkataramani; F L Ricklefs; D Heiland
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma (GB) is a particularly aggressive brain tumor which is characterized by a low overall survival due to rapid formation of neuron-tumor-networks. The neural epigenetic subtype was linked to increased tumor-neural connectivity but the mechanisms underlying this integration remain poorly understood. Here, we aim to investigate the impact of the microenvironmental ecosystem on neuron-tumor synaptogenesis leveraging a human cortical slice model and single cell spatially resolved transcriptomic analysis.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A human cortical slice model was employed to visualize and assess tumor-neuronal interactions using advanced retrograde tracing techniques in human derived cell lines (n = 12). This system was based on an EnvA-pseudotyped G-protein-deleted rabies virus. Spatial transcriptomics was conducted using multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis (MERFISH). Additionally, we conducted immunohistochemical staining and confocal microscopy.
RESULTS
Spatial transcriptomic evaluation of neural high and low tumors revealed distinct microenvironmental ecosystems within the infiltrating rim of the tumors. Neural-high tumors exhibited a higher presence of synaptogenesis-inducing inflammatory myeloid cells driving neuronal synaptogenesis. Retrograde tracing of neural high vs low cell lines confirmed increased synaptic density and neuronal coupling in the neural high phenotype, which were associated with higher invasiveness, supported by stRNA-seq, which identified genes linked to synaptogenesis and connectivity.
CONCLUSION
Neural-high GB shows enhanced neuronal connectivity and invasiveness, contributing to accelerated tumor progression, which underlines the prognostic value of epigenetic tumor profiling and opens ways for novel therapeutic approaches.

title: P02.16.A IN VIVO TEMPORAL METABOLIC PATTERNS OF GLIOBLASTOMA MICROENVIRONMENT IN A XENOGRAFT MODEL
authors: F Monedeiro; D Schimek; E Zügner; T Altendorfer-Kroath; T Birngruber; C Magnes
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Glioblastoma is marked by a poor prognosis and profound metabolic reprogramming. Mapping its metabolic dynamics is valuable for identifying therapeutic targets. Cerebral open flow microperfusion (cOFM) enables orthotopic implantation of glioma cells and time-resolved, atraumatic sampling of brain interstitial fluid (ISF) directly from the tumor microenvironment (TME) in vivo. Here, ISF and plasma (PL) metabolomics were performed to characterize local and systemic metabolic alterations during tumor progression in a murine xenograft model.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Via cOFM, U-87 MG cells were orthotopically implanted in mice, and ISF was sampled from tumor-bearing (GB) and control animals (CTRL) at days 7, 10, and 15 post-implantation (d07, d10 and d15, respectively). PL was collected at baseline (d0) and matched time points. Metabolomics was performed using HILIC UHPLC-HRMS. Data were analyzed using univariate and multivariate methods and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis (PA).
RESULTS
The ISF metabolome of CTRL and GB exhibited distinct patterns at all time points, primarily driven by differences in the levels of amino acids and glycolysis intermediates, indicating active modulation of tumor energy metabolism. In GB, ISF at d07 and d10 showed elevated fatty acids and lipids compared to CTRLs, a trend no longer evident at d15. Tumor progression was linked to increased markers of inflammation and oxidative stress, and decreased energy substrates. Only in GB, significant correlations were observed between elapsed time and the increase in the levels of kynurenine, as well as the decrease in polyunsaturated fatty acids and glutamine. In contrast to ISF, PL in the GB group showed early (d07-d10) depletion of lipids and fatty acids. In PL, tumor progression over time was correlated with a significant decrease in the levels of carbohydrates, and an increase in the levels of ketone bodies and markers of muscle catabolism. PA of ISF data revealed that significant pathway alterations in the TME expanded from d10 onward, mainly affecting amino acid, lipid, and signaling processes. By d15, broader disruptions emerged in the TME, with many pathways exhibiting metabolic depletion compared to d07. Compared to ISF, PL metabolome changes were concentrated in core metabolic pathways and processes related to nutrient digestion and absorption. Systemic metabolic alterations peaked at d07. Relative to d0, PL at d15 indicated progressive disruption of energy metabolism and the emergence of additional cancer-associated metabolic traits.
CONCLUSION
Glioblastoma progression drove dynamic, compartment-specific metabolic reprogramming, with early systemic disruption and gradual but extensive remodeling of TME that was marked by evolving metabolic demands and enhanced inflammation-related signaling, indicating critical windows for therapeutic intervention.

Cerebral open flow microperfusion (cOFM) enables orthotopic implantation of glioma cells and time-resolved, atraumatic sampling of brain interstitial fluid (ISF) directly from the tumor microenvironment (TME) in vivo. Here, ISF and plasma (PL) metabolomics were performed to characterize local and systemic metabolic alterations during tumor progression in a murine xenograft model.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Via cOFM, U-87 MG cells were orthotopically implanted in mice, and ISF was sampled from tumor-bearing (GB) and control animals (CTRL) at days 7, 10, and 15 post-implantation (d07, d10 and d15, respectively). PL was collected at baseline (d0) and matched time points. Metabolomics was performed using HILIC UHPLC-HRMS. Data were analyzed using univariate and multivariate methods and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis (PA).

By d15, broader disruptions emerged in the TME, with many pathways exhibiting metabolic depletion compared to d07. Relative to d0, PL at d15 indicated progressive disruption of energy metabolism and the emergence of additional cancer-associated metabolic traits.
CONCLUSION
Glioblastoma progression drove dynamic, compartment-specific metabolic reprogramming, with early systemic disruption and gradual but extensive remodeling of TME that was marked by evolving metabolic demands and enhanced inflammation-related signaling, indicating critical windows for therapeutic intervention.

title: P02.17.B CREB REGULATES PRO-TUMOR MACROPHAGE POLARIZATION IN GBM AND CAN BE TARGETED TO REVERSE IMMUNOSUPPRESSION
authors: S Widodo; M Dinevska; L Cook; S Stylli; T Mantamadiotis
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The cAMP Responsive Element Binding (CREB) protein is a kinase-inducible transcription factor with prominent roles in the brain, immune cells and tumor cells. We investigated CREB activation in immune cells, in glioblastoma (GBM). As tumor associated macrophages (TAM) are key regulators of tumor immunosuppression, we hypothesized that CREB is an important regulator of macrophage polarization in GBM.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We characterized CREB phosphorylation in pro-tumor immunosuppressive and anti-tumor inflammatory TAMs in the GBM tumor microenvironment, using spatially resolved multiplex immunohistochemistry. To test if macrophages respond to GBM cell secreted factors and that these factors regulate TAMs, we performed in vitro experiments using macrophage-differentiated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and stimulated these with GBM cell conditioned media (CM), to measure changes in pCREB expression by western blotting (WB). To test whether CREB directly regulates pro-tumor immunosuppression, we used a CREB inhibitor. To identify CREB target genes in GBM TAMs, we used RNA-seq and Olink proteomics in TAMs, which were either GBM-CM stimulated or not, in the presence or absence of the CREB inhibitor.
RESULTS
Spatial data revealed that circulating bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) arrive at the tumor, expressing inflammatory biomarkers and are rapidly polarized toward an immunosuppressive state when they encounter the GBM tumor parenchyma. TAM immunosuppression correlated with CREB activity, where almost all CD163+ TAMs were also pCREB+, while CREB163- TAMs were pCREB-. In vitro data showed that GBM cell secreted factors provide the necessary signals for CREB activation and pro-tumor TAM polarization. Use of cell signaling inhibitors identified that the cAMP pathway regulates CREB activation in GBM TAMs. Differential expression analysis identified key CREB target genes which regulate TAM immunosuppression.
CONCLUSION
GBM cell-derived factors are sufficient for pro-tumor M2-like macrophage polarization, which is regulated by a cAMP-CREB signaling-transactivation axis. This study also defines a set of CREB regulated target genes encoding for cytokines and chemokines expressed by GBM-TAMs. Importantly, the expression of these immunosuppressive factors in TAMs can be inhibited by pharmacological targeting of CREB, resulting in reversal of pro-tumor M2-like TAM polarization.

title: P02.18.A TUMOR-SECRETED (R)-2-HYDROXYGLUTARATE ACTIVATES NEURONS TO PRODUCE MITOGENS THAT PROMOTE IDH MUTANT GLIOMA GROWTH, FOSTERING A PARACRINE SIGNALING LOOP WITHIN THE TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
authors: C K Lee; H Nagashima; S Cash; J J Miller; H Wakimoto; D P Cahill
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Lower grade gliomas with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)1/2 gene mutation produce the oncometabolite (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG) at a high concentration. 2HG is toxic to glioma cells in vitro, yet has the net result in vivo of promoting gliomagenesis, pointing toward a strong context-specific effect. Here, we investigated the tumor microenvironment of IDH mutant gliomas and uncovered bidirectional neuron-glioma communication that promotes tumor growth.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
To investigate how (R)-2-hydroxyglutarate (2HG) influences neuronal activity and subsequently impacts the growth of IDH mutant gliomas, we performed time-lapse imaging of murine primary dissociated neurons engineered to express the fluorescent calcium indicator GCaMP6s. We tested changes in activity resulting from exposure to 2HG. We then used endogenous IDH mutant glioma lines (TS603 and MGG119) to test whether mitogens released by 2HG-activated neurons increased tumor proliferation rates.
RESULTS
Consistent with previous reports showing increased neuronal activity with exogenous exposure to 2HG, we triggered an increase in calcium imaging signals of neuronal activity with 2HG application. Furthermore, this activity was similarly provoked by 2HG secreted locally from co-cultured patient-derived IDH mutant cell lines. Activity was completely reversed with IDH inhibitor treatment. In turn, IDH mutant glioma cell proliferation was induced by neuron-conditioned media containing secreted mitogens. Proliferation was dramatically accelerated by conditioned media from 2HG-treated neurons, with concomitant upregulation of MAPK pathway activation in the tumor cells. Conversely, 2HG-stimulated mitogen release was blocked by glutamate receptor inhibition, demonstrating activity-dependence.
CONCLUSION
Our data provide evidence of a 2HG-driven neuron-glioma feed-forward mechanism in IDH mutant tumors, similar to what has been observed in IDH wild-type gliomas. These findings can explain how the inherent growth-suppressive effect of 2HG is overcome in vivo by microenvironmental remodeling. Importantly, the contribution of 2HG-driven aberrant neuronal activity to tumor proliferation in IDH mutant gliomas supports the role of mutant IDH inhibitors and neuromodulation as therapeutic modalities for patients with these tumors.
