title: P10.18.A THE IMPACT OF PUBERTAL STATE ON THE ONSET AND PROGRESSION OF PEDIATRIC LOW-GRADE GLIOMAS: CAUSAL ASSOCIATION OR UNDERLYING BIOLOGICAL MECHANISM?
authors: F D’antonio; S Rossi; A CARAI; G Colafati; A Deodati; G Megaro; V Di Ruscio; G Del Baldo; A Mastronuzzi; A Cacchione
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG) are the most common central nervous system tumors in children, with an incidence of 10-12 cases per million annually. Estrogen receptors (ER-α, ER-β, and GPER) are expressed in pLGG and have been implicated in the activation of the MAPK/ERK pathway, which may influence tumor behavior (Hirtz et al., 2020)(Tavares et al., 2018). Experimental studies have shown that estradiol stimulates astrocyte proliferation and gene expression associated with the cell cycle and angiogenesis(Madeshwaran et al., 2024). During puberty, there is an increase in estrogen levels not only in women but also in men, driven by the conversion of androgens to estrogens via aromatase. Several case reports have described children with precocious puberty and pLGG who experienced tumor reduction after hormone-blocking therapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy. These findings suggest that sex hormones may play a role in the behavior of pLGG(De Lucio Delgado et al., 2023)(Kang et al., 2024).
METHODS
Our study included patients with pLGG treated at Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital in Rome between January 2015 and December 2025, for whom follow-up data were available. Demographic, clinical, surgical and histological data were collected. Clinical and radiological outcomes, including hormonal assessment with objective pubertal state (Tanner stage) were monitored during follow-up.
RESULTS
This retrospective observational study included 215 patients diagnosed with pLGG. The median age at diagnosis was 13.9 years (range 1-16 years), with 95 females (44.2%) and 120 males (55.8%). Among the entire cohort, 48 patients (22.3%) with Tanner stage >3 received a diagnosis of pLGG or experienced disease progression; of these, 12 patients (25.0%) had a diagnosis of precocious puberty. Among patients with precocious puberty, 10 (83.3%) were diagnosed with precocious puberty concurrently with or prior to the diagnosis of low-grade brain tumor, while 3 patients (25.0%) developed precocious puberty at the moment of tumor progression.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings suggest that hormonal changes during puberty, particularly increased estrogen levels, may influence the development and progression of pLGG. The association between pubertal stage, precocious puberty, and tumor dynamics highlights the potential role of sex hormones in modulating tumor behavior. Further prospective studies are needed to better understand the biological mechanisms underlying this relationship and to explore potential therapeutic implications.

title: P10.19.B SINGLE INSTITUTION 15-YEARS EXPERIENCE IN TREATING PEDIATRIC DIFFUSE MIDLINE GLIOMA H3-K27 ALTERED PATIENTS
authors: A Cacchione; V Di Ruscio; S Chiesa; A Carai; G S Colafati; C D’Orazio; F D’Antonio; S Mariani; S Rossi; G Megaro; G Del Baldo; A Mastronuzzi
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Pediatric diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs), H3 K27-altered, represent the 5-10% of all pediatric brain tumors. The preferential location is the brainstem (diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, DIPG). Median overall survival is 11 months. In this study, we report about treatment and survival on one of the largest known single-institution cohort of DMGs.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The study included patients between 3 and 22 years, affected with DMGs. Primary endpoint was the comparison of median progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in different front line treatment: group A (intravenous nimotuzumab- vinorelbine scheme) and group B (oral temozolomide) in combination with external beam radiotherapy (RT). The secondary endpoint was to assess the impact of reirradiation at first progression in the two cohorts. Nimotuzumab was administered at 150 mg/m2 weekly for 12 weeks and then every two weeks; vinorelbine was administered 20 mg/m2 weekly and then 25 mg/m2 every two weeks. Temozolomide was administered 75 mg/m2 during RT and then 150-200 mg/m2/day, 5 days/month in 28- day cycles. Focal radiotherapy was delivered at total dose of 54 Gy in first line and at 19 Gy at first progression. Response was evaluated based on radiological findings according to RAPNO criteria. Adverse events (AE) were evaluated in both groups according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTC-AE) Version 5.0 (CTC-AE5).
RESULTS
one hundred five patients (median age 9 years) were treated for DMG H3K27 altered in our institution between 2009 and 2024. First-line treatment, in the entire cohort (105 patients, 100%), involved focal radiotherapy; 86 patients (82%), group A, received concomitant first-line medical treatment with nimotuzumab vinorelbine, and the remaining 19 patients (18%), group B, were treated with temozolomide. Median OS and PFS were superposable between the two groups, specifying that 24 patients in group A were excluded from the analysis because enrolled in the ongoing trial. OS in group A was 14.6 months (range 4.8-57.8 months) vs 14.4 months in group B (range 1.9-115.6 months). The median PFS was 8 months (range 2.5-19.6 months) in group A and 8.2 months (range 1.9-93 months) in group B. An increase in the median OS was observed in group A versus group B (respectively 17.38 vs 10.9 months, p = 0.0004) in the reirradiation at first progression. Most common drug-related AEs were hematological with 10 events grade 4 in group B, while mostly of hematological toxicities were mild (grade 1-2) and no severe toxicity grade 4 was reported in group A.
CONCLUSIONS
Nimotuzumab-Vinorelbine scheme in an outdoor setting was well tolerated and had comparable efficacy in terms of median PFS and OS respect to the use of oral temozolomide in DMGs.

title: P10.20.A RADIOMICS-BASED GRADING OF PAEDIATRIC GLIOMAS USING [18F] F-DOPA PET/CT: INSIGHTS FROM THE PERITUMORAL BORDER

[18F] F-DOPA PET imaging plays a crucial role in their assessment. Differentiating high-grade (p-HGG) from low-grade gliomas (p-LGG) is essential for treatment planning, and non-invasive tools are particularly needed for lesions located in hard-to-reach areas. To this end, we developed a machine learning pipeline to assess whether radiomic features from PET imaging can enhance glioma grading, focusing on tumour borders due to the high prevalence (77%) of diffusely infiltrating lesions in our dataset.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We retrospectively analysed [18F] F-DOPA PET scans of 103 paediatric patients diagnosed with p-HGG (n = 65) and p-LGG (n = 38) referred to Galliera Hospital between 2011 and 2024. Lesions were segmented using LIFEx, considering two volumes of interest (VOIs): (i) the whole tumour, defined as uptake >50% SUVmax; and (ii) a 5 mm peripheral margin. We extracted static metrics such as tumour-to-striatum (T/S) and tumour-to-background (T/N). We then computed 107 radiomic features via Pyradiomics and harmonised using Combat to address scanner variability. A nested cross-validation framework (5 outer, 10 inner folds) was adopted. title: P10.21.B DIFFUSE MIDLINE GLIOMA, H3 K27 AND BRAF/FGFR1 CO-ALTERED: DISTINCT BIOLOGY AND THERAPEUTIC OPPORTUNITIES
authors: L Auffret; C Barry; Y Ajlil; A Tauziede-Espariat; M Simbozel; L Mayr; T Kergorhen; C Puiseux; L Riffaud; P Blouin; A Bertozzi; P Leblond; K Blomgren; S Froelich; A Picca; M Touat; M Sanson; K Beccaria; T Blauwblomme; V Dangouloff-Ros; N Boddaert; J Gojo; M Filbin; P Varlet; M Debily; J Grill; D Castel
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) H3 K27-altered are incurable WHO grade 4 gliomas that pose a significant therapeutic challenge in neuro-oncology. The 2021 WHO Classification of CNS Tumors recognizes four subtypes of DMG, yet clinical and molecular diversity suggests additional subgroups may exist. We recently identified a novel subtype of DMG characterized by concurrent BRAF or FGFR1 mutations alongside H3K27M mutations or EZHIP overexpression, suggesting a unique clinical entity within this category.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A retrospective cohort of 60 adult and pediatric DMG cases was assembled, all exhibiting both MAPK pathway alterations (BRAFV600E or FGFR1 mutations) and either H3K27M mutations or EZHIP overexpression. These cases underwent comprehensive clinical, radiological, histopathological, and genomic analysis. DNA methylation profiling was performed to assess epigenetic distinctions, and transcriptomic analyses were used to explore pathway activation and gene expression signatures. Additionally, patient-derived models were developed to study therapeutic responses, and specific clinical response in patient are reported.
RESULTS
This newly characterized DMG subtype shows distinct features: a higher incidence in the thalamus (27% overall; 70% for BRAFV600E and 58% for FGFR1MUT cases), and greater prevalence in adults for FGFR1MUT tumors. These tumors are associated with improved overall survival, with a median exceeding three years. Unsupervised methylation analysis revealed a unique cluster, distinct from both classical DMG H3K27-altered and lower-grade midline gliomas with MAPK alterations. Radiologically and histologically, these tumors often exhibit calcifications and a solid component—features uncommon in canonical DMG. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a senescence-associated expression profile involving the TP53/CDKN1A axis and marked PI3K/AKT pathway upregulation. Additionally, preliminary clinical data indicate enhanced sensitivity to everolimus in this subgroup.
CONCLUSION
DMG H3 K27 and BRAF/FGFR1 co-altered represent a novel and distinct molecular subtype of DMG with unique radiological, histopathological, and prognostic characteristics. Their distinct biology, improved prognosis, and differential drug response profile support their recognition as a separate entity, warranting specific stratification in future clinical trials and personalized therapeutic approaches.

title: P10.22.A UNRAVELLING MOLECULAR HETEROGENEITY IN DIFFUSE HIGH-GRADE GLIOMAS OF PEDIATRIC, ADOLESCENT, AND YOUNG ADULTS THROUGH DNA METHYLATION PROFILING
authors: S BHARDWAJ; S Singh; J Singh; M Sharma; V Suri
abstract:
BACKGROUND
High-grade gliomas (HGGs) are among the most aggressive CNS tumors in pediatric, adolescent, and young adult (AYA) populations, marked by rapid progression and poor survival. These tumors show considerable histopathological and molecular heterogeneity, complicating diagnosis and treatment. Although WHO CNS5 distinguishes adult and pediatric HGGs, the pediatric and AYA subgroup remains a heterogeneous group with overlapping features and considerable molecular variability.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A total of 61 pediatric and AYA cases of diffuse HGG, CNS WHO Grade-4, NOS (median age: 19 years; M: F = 1.6: 1), were included in the study. Whole-genome DNA methylation profiling was performed for all cases along with eight controls and classified on the online available Epignostix brain tumor classifier (v12.8), and Methylscape. Additionally, next-generation sequencing (NGS) and RNA fusion analysis were conducted where appropriate, based on insights from methylation-based classification.
RESULTS
Tumors initially labeled as diffuse HGG, CNS WHO Grade 4, NOS were reclassified into distinct methylation classes. Pediatric HGGs, H3-WT/IDH-WT accounted for 20% (12/61), with 42% (5/12) showing H3K27me3 loss, deviating from WHO criteria. RTK1 subtype was enriched in MMR-deficient and radiation-induced gliomas. Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype comprised 18% (11/61), including 45% (5/11) pediatric cases. Adult-type glioblastoma, subtype B (5%, 3/61) showed MAPK pathway alterations of therapeutic relevance. Diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3K27M-altered was identified in 6.5% (4/61) of cases, including one located in the temporal lobe—challenging conventional anatomy-based classification. Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA) was seen in 8.2% (5/61), all of which had poor survival outcomes. Other reclassified entities included DHG, H3G34-mutant (n=2), pilocytic astrocytoma (n=3), HGAP (n=1), MPNST (n=2), CNS-BCOR ITD (n=1), neuroepithelial tumor with PATZ1-fusion (n=1), and DLGNT (n=1). Methylation profiling refined diagnoses in 48%, changed them in 16%, confirmed in 15%, while 12% were misdiagnosed and 10% remained unclassified.
CONCLUSION
Methylation profiling revealed substantial molecular diversity in pediatric and AYA diffuse HGGs, enabling refined classification and identification of rare, clinically relevant subtypes. Deviations from WHO criteria highlight the need to update diagnostic frameworks to better capture subgroup variability. Expanding classifier datasets to include diagnostically challenging cases may enhance prognostic accuracy and clinical relevance. This comprehensive approach advances molecular understanding, diagnostic precision, and better informs targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: P10.23.B UNCOVERING THERAPEUTIC VULNERABILITIES IN PEDIATRIC BCOR/L1-DRIVEN CNS TUMORS THROUGH MULTI-OMICS PROFILING
authors: D Lötsch-Gojo; L Gabler-Pamer; K Bruckner; D Kirchhofer; J LaBelle; A Beck; S Wang; D Al Tukmachi; J Quack; S Madlener; D Senfter; A Federico; C Dorfer; T Eder; F Grebien; A Tauziede-Espariat; J Pahnke; J Bunt; V Hovestadt; J Schueler; C Haberler; M G Filbin; M Kool; W Berger; J Gojo
abstract:
BACKGROUND
BCOR and its homologue BCORL1 are core components of the non-canonical polycomb repressor complex (PRC) 1.1, playing a central role in epigenetic gene silencing and transcriptional repression. Genomic alterations involving BCOR/L1, primarily BCOR internal tandem duplications (ITD) or BCOR/L1 fusions, occur in central nervous system (CNS) tumors with distinct molecular characteristics and poor clinical outcome. Thus far, the impact of these BCOR/L1-alterations on PRC1.1 functionality in CNS tumors remains elusive. Therefore, a better understanding of the underlying biology is essential to develop improved therapies
MATERIAL AND METHODS
By analyzing bulk, single-cell RNA and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) sequencing data in tissue samples, we explored whether BCOR-ITD or BCOR/L1 fusions share molecular mechanisms and target gene activation patterns in brain tumors. The functionality and targetable vulnerabilities of identified BCOR/L1 targets were confirmed in-vitro and in-vivo using patient-derived and transgenic cell as well as xenograft models.
RESULTS
BCOR-altered CNS tumors harbor a unique transcriptomic gene signature, indicative of impaired PRC1.1 repressive functions. This dysregulation leads to activation of distinct BCOR-mediated (FGF/FGFR, PDGFR) and PRC1.1 target genes (GATA6). ChIP-Sequencing analyses confirmed recruitment of activating histone marks (H3K27ac), despite binding of KDM2B and mutant BCOR/L1 to the respective target loci. In parallel, PRC1/2-mediated repressive histone modifications, H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub, were absent. Single-cell RNA sequencing further uncovered a distinct tumor cell population enriched for GATA6 and FGF/FGFR expression. Finally, the dependency on receptor tyrosine kinase signaling activity, identified in BCOR/L1-altered tumors, was confirmed by drug screening, revealing FGFR/PDGFR inhibitors as highly active compounds. The multikinase inhibitor nintedanib not only showed anti-cancer activity in a BCORL1-fused PDX model, but also clinical activity in two patients affected by progressive BCOR/L1-driven CNS tumors.
CONCLUSION
We deciphered key oncogenic pathways driven by BCOR/BCORL1 alterations in CNS tumors and identified potential targeted therapeutics, which may be leveraged for improved therapy of patients suffering from these aggressive malignancies.

title: P10.24.A TARGETING NON-GENETIC KINASE-DEPENDENT SIGNALING TO PREVENT GROUP 3 MEDULLOBLASTOMA RECURRENCE
authors: H Kuzmychova; U Chawla; E Martell; H Senthil; A Grewal; C Jain; C Venugopal; S K Singh; T Sharif
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Brain tumors are the leading cause of cancer-related death in children, with medulloblastoma (MB) comprising 20-25% of cases. Proteogenomic profiling categorizes MB into four subgroups: Wingless (WNT), Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Group 4 (G4), and Group 3 (G3), with G3 MB being the most aggressive one. Despite intensive chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which often leads to long-term side effects, G3 MB is prone to develop treatment-resistant relapse tumors, resulting in a five-year survival rate below 60%. Genomic analyses show that recurrent tumors retain their original genomic features, suggesting that changes in non-genomic signaling pathways drive relapse. Kinases, as central regulators of phosphorylation-driven signaling, can control pathways involved in proliferation, migration, and survival. We hypothesize that kinase-driven changes in signaling pathways underlie treatment resistance and tumor relapse in G3 MB. Understanding these adaptations will provide insights into novel therapeutic strategies for targeting recurrent MB.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We used well-characterized MB cell lines and orthotopic intracerebellar patient-derived xenograft (PDOX) mouse models treated with a clinically relevant CRT regimen. Kinase activity changes were assessed via human phospho-kinase arrays, immunoblotting, and immunohistochemistry. The efficacy of kinase inhibitors in combination with CRT treatment was evaluated in vitro using viability, tumorsphere formation, and migration assays, and in vivo by assessing tumor progression and animal survival.
RESULTS
CRT-resistant G3 MB cells showed elevated activating phosphorylation of Src kinase and its downstream targets, with minimal changes in other key oncogenic kinases. Notably, upregulation of p-Src was not observed in CRT-treated SHH MB cells or normal human stem cells, suggesting a tumor- and subgroup-specific adaptation. G3 MB CRT-resistant cells demonstrated marked sensitivity towards repurposed FDA-approved brain-penetrant Src inhibitors, which significantly impaired their stemness and migratory potential in vitro and extended animal survival in the CRT PDOX animal model.
CONCLUSION
These results identify Src signaling as a subgroup-specific driver of therapy resistance and recurrence in G3 MB. Targeting this pathway may offer a promising therapeutic strategy to combat CRT resistance in recurrent G3 MB to ultimately improve patient outcomes.
SUPPORT
This work was supported by the Canadian Institute of Health Research (CIHR), Canadian Cancer Society (CCS), Cancer Research Society (CRS), and Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).

title: P10.25.B STIMULATED RAMAN HISTOLOGY FOR INTRAOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS OF PEDIATRIC BRAIN TUMORS
authors: J Makolli; L Körner; G Kucinska; R Mödl; C C Vogel; E Krause; G Widhalm; C Dorfer; C Haberler; T Roetzer-Pejrimovsky; B Kiesel
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Intraoperative frozen sections are an essential part of neuropathological evaluation during pediatric neurosurgical tumor resections. However, tissue processing and analysis can take up to 45 minutes. Recently, stimulated Raman histology (SRH) has been introduced as a rapid technique for obtaining high-resolution digital images of unprocessed tissue samples directly in the operating room. This study aimed to assess the application of SRH in pediatric brain tumor surgery.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patients aged 18 years or younger undergoing biopsy or resection of a suspected tumor were included. Tissue samples were collected intraoperatively, first examined using SRH directly in the operating room, and subsequently processed for conventional frozen section analysis. A pathologist attempted to classify diagnoses based on SRH images, comparing them with hematoxylin-eosin (HE)-stained sections for mitotic activity, cell density, and vascular density. The representativeness of SRH images was also evaluated.
RESULTS
A total of 66 patients were included, with a median age of 9.4 years (30 female, 36 male). Based on SRH images, the pathologist was able to correctly establish the diagnosis in 78.8% (52 cases). Incorrect diagnosis was made in 12.1% (8 cases), and in 9.1% (6 cases), a diagnosis could not be made due to the absence of tumor cells in the SRH sample, attributed to a sampling error. The interpretability of mitotic activity was rated as identical between SRH and HE-stained sections in 100% of applicable cases. Cell density was rated correctly in 86.4% (57 cases) whilst vascular density was rated correctly in 93.9% (62 cases). The representativeness of SRH images was rated as high in 59.1% (39 cases), moderate in 30.3% (20 cases), low in 9.1% (6 cases), and non-representative in 1.5% (1 case).
CONCLUSION
Stimulated Raman histology serves as an important intraoperative diagnostic tool, providing rapid, high-resolution images comparable to conventional frozen section analysis, aiding neurosurgeons in optimizing surgical decision-making.

Stimulated Raman histology serves as an important intraoperative diagnostic tool, providing rapid, high-resolution images comparable to conventional frozen section analysis, aiding neurosurgeons in optimizing surgical decision-making.

title: P10.26.A AN EVALUATION OF THE DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF A MINIMAL IMMUNOHISTOCHEMICAL PANEL FOR ATYPICAL TERATOID/RHABDOID TUMOR (AT/RT) MOLECULAR SUBTYPING, BENCHMARKED AGAINST DNA METHYLATION PROFILING
authors: S Mahajan; V Suri; M C Sharma
abstract:
BACKGROUND
AT/RT are aggressive pediatric central nervous system (CNS) malignancies, characterized by biallelic inactivation of either SMARCB1 (95%) or SMARCA4 (5%). Transcriptomic and DNA methylation analyses classify AT/RT into three molecular subgroups: SHH (marked by neurogenesis and NOTCH pathway gene expression, e.g., ASCL1), TYR (expressing melanosomal markers such as TYR, MITF and OTX2), and MYC (overexpressing MYC and HOXC clusters). Given that they can differ in tumor location, age of onset, and possibly overall survival rates, molecular classification of ATRT is anticipated to impact clinical decision-making. However, due to availability and financial constraints, resource limited institutes are unable to use DNA methylation profiling as a first-line approach and hence immunohistochemical (IHC) surrogates are needed.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We analysed a case series of 10 pediatric AT/RTs—nine SMARCB1-deficient and one SMARCA4-deficient—to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of an IHC marker panel (3 antibodies; Tyrosinase, SOX11 and MYC) and its concordance with DNA-methylation profiling in predicting molecular subgroups.
RESULTS
In this study, 9 out of 10 cases were consistently assigned to a specific AT/RT molecular subgroup with high confidence (calibrated score ≥ 0.9), including 4 MYC, 2 SHH, and 3 TYR subtypes based on methylation profiling. The remaining one case was ambiguously classified as either AT/RT-TYR or cribriform neuroepithelial tumor with SMARCB1 alteration, with a low calibrated score. As a result, 9 well-defined AT/RT cases were included for comparison with IHC subtyping. Among these, the concordance between IHC and DNA methylation profiling was nearly perfect, with a κ coefficient of 0.90 and only one discrepant case. Specifically, there was 100% agreement for the TYR and SHH subgroups. The discrepant case classified as AT/RT-MYC on methylation showed SOX11 immunoexpression, supporting the notion that MYC IHC should be negative when SOX11 is positive, to favor an AT/RT-SHH diagnosis. Thus high sensitivity and specificity of the IHC markers, along with the strong concordance between IHC and DNA methylation profiling, highlight the reliability of this method for accurately identifying AT/RT molecular subtypes.
CONCLUSION
Though our study is limited by small number of cases, however we suggest that incorporating MYC, SOX11, and Tyrosinase into immunohistochemical panels for subtyping, and including them in future clinical trials, may help elucidate their clinicopathological significance and further establish their utility as surrogate markers for AT/RT molecular subgroups, particularly in resource-limited settings.

title: P10.27.B PRECLINICAL MODELLING AND DRUG SENSITIVITY DISCOVERY USING PATIENT- AND PDX-DERIVED TUMOROIDS OF HIGH RISK MEDULLOBLASTOMA
authors: C Meulenbroeks; P Stathi; C Giebel; M van de Wetering; B Schwalm; N Mack; N Geisemeyer; S L A Plasschaert; S M Pfister; M E G Kranendonk; E W Hoving; J Bunt; M Kool
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Medulloblastoma (MB) is one of the most common malignant embryonal brain tumor types, subdivided into four major molecular groups: WNT, SHH, Group 3 (G3), and Group 4 (G4). Current therapy includes resection, chemotherapy, and cranio-spinal irradiation. MB prognosis is amongst others dependent on molecular group, subtype, and molecular alterations. High-risk MB subgroups, including TP53-mutant SHH, MYC-amplified G3 and relapsed MB, all require more effective treatments. Therefore, we aim to generate more advanced preclinical models, recapitulating these very high-risk MB subtypes, to identify novel therapeutic strategies.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Long-term in vitro MB tumoroid models have been established and molecularly characterized from patient- and PDX-derived tumor material. High-throughput drug screening with ~225 compounds was used to identify (MB type-specific) drug sensitivities and synergistic combinations.
RESULTS
Thus far, we established 19 MB tumoroid models from SHH TP53-mutant (n=6), G3 MYC-amplified (n=8), and G3 non MYC-amplified (n=4) tumors, including five relapse models. DNA methylation and transcriptome analyses demonstrates that these tumoroids retain their parental tumor identity after long-term culture (>5 passages). Analyses of high-throughput screens show MB-wide and molecular group-specific drug sensitivities. Notably, inhibitors of BCL2, CDK7, CDK12, HDAC, and CHECK1 demonstrate efficacy in all tumors, while MCL1 inhibitors appear to be more effective in TP53-mutant SHH compared to G3 MB. Combinatory screens in TP53-mutant SHH MB reveal synergistic drug combinations, including MCL1 with BCL2 inhibitors and CDK12/13 with MTOR inhibitors.
CONCLUSION
We have established a large cohort of high-risk MB tumoroid models from patient and PDX tumors that reflect the parental tumor. These in vitro models are highly relevant and provide the basis for future preclinical studies, accelerating the discovery of new treatment modalities in MB. Our current data reveal novel drug combinations for high-risk TP53-mutant SHH MB that we are further validating in vitro before testing in vivo using PDX models.

title: P10.28.A PATTERN OF FAILURE IN PEDIATRIC HIGH GRADE GLIOMAS TREATED WITH FOCAL RADIOTHERAPY
authors: I Desideri; D Greto; B Castelli; M Tellini; C Fonte; M Guidi; L Giunti; M Di Nicola; A Buccoliero; L D’Incerti; F Giordano; L Genitori; P Papadopulos; L Livi; I Sardi
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Radiotherapy (RT) is the backbone of treatment of pediatric high grade gliomas (pHGGs), tipically characterized by very high rates of treatment failures. The aim of the present study was to describe the recurrence patterns (POF) after focal RT.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We retrospectively compared RT plans with MRI imaging at relapse of an institutional series of pHGG-patients (pts) to describe the pattern of treatment failure. Local Failures(LFs) were mapped to the planning target volume (PTV) and classified as in-field (completely within the PTV), marginal (partially within the PTV), or out-of-field (completely outside the PTV).
RESULTS
34 relapsed HGG pts, 17 females and 17 males, with a median age of 11 years (3-21), accrued from 2012 to 2022 were retrospectively evaluated. Primary sites consisted of diffuse cerebral lesions compatible with gliomatosis cerebri (GC) in 5 (13.8%), while among focal disease presenting cases, 15 were supratentorial, 2 cerebellar and 12 located in the brainstem. 24/34 (70.5%) patients received surgery after first imaging, with 1 gross total resection, 13 partial resection and 10 biopsies. Histological analysis identifed diffuse pediatric HGG H3 wild type, IDH 1/2 wild type in 1 case, diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34-mutant in four cases, diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered in four case, IDH1-mutant grade 3 astrocytoma in 1 case, BRAFV600E mutated anaplastic pleomorphic xantoastrocytoma in one case, while for 10 patient the diagnosis could only be HGG. Almost all (33/34, 97%) underwent to focal tumour bed irradiation, except one patient that received whole brain irradiation according to pGBM-WBRT/DOX2020 clinical trial (Eudract 2020-005131-74). All patients also underwent concomitant and adjuvant chemotherapy based mainly on temozolomide (TMZ) in 19 cases, nimotuzumab plus vinorelbine in 4 cases, and with a combination of TMZ and doxorubicine according to GBM TMZ/DOX 2015 Eudract: 2015-002307-28p) and GBM-WBRT/DOX2. Radiotherapy was performed with VMAT technique for a mean dose of 59,4Gy (range 54-59.4). At a median time of 7 months (range 3-39) 24 LFs were in field, 4 out-of-field, 3 marginal and 3 mixed (both in and out-of-field). All out-of-field LFs were diagnosed in supratentorial pts.
CONCLUSION
In supratentorial pediatric HGG POF may justify a different approach in terms of RT volumes (e.g. whole brain RT) in order to achieve a better outcome and possibly facilitating a higher penetrability of active drugs through the brain-blood barrier.

title: P11.01.B THE IMPACT OF SURGICAL RESECTION OF SMALL CELL LUNG CARCINOMA BRAIN METASTASES ON OVERALL SURVIVAL
authors: R Gabay Yehezkely; A R Eisenberg; I Livneh; R Grossman
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC), accounting for 15% of lung cancers, is highly prone to brain metastases, occurring in up to 70% of patients at diagnosis. Brain metastases are associated with a poor prognosis, with median survival dropping to 5 months. Whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) was the standard treatment, but in the past decade, local treatment with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) has become more common, sparing patients the side effects of WBRT. Surgical resection has not been considered relevant, even for solitary or oligo brain metastases.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
This retrospective cohort study evaluates the impact of surgical resection on overall survival in SCLC patients with brain metastases, compared to radiotherapy (RT). Data was collected from patients treated at a single neurosurgery department between 2011 and 2025. Key variables included demographics, Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), tumor characteristics, and survival outcomes.
RESULTS
Of 226 patients diagnosed with SCLC, 79 developed brain metastases. Fifteen patients underwent surgical resection followed by RT (surgical group) and 64 received only RT. The analysis included patients with up to 3 lesions, totaling 26 in the RT group. The mean age in the surgical and RT groups was 60.5±9.33 and 64.7±6.32, respectively (p>0.05). The mean KPS was 82.3±10.78 and 70.8±16.26, respectively (p>0.05). Median overall survival was 25.0 months (95% CI: 7.81-42.19) for the surgical group, compared to 5.97 months (95% CI: 1.64-10.29) for the RT group (p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS
Surgical resection followed by RT in SCLC patients with brain metastases is associated with significantly improved survival compared to RT alone. Surgery may be an effective treatment option for patients with solitary or oligo brain metastases. Further studies with larger cohorts and long-term follow-up are needed to define patient selection for surgery.

title: P11.02.A PRECLINICAL STUDY TO OVERCOME METHOTREXATE-RESISTANT MOUSE LEPTOMENINGEAL CARCINOMATOSIS: INTRATHECAL METHOTREXATE AND ORAL 6-THIOGUANINE
authors: H Nakagawa; Y Yui; S Sasagawa; M Tamura; M Yamada; M Kawaichi
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (MC) is a severe complication of advanced cancer with limited therapeutic options. Methotrexate (MTX) is one of the most commonly used drugs for treating MC. However, MTX resistance is frequently observed before and during intrathecal chemotherapy. In this study, we aimed to develop a method to overcome MTX resistance in a preclinical model.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
MM46 transplantable ascitic breast cancer cells (O-MM46) were used, and MTX-resistant MM46 cells (R-MM46) were established through repeated intra-abdominal MTX administrations, starting at a low dose and increasing to 20 μg/mL, thrice per week. MTX resistance was confirmed by increased dihydrofolate reductase activity (O-MM46, 0.197; R-MM46, 1.253 μmol/min/mg protein) and the lack of survival benefit in MTX-treated mice bearing R-MM46 cells, in contrast to the significantly increased survival in MTX-treated mice bearing the parent O-MM46 cells. Subsequently, we assessed pyrimidine and purine metabolic activity after intra-abdominal administration of MTX (50 mg/kg) in O-MM46 and R-MM46 transplantable ascitic mammary cancer cells by measuring the levels of orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, thymidine kinase, 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, and guanine phosphoribosyltransferase. Based on the observed activation of the purine salvage pathway in R-MM46 cells, we determined to use oral administration of 6-thioguanine (6-TG), a purine antagonist, as an adjuvant drug. Finally, we assessed the synergism between intrathecal MTX and oral 6-TG by adjusting their administration time in the treatment of MTX-resistant MC.
RESULTS
Mice with MC were divided into six groups (n = 10/group): control (sham intrathecal phosphate-buffered saline), MTX only (12.5 μg/0.05 mL), 6-TG only (0.04 mg/body), simultaneous MTX and 6-TG, MTX 2 h after 6-TG, and 6-TG 2 h after MTX. All treatment groups, except the MTX-only group, demonstrated significantly longer survival than that of the control group. Survival (mean ± standard error of the mean, days) is as follows: control, 16 ± 0.3; MTX only, 17.4 ± 0.3; 6-TG only, 21.8 ± 0.5; simultaneous MTX and 6-TG, 24.6 ± 0.5; MTX 2 h after 6-TG, 27.1 ± 0.5; and 6-TG 2 h after MTX, 28.0 ± 0.7. Notably, survival was longest in the group receiving 6-TG 2 h after MTX (simultaneous MTX and 6-TG vs. 6-TG 2 h after MTX pretreatment; p < 0.005).
CONCLUSION
These findings indicate that an oral chemotherapeutic protocol with 6-TG after intrathecal MTX injection may be effective for treating MTX-resistant MC. Based on these preclinical results, we applied this approach for clinical use.

title: P11.03.B EFFICACY AND SAFETY OF CHIMERIC ANTIGEN RECEPTOR (CAR)-T CELL THERAPY IN PATIENTS WITH SECONDARY CNS LYMPHOMA: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
authors: T B Schuster; G N de Medeiros; M D Santos; A V de Jesus; R A Pachega; N M Rodrigues; D A Barbosa; W F Amador; T A Gonçalves; C D Donadel; T P Fagundes
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has demonstrated efficacy in relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (B-NHL), but its role in patients with secondary central nervous system (CNS) involvement is less established. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of CAR T-cell therapy in this specific population.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to March 2025 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies of CAR T-cell therapy in adult patients with B-NHL and secondary CNS involvement. Outcomes of interest included Complete response, CNS response, progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and adverse events such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS).
RESULTS
We included 19 studies with 518 patients of whom 289 had systemic disease at time of CAR-T therapy. Complete response rates were observed in 54% of patients (95% CI 0.43-0.65; I²=78%), while CNS response rates were reported in 58% of patients (95% CI 0.28-0.87; I²=89%). Proportions of adverse events including CRS (95% CI 0.72-0.96; i²=88%) and ICANS (95% CI 0.37-0.59; i²=78%) were 84% and 48%, respectively.
CONCLUSION
These findings suggest that CAR T-cell therapy provides significant systemic and CNS responses and reduces progression in B-NHL patients with secondary CNS involvement, though neurotoxicity remains a notable concern for neuro-oncology practice.

title: P11.04.A BREAKING THE BRAIN’S DEFENSE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF IMMUNE-EVASION MECHANISMS IN GLIOBLASTOMA AND CNS METASTASIS
authors: M Alnahdi
abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain tumor that evades immune detection, promoting tumor progression and metastasis within the CNS. This systematic review examines immune-evasion mechanisms in GBM and their role in CNS metastasis, focusing on immune checkpoints, tumor-associated macrophages, microglia, and exosome-mediated immune modulation.
METHODS
A systematic literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted, reviewing studies from 2010 to 2025. Databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched using keywords related to GBM, immune evasion, CNS metastasis, immune checkpoints, TAMs, microglia, and exosomes. A total of 150 studies were identified, and after screening, 30 studies met the inclusion criteria. Both preclinical and clinical studies were included.
RESULTS
Key immune-evasion mechanisms identified include upregulation of immune checkpoint pathways (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4), polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) towards an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype, microglial reprogramming, and exosomal secretion of immunosuppressive molecules. Cytokines like TGF-β, IL-10, and VEGF also foster immune tolerance and promote metastatic spread within the brain.
CONCLUSION
GBM’s immune evasion strategies are critical to its aggressiveness and resistance, especially in CNS metastasis. Our review highlights how GBM manipulates immune checkpoints, recruits immunosuppressive TAMs, and exploits the immune-privileged brain environment to promote tumor spread. Targeting these mechanisms alongside conventional therapies offers a promising approach to improve GBM patient outcomes and combat metastasis, paving the way for personalized immunotherapies that could significantly alter the prognosis for GBM patients globally.

This systematic review examines immune-evasion mechanisms in GBM and their role in CNS metastasis, focusing on immune checkpoints, tumor-associated macrophages, microglia, and exosome-mediated immune modulation.
METHODS
A systematic literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted, reviewing studies from 2010 to 2025. Databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched using keywords related to GBM, immune evasion, CNS metastasis, immune checkpoints, TAMs, microglia, and exosomes. A total of 150 studies were identified, and after screening, 30 studies met the inclusion criteria. Both preclinical and clinical studies were included.
RESULTS
Key immune-evasion mechanisms identified include upregulation of immune checkpoint pathways (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4), polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) towards an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype, microglial reprogramming, and exosomal secretion of immunosuppressive molecules. Cytokines like TGF-β, IL-10, and VEGF also foster immune tolerance and promote metastatic spread within the brain.
CONCLUSION
GBM’s immune evasion strategies are critical to its aggressiveness and resistance, especially in CNS metastasis. Our review highlights how GBM manipulates immune checkpoints, recruits immunosuppressive TAMs, and exploits the immune-privileged brain environment to promote tumor spread. Targeting these mechanisms alongside conventional therapies offers a promising approach to improve GBM patient outcomes and combat metastasis, paving the way for personalized immunotherapies that could significantly alter the prognosis for GBM patients globally.

title: P11.05.B BENEFITS OF SODIUM FLUORESCEIN IN RESECTION OF BRAIN METASTASES
authors: A Neumeister; T Meier; L Karamani; S Kubon; N Andreas; D Taeuscher; P Bank; T Ernst; K Pietschmann; C Senft
abstract:
BACKGROUND
For central nervous system (CNS) tumors, the use of intraoperative fluorophores can significantly improve resection in several ways. Although sodium fluorescein (Na-Fl) has been used for CNS tumors since the 1940s, experience and use of Na-Fl is relatively limited. To date, existing studies of Na-Fl assisted resection of brain metastases (BM) have involved a limited number of patients.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Any patient at our institution who underwent resection of a cerebral lesion suspected of being BM between November 2023 and March 2025 received 200 mg 10% Na-Fl solution during induction of anaesthesia. The multidisciplinary tumor board confirmed the indication for any BM resection. A 560 nm filter microscope was used for intraoperative fluorescence guidance. Fluorescence patterns and extent of resection according to early postoperative cT1w MRI were recorded. Postoperative overall survival was determined for the available cases.
RESULTS
We enrolled 67 patients (28 females, mean age of 64 ±10 years) who underwent resection of at least 1 BM using intraoperative Na-Fl induced fluorescence. 43 patients had singular and 25 patients had multiple BM. Na-Fl fluorescence was positive in 94%, negative in 3% and not documented in another 3% of cases. Most common primary cancers were non-small cell lung cancer (43.3%), gastrointestinal carcinoma (13.4%), and malignant melanoma (10.4%). No negative side effects of Na-Fl were observed in any patient. Cost per patient was 12€. According to postoperative MRI, a gross total resection could be achieved in 64.2% of cases. Long-term data were available for 32 patients. Median follow-up time was 3.9 months (SD 3.8), and 6-month survival rate was 46.9%. Overall survival was statistically significantly different between patients with singular or multiple metastases (p<0.006, Log rank test).
CONCLUSION
Na-Fl facilitates intraoperative detection of BM. It appears to be safe, inexpensive and easy to use. However, Na-Fl also appears to accumulate in the adjacent areas of impaired blood-brain barrier. Further studies are warranted to investigate the benefits of using Na-Fl to improve the extent of resection.

title: P11.06.A PATTERNS OF PSTAT3 EXPRESSION IN REACTIVE ASTROCYTES OF BRAIN METASTASES FROM NON-SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER AND CORRELATIONS WITH OUTCOME
authors: A Pellerino; D Wasilewski; L Bertero; A Ricci; A Mangherini; A Bianconi; D Garbossa; P Cassoni; N Priego; M Valiente; R Soffietti; R Ruda
abstract:
BACKGROUND
pSTAT3 expression in peritumoral reactive astrocytes (RA) of brain metastases (BrM) from breast cancer may favor a pro-metastatic environment and negatively affect the intracranial progression-free survival (i-PFS) (Pellerino, Neurooncol Adv. 2023). We aim to evaluate whether pSTAT3 plays the same role also in BrM from NSCLC.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Seventy-two BrM specimens from NSCLC were identified from the biobank of Pathology Unit of University of Turin and Berlin. pSTAT3 expression was scored in RA of peritumoral tissue according to Priego et al. (Nat Med 2018). Clinical and molecular data, and i-PFS were retrospectively retrieved.
RESULTS
Median age was 64 years (95%CI 59-67). Immunohistochemistry for GFAP and pSTAT3 was feasible in 66/72 (91,6%). 42/66 (63,6%) had BrM with druggable mutations, while 24/66 (36,4%) did not show any actionable mutations. Druggable mutations were as follows: 8/42 (19,1%) KRAS G12C, 6/42 (14,3%) EGFR, 5/42 (11,9%) ALK, 1/42 (2,4%) BRAFv600E, 31/42 (73,8%) PDL1 expression. Overall, 53/66 (80,3%) showed positive staining of pSTAT3: 22/66 (33,3%) with score 3, 21/66 (31,8%) with 2, 10/66 (15,1%) with 1, and 12/66 (19.8%) with 0 (negative). High pSTAT3 expression (score 2-3) was observed in 32/42 (76,2%) BrM with actionable mutations and in 12/24 (50%) without actionable mutations (p 0,031). PDL1 expression was significantly correlated with high pSTAT3 expression (29/31, 93,5%), while most of BrM without PDL1 (20/35 - 57,1%) had low or absent pSTAT3 (score 0-1) (p<0,0001). Median i-PFS was 12 months (95%CI 8-23): low pSTAT3 BrM had a median i-PFS of 18 months (95%CI 14-28) versus 9 months (95%CI 8-12) for high pSTAT3 BrM (HR 5,3;p 0,0001).
CONCLUSION
pSTAT3 overexpression in RA is associated with PDL1 expression and may negatively impact the i-PFS in BrM from NSCLC. These data support the investigation of STAT3 inhibitor silibinin in preventing intracranial recurrence in a clinical trial (NCT05689619).

title: P11.07.B MR IMAGING FOR INITIAL DIAGNOSIS OF LEPTOMENINGEAL METASTASES FROM SOLID CANCERS: AN EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS OF 227 PATIENTS IN A SINGLE INSTITUTE
authors: Y Nakasu; S Deguchi; K Nakashima; K Mitsuya; S Nakasu
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a life-threatening and quickly advancing complication in patients with solid cancers. Reliable and rapid initial diagnosis is a challenge to this urgent disease. Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging is characterized by less-invasiveness and immediate information including patterns of LM spread, brain parenchymal metastases (PM), and hydrocephalus. The priority of MR imaging remains controversial in initial diagnosis and decision-making for patients with LM.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
After approval by the Institute Review Board, retrospective search was conducted on 227 patients with LM who underwent consultation in the CNS Cancer Board between 2007 and 2023. Data on patient characteristics, MR findings (conventional postcontrast T1-weighted images at 1.5 or 3T), and outcomes were collected. Statistical analyses were performed using the chi-squared test, Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank test, and multivariate Cox regression analysis.
RESULTS
Primary cancers included lung (66%), breast (15.9%), and gastrointestinal (GI) cancers (12.8%). The mean follow-up duration was 8.6 months. The median OS from the diagnosis of LM was 3.8 months [95%CI: 3.3-4.5]. All patients underwent MR imaging, and 47.1% CSF cytology test. Initial diagnosis of LM was made via MR imaging and neurological manifestations in 98.2% of patients, and via CSF cytology alone in 1.8%. Postcontrast MR images showed mixed pattern in 43.6% of cases, linear in 41.9%, nodular in 8.8%, or no enhanced lesions in 5.7%, also hydrocephalus in 39.2%. PM developed in 52.9% of LM patients, of whom 11.5% had pre-existed PM (prePM), 41.4% had concurrent PM (conPM), and 47.1% LM only. MR mixed pattern made up 81.9% in conPM group, linear pattern 76.6% in LM only group, however, no dominant pattern was observed in prePM group (P<0.001). OS was not significantly different among the prePM, conPM or LM only groups (P=0.301). By multivariate analysis, prognostic factors for longer OS included age younger than 60 years (HR0.67 [95%CI: 0.46-0.96] p=0.030), lung cancer compared with breast cancer (HR0.62 [95%CI: 0.42-0.94] p=0.023), and synchronous LM at the diagnosis of primary cancer (HR0.49 [95%CI: 0.31-0.78] p=0.002). Factors for significantly increased mortality included GI cancer compared with breast cancer (HR2.13 [95%CI: 1.26-3.60] p=0.005), mixed pattern compared with nodular one (HR1.68 [95%CI: 1.01-2.79] p=0.047), and hydrocephalus (HR1.44 [95%CI: 1.08-1.94] p=0.015).
CONCLUSION
This study showed that MR imaging demonstrates worse outcomes in LM with mixed pattern, and that it immediately offers diagnosis of associated hydrocephalus and concurrent PM that need urgent treatment decisions. Further research is required to specify a less-invasive and in combination with biomarker-driven approach to LM.

title: P11.08.A CLINICAL OUTCOMES AND BIOMARKER SHIFTING OF BREAST CANCER BRAIN METASTASES - A SINGLE INSTITUTION EXPERIENCE
authors: R Wang; Q Zhang; J Megyesi
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Breast cancer brain metastases (BCBMs) are a feared complication of breast cancer and associated with a poor prognosis. The molecular and biological events that give rise to BCBMs are not fully understood. The project aims are to characterize the clinicopathological outcomes of patients who underwent surgical resection or biopsy of BCBMs at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and further compare the biomarker profiles between primary tumor and BM.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patients who had BCBMs surgically-resected or biopsied at LHSC were identified. Retrospective chart review was conducted to collect patients demographics, details on primary BC and BM diagnoses and treatments, pathology details, and clinical outcomes. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated and uni- and multivariate Cox-regression analyses were conducted to determine clinical outcome predictors.
RESULTS
Seventy-five female patients were identified. Mean age at BCBM diagnosis was 56.1 years and mean time to developing BCBM was 5.4 years (range: 0-23.0 years). Triple-negative (18/75, 24.0%) and HER2+ (14/75, 18.7%) were the most common subtypes. Median overall survival (OS) after BCBM diagnoses was 2.4 years. Solitary BCBM (p=0.0276) and no extracranial systemic disease (p=0.0276) were associated with longer OS after BCBM diagnosis. 51 patients had paired immunohistochemistry (IHC) markers of their primary BC and BMs. 12/51 (23.5%) patients exhibited a subtype switch with hormone receptor loss (5/12, 41.7%) being the most common change. Univariate Cox-regression analyses for these 51 patients demonstrated that triple-negative subtype (HR 2.81, p=0.0075), multiple BMs (HR 3.23, p=0.0024), neurological deficits (HR 3.06, p=0.0058), tumor >3 cm (HR 2.84, p=0.013), and hydrocephalus (HR 4.13, p=0.014) were negative prognostic factors. After multivariate Cox-regression, only triple-negative subtype (3.52, p=0.0033) and multiple BMs (2.34, p=0.047) remained significant. Subtype switching did not appear to impact OS (p=0.27).
CONCLUSION
The management of BCBM remains challenging with overall survival remaining poor, especially in those with triple-negative disease, multiple BMs, and widespread metastatic disease. Within our cohort, a noticeable proportion of patients exhibited biomarker profile shifting between the primary BC and BCBM. This may have clinical implications and further investigations are required.

title: P11.09.B PREDICTIVE MODEL FOR RADIATION NECROSIS AFTER STEREOTACTIC RADIOSURGERY FOR BRAIN METASTASES BASED ON THE V12 PARAMETER AND INFLAMMATION-RELATED PLASMA BIOMARKERS
authors: P A Jablonska; D Serrano; N Galan; J Barranco; S Leon; A Calvo; J Aristu
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Cerebral radiation necrosis (RN) is a deleterious adverse event following stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for brain metastases (BMs). Although the volume of brain tissue receiving 12 Gy (V12) is a recognised predictor of RN, its predictive performance remains suboptimal. Prior authors demonstrated that radiation-induced brain injury can be traced in peripheral blood. We sought to identify predictive biomarkers of symptomatic RN in liquid biopsies from BMs patients at the time of SRS and to develop a risk prediction model integrating both V12 and biomarker data.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A case-control study was designed using plasma samples from BMs patients treated with SRS. Olink 96 Target Immuno-Oncology Panel was performed to analyse 92 immune-related human proteins using oligonucleotide-bound antibodies and real-time polymerase-chain reaction. Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.0. Receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curves were performed for selected biomarkers. Multivariate Cox proportional hazard (PH) regression was conducted to assess predictor variables related to patients, SRS treatment and baseline plasma biomarkers, and the subsequent development of RN. Multiplex immunophenotyping in RN tissue was performed in available cases to validate the presence of a pro-inflammatory microenvironment.
RESULTS
A total of 47 patients were included, comprising 21 individuals who developed RN post-SRS and 26 matched controls with successful ablation of BMs without RN. Plasma analysis at the time of SRS revealed significantly elevated CD8a levels and significantly decreased MUC-16 and IL-8 levels (p<0.05) in patients who later developed RN. Multivariate Cox PH analysis identified V12 (p<0.01), IL-8 (p<0.01), and CXCL11 (p<0.001) as independent predictors of RN. Development of a necrosis prognostic index (NPI) combining V12, MUC-16, CD8a, CXCL11, and IL-8 substantially improved predictive performance, with the ROC area under the curve (AUC) increasing from 0.77 (V12 alone) to 0.91 (p=0.097). Histopathological analysis confirmed enhanced inflammatory infiltrates (CD4+, CD8+, GFAP+STAT3+, and CD68+iNOS+ cells) in RN specimens, supporting an enhanced inflammatory response.
CONCLUSION
The predictive accuracy of the V12 dosimetric parameter for RN can be significantly augmented by integrating plasma-derived inflammatory biomarkers measured at the time of SRS. Prospective validation of this model may enable early identification of BMs patients at higher risk of radiation-induced brain toxicity, facilitating the development of personalised SRS treatment strategies to mitigate RN incidence.

title: P11.10.A BEYOND BIOLOGY - PSYCHOLOGICAL PREDICTORS OF QUALITY OF LIFE IN PATIENTS WITH BRAIN METASTASES BEFORE RADIOTHERAPY
authors: E E van Grinsven; K Adriaensen; F Cialdella; J Verhoeff; M Philippens; M J van Zandvoort
abstract:
BACKGROUND
With the rising incidence of brain metastases (BMs) and extended survival due to improved oncological treatments, preserving quality of life (QoL) has become a central goal in cancer care. QoL is influenced not only by physical health but also by psychological factors, including personality traits and coping styles. This study examined whether personality and coping predict QoL in patients with BMs prior to radiotherapy, and whether coping mediates these relationships.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Personality was assessed using the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (neuroticism, extraversion), and coping was measured with the Utrecht Coping List (UCL-90), categorized into engagement (i.e. actively approaching stressor) and disengagement coping (i.e. orienting away from stressor). QoL was evaluated using the EORTC QLQ-C30 summary score (overall QoL) and the EQ-VAS (health-related QoL, HRQoL). Mediation analyses were conducted using Model 4 of the PROCESS macro for SPSS, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
RESULTS
170 patients (79 females; age 32-82) referred for radiotherapy were included. Higher neuroticism and lower extraversion were significantly associated with more disengagement coping (p<.001 and p=.013, respectively), which in turn was linked to poorer overall QoL (both p≤.001). Mediation analyses showed that disengagement coping, but not engagement coping, significantly mediated the relationship between both traits and overall QoL. However, neither personality traits nor coping showed significant direct or indirect effects on HRQoL in the mediation analyses.
CONCLUSION
This study highlights the importance of psychological characteristics—particularly neuroticism, extraversion, and disengagement coping—in understanding variations in QoL among patients with BMs prior to radiotherapy. Disengagement coping emerged as a key psychological factor linking personality traits to perceived overall QoL. The results support integrating early psychological screening to identify at-risk profiles and tailor psychosocial interventions, potentially enhancing treatment readiness, resilience, and outcomes in this vulnerable population.

title: P11.11.B EVALUATION OF THE PROGNOSTIC SIGNIFICANCE OF BRAIN METASTASIS VELOCITY IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING INTRACRANIAL STEREOTACTIC RADIOTHERAPY
authors: F Sert; N Bozbas Yalcin; S Kamer
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Despite the availability of targeted therapies, brain metastasis (BM) continue to pose a significant challenge, especially in the context of solid organ tumors, with lung cancer being the most affected. Stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) plays a crucial role in the treatment of BM by providing effective local control while minimizing damage to healthy brain tissue. Brain metastasis velocity (BMV) has been suggested as a prognostic factor for overall survival (OS) in patients with BM. title: P11.12.A A PAN-CANCER ATLAS OF LEPTOMENINGEAL DISEASE REVEALS BRANCHED CHAIN KETO ACIDS DRIVE IMMUNOSUPPRESSION AND NEURODEGENERATION
authors: M Khaled; E Vallebuona; Y Ren; V Law; M Boozo; Z Chen; B Evernden; O Ospina; M Liu; M Hall; L Darville; V Izumi; S Pilon-Thomas; J Koomen; M Jain; A Gomes; R Kundalia; G Wallace; A Chen; P Stewart; S Corallo; S Holmen; F Locke; P Forsyth; I Smalley
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is one of the most devastating complications of advanced cancer, resulting in severe neurological deterioration and poor survival outcomes.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Using single-cell transcriptomics and multi-omics profiling of patient specimens, we created a comprehensive LMD atlas that revealed two hallmarks of LMD: an immunosuppressive cellular microenvironment and an environment promoting neurodegeneration.
RESULTS
We report that toxic branched-chain keto acids (BCKAs) accumulate in the cerebrospinal fluid of LMD patients and drive both immunosuppression and neurodegeneration, presenting a novel therapeutic target. Mechanistically, there is a profound BCKA-mediated disruption of T cell function and neuronal integrity. Strikingly, BCKA-reducing therapy using sodium phenylbutyrate improved survival and neurological outcomes in preclinical models while enhancing the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy.
CONCLUSION
BCKA accumulation is a central mediator of LMD progression and treatment resistance and provides an actionable therapeutic opportunity through drug repurposing. Importantly, our pan-cancer atlas of human LMD delivers a framework for understanding disease mechanisms and developing novel therapeutic strategies for this urgent unmet clinical need.

title: P11.13.B INTRAOPERATIVE DISCRIMINATION OF TUMOR MARGINS IN BRAIN METASTASES USING A LABEL-FREE NANOPLASMONIC BIOSENSOR, A PROOF OF CONCEPT.
authors: V García-Milán; A Franco; S Marcos; L Bauluz Olmedo; R Martín-Láez; M Ortiz; F Moreno; J Fernández-Luna; C Velásquez
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Complete resection of brain metastases may be challenging in infiltrative lesions lacking a clear tumor-parenchyma border. Current intraoperative tools to discriminate the margins usually need exogenous contrast agents, often have poor resolution and are limited by subjectivity. We evaluated a nanoplasmonic biosensor based on extraordinary optical transmission (EOT) as a label-free, real-time method to discriminate between tumor and peritumoral brain tissue during surgery.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
In this prospective study, ex vivo tissue samples were obtained intraoperatively from patients with histologically confirmed brain metastases. Paired samples from the edge tumor and adjacent peritumoral tissue were collected, and their nature was confirmed independently by the Department of Pathology. Samples were subsequently analysed using an EOT-based nanoplasmonic biosensor, and their refractive index (RI) values were recorded. A diagnostic threshold was determined based on the distribution of RI values, and classification performance was assessed by calculating the percentage of correctly classified samples. This study is ongoing, and additional cases are being collected to refine the diagnostic threshold and validate these preliminary findings.
RESULTS
A total of 8 paired tissue samples were analysed. RI values were consistently higher in tumor tissue compared to peritumoral samples (median RI: 1.352 vs. 1.345). Using an empirically determined threshold of 1.347, the biosensor correctly classified 75% of the samples overall. Specifically, it achieved a sensitivity of 87.5% for tumor detection and a specificity of 62.5% for peritumoral tissue identification. These preliminary results suggest that the EOT-based biosensor can differentiate between tumor and peritumoral brain tissue, although further validation with a larger cohort is required.
CONCLUSION
The EOT-based nanoplasmonic biosensor successfully discriminated ex vivo between tumor and peritumoral brain tissue in brain metastases. These findings are consistent with previous work from our group in glioblastoma using the same biosensor platform. It requires no contrast agents, no tissue processing, and no interpretation by a trained pathologist, providing objective and immediate feedback. These characteristics make it a promising tool for improving intraoperative margin assessment and guiding surgical decision-making in patients with brain metastases.

title: P11.14.A STEREOTACTIC RADIOSURGERY FOR OVARIAN CANCER BRAIN METASTASES: AN INTERNATIONAL RADIOSURGERY RESEARCH FOUNDATION RETROSPECTIVE STUDY
authors: D Mathieu; M Billau; A Hamel; E Adam; C Iorio-Morin; R Liscak; J May; A Niranjan; Z Wei; L Lunsford; D Luy; S Jose; S Scanlon; J Silverman; R Mullen; K Bernstein; D Kondziolka; S Peker; Y Samanci; A H Düzkalir; S E Braunstein; C Phuong; J Sheehan; S Pikis; J Kosyakovsky; R N Prasad; J D Palmer; D Bailey; B E Zacharia; C Cifarelli; D Cifarelli; D Arteaga Icaza; R E Wegner; M J Shepard; G N Bowden; N Wandrey; C G Rusthoven; E B Hintz; M Schulder; A Goenka; J Peterson
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Ovarian cancer rarely metastasises to the brain, thus studies reporting the outcomes of affected patients are lacking. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is now the mainstay of management for patients with brain metastases (BM) from most primary sites, but little evidence of its efficacy in ovarian cancer is available. The current study was undertaken to provide guidance for SRS management using pooled data from multiple institutions.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Centers participating in the IRRF (International Radiosurgery Research Foundation) were asked to provide outcome data for patients who had SRS for ovarian cancer brain metastases between 2020 and 2024 and at least one clinical and imaging follow-up after the procedure. Primary endpoints included survival from SRS, local tumor response according to RANO-BM criteria and occurrence of adverse radiation effects (ARE). Cox regression analyses were performed to identify variables impact each endpoint.
RESULTS
128 patients had SRS for a total of 532 BM treated. Epithelial histology was the most common (91%). Median age at SRS was 62 years (IQR 56-70). Median KPS was 80% (IQR 80-90%) and 71.9% of patients had neurological symptoms at presentation. Other active systemic metastases were present in 41.4%. The median number of treated BM was 2 (IQR1-3) and the median cumulative treatment volume was 6 cc (IQR 2-12.9). The median margin dose was 18 Gy (IQR 16-20). At last follow-up, 19.5% of patients were still alive. The median overall survival (OS) after SRS was 27 months, and 6-, 12- and 24-month OS was 83.8%, 74.2% and 52.2%, respectively. Multivariate analyses revealed that increasing age at SRS (HR 1.02, p=0.05), active systemic metastases (HR 2, p=0.005) and increasing number of brain metastases (HR 1.05, p=0.04) were associated with worse survival, while repeating SRS (HR 0.4, p=0.002) led to improved survival. Local failure occurred in 12.8% of treated BM. Actuarial progression-free survival (PFS) at 6, 12 and 24 months was 92.3%, 86.6% and 70.3%, respectively. Only prior WBRT (HR 4.36, p=0.03) led to worse local control on multivariate analyses. New remote BM appeared in 49.5% of patients and 14.5% suffered from leptomeningeal dissemination. ARE were seen in 12.1% of BM but were symptomatic in only 3.2%. On multivariate analyses, prior SRS (HR 3.13, p=0.002) was associated with increased risk of ARE.
CONCLUSION
Ovarian cancer brain metastases can be safely and effectively managed with SRS as the primary treatment modality in most patients.

title: P11.15.B TUMOUR-SECRETED PHOSPHOPROTEIN 1 (SPP1) VIA ACTIVATION OF MICROGLIA CONTRIBUTES TO THE FORMATION OF THE BREAST AND LUNG CANCER BRAIN METASTASES
authors: B Kaminska; K Waśniewski; K Poleszak; A M Lenkiewicz; B Kaza; L Jassowicz; C Park; C Herold-Mende
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Brain metastases (BrMets) occur in 20%-40% of patients with breast and lung cancers and contribute significantly to morbidity and/or mortality. The molecular mechanisms that drive and permit the progression of metastasis in the brain are poorly understood. Identifying components of the metastatic niches and propensities of primary tumors towards the brain microenvironment are essential to improve our understanding of BrMet development, patient management and outcomes. We have previously demonstrated the pivotal role of microglia, brain resident myeloid cells, in progression of malignant gliomas. SPP1 (a secreted phosphoglycoprotein 1) is a tumour derived potent activator of microglia (brain resident myeloid cells).
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Expression of SPP1 was analysed in public datasets of breast and lung cancer brain metastasis and by qPCR and ELISA in a number of patient derived cell lines. Cancer cells cancer proliferation and cell invasion was evaluated in Matrigel assay in microglia-cancer cell co-cultures. Expression of genes supporting tumour invasion and immunosuppression was determined by qPCR. The effects of the 7aaRGD interfering peptide, or Minocycline (MINO). Intracranial growth of patients derived xenograft (PDX) in nude mice was evaluated histologically and by measuring luminescence of stably labelled malignant cells, and myeloid cell accumulation was determined with immunofluorescence.
RESULTS
We found upregulated expression of SPP1 is elevated in breast and lung cancer brain metastasis and a number of patient derived cell lines. Cancer cells-derived SPP1 strongly activate microglia in ex vivo co-cultures, increases cancer cell invasion in Matrigel assay and upregulated a number of genes supporting tumour invasion and immunosuppression. Blocking SPP1-mediated cancer-microglia communication with the 7aaRGD interfering peptide and MINO abolished microglia-dependent cancer cell invasion. The intracranial growth of the patient derived xenografts injected to nude mice was established, and staining for microglia markers TMEM119 and Sal1 were performed.
CONCLUSION
The results highlight the important role of breast and lung cancer BrMet-derived SPP1 in shaping the permissive microenvironment of BrMets, and indicate a potential of the 7aaRGD peptide or minocycline to be new therapeutics in brain metastasis treatment. Studies were supported by the TRANSCAN-3/1/168/2022 ImmuMet project funded by National Center for Research and Development, Poland.

title: P11.16.A HER2 HETEROGENEITY BETWEEN PRIMARY CANCERS AND BRAIN METASTASES: A RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS OF 185 MATCHED PAIRS ACROSS MULTIPLE CANCER TYPES
authors: J Lee; J Koo; N Kim; S Kim; H Shim; M Yi; R Lee; S Park; T Jung; K Moon; K Lee
abstract:
BACKGROUND
HER2 overexpression drives tumor aggressiveness and poor prognosis, serving as a crucial therapeutic target in various malignancies. While HER2’s role in breast cancer metastasis and prognosis is well-documented, its heterogeneity in brain metastases (BM) across different primary tumors remains understudied. This investigation examined HER2 status in matched primary cancers and BM across multiple cancer types to evaluate HER2 alterations during metastases.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a retrospective analysis of 185 matched primary tumor-BM pairs. HER2 expression was assessed using immunohistochemistry (IHC), with equivocal cases (IHC 2+) further evaluated by silver-enhanced in situ hybridization (SISH). We analyzed associations between HER2 positivity, clinicopathological factors, and survival outcomes.
RESULTS
Of the 185 matched cases, lung, breast, and colorectal cancers were predominant, with breast cancer showing the highest HER2 positivity rate (61.5%, P < 0.001). HER2 positivity was detected in 14.1% (26/185) of primary tumors and 15.1% (28/185) of BM with a 7.6% (14/185) discordance rate between primary and metastatic sites. HER2 positivity in BM significantly correlated with age, primary cancer type, and BM location (P = 0.040, P < 0.001, P = 0.045, respectively). Age, BM location, BM size, BM multiplicity, and presence of other organ metastases were identified as independent prognostic factors.
CONCLUSION
Our findings reveal significant HER2 heterogeneity between primary tumors and matched BM across cancer types. The observed discordance in HER2 status, particularly notable in breast cancer, underscores the necessity of HER2 status reassessment in BM for optimal targeted treatment strategies.

title: P11.17.B PD-L1 DETECTION IN CEREBROSPINAL FLUID OF LEPTOMENINGEAL METASTASIS BASED ON THINPREP CYTOLOGY
authors: G Yang; Z Pan; H Lei; Y Huang; M Liu; P Tai; X Chen; Y Zhang; L Wang
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) involves tumor cell dissemination within the leptomeninges and subarachnoid space. Intrathecal anti-programmed death 1 immunotherapy has been explored clinically for LM. Programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) is currently the only approved immunotherapy marker. This study aims to detect PD-L1 expression in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from LM patients based on ThinPrep cytology method.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Cell lines (lung adenocarcinoma: NCI-H358, A549; breast cancer: MDA-MB-231, MCF7; gastric adenocarcinoma: SGC-7901, AGS) with confirmed high/low PD-L1 expression were processed via ThinPrep liquid-based cytology and cell-block sections. CSF tumor cells from LM patients underwent ThinPrep slide preparation. Immunocytochemical analysis with PD-L1 antibodies (Ventana SP263 and Dako 22C3) was performed. Five independent observers assessed PD-L1 expression using the tumor proportion score (TPS), defined as the percentage of viable tumor cells showing membrane staining among ≥100 evaluable cells (positive threshold: TPS ≥1%) with absolute cell counts recorded for specimens containing <100 tumor cells, and inter-assay concordance was determined using Cohen’s κ statistics.
RESULTS
Cell lines with high PD-L1 gene expression (NCI-H358, MDA-MB-231, SGC-7901) demonstrated strong membranous PD-L1 protein expression (TPS range: 94-100%) by both 22C3 and SP263 assays. In contrast, low-expressing lines (A549, MCF7, AGS) showed minimal staining (TPS <1%) with either antibody. PD-L1 expression showed excellent concordance between ThinPrep slides and cell-block sections. In clinical specimens, analysis of 88 CSF samples from 44 LM patients (37 lung adenocarcinomas, 5 breast cancers, and 2 gastric adenocarcinomas) revealed PD-L1 positivity rates of 45% (20/44) with 22C3 and 52% (23/44) with SP263, demonstrating a high inter-assay concordance (Cohen κ=0.86). Among 44 slides with <100 tumor cells, PD-L1 expression was as follows: 27 within TPS <1% (14 for 22C3 and 13 for SP263), 15 within TPS 1-49% (7 for 22C3 and 8 for SP263), and 2 within TPS ≥50% (1 for 22C3 and 1 for SP263). All CSF specimens from breast cancer and gastric adenocarcinoma patients showed negative PD-L1 expression. Among lung adenocarcinoma cases, the assays demonstrated Cohen κ of 0.84, with positivity rates of 54% (20/37) for 22C3 and 62% (23/37) for SP263.
CONCLUSION
Immunocytochemical analysis of PD-L1 expression in CSF specimens from LM patients using ThinPrep cytology demonstrated feasibility, showing good concordance between the Ventana SP263 and Dako 22C3 assays.

title: P11.18.A ROLE OF RADIOTHERAPY IN RESECTED NON-SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER BRAIN METASTASES TREATED WITH CNS-ACTIVE TYROSINE KINASE INHIBITORS
authors: A Choudhury; F K Keane; L L Zhu; S Waliany; A E Marciscano; J F Gainor; Z Piotrowska; J J Lin; K S Oh; D P Cahill; P Brastianos; H Willers; H A Shih; M J Khandekar
abstract:
BACKGROUND
For patients (pts) with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with targetable genomic alterations (TGAs), the increased CNS activity of 2nd/3rd-gen tyrosine kinase inhibitors (CNS-TKIs) has transformed the treatment of intact brain metastases (BMs). For pts with resected BMs, radiation therapy (RT) reduces the risk of local recurrence (LR). To our knowledge, there are no reports of the comparative benefits of adjuvant RT with TKI vs TKI alone for pts with resected NSCLC BMs with TGAs. We hypothesized that omitting cranial RT may alter patterns of failure after craniotomy. Here we compare clinical outcomes of pts with NSCLC with TGAs and resected BMs treated with CNS-TKIs, with and without adjuvant RT.
METHODS
We performed a retrospective analysis of consecutive pts with NSCLC with TGAs without prior CNS-TKI exposure who underwent craniotomy for BM at a single institution from March 2015 to October 2024. CNS-TKIs were defined as TKIs with >50% intracranial response rate in published studies. Data for overall survival (OS), time to intracranial recurrence (ICR), and LR were extracted by chart and imaging review. Analysis was performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, and statistical significance was calculated using the log-rank test. Group comparisons were made using Fisher’s exact test.
RESULTS
We identified 38 pts, 21 of whom underwent RT and 17 of whom did not undergo RT with a median follow up of 25 months from craniotomy (range 10.3-83.1). The median age was 68 (range 36-81). The pts had the following TGAs: EGFR classical mutations (n=25), ALK fusion (4), ROS1 fusion (4), METex14 skipping mutation (3), and RET fusion (2), with no difference in distribution of TGAs between the groups (p=0.40). More pts had a single BM in the RT arm (48% in RT+TKI vs. 12% in TKI (p=0.03)). 68% of pts had gross total resection (66.7% with RT+TKI, 70.1% with TKI). Of the pts undergoing RT after resection, 3 received stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS, defined as <5 fractions), 17 fractionated RT to the cavity (median dose 30 Gy (range: 30-42 Gy) in 10 fractions (range 10-14)), and 1 hippocampal avoidant whole brain RT (HA-WBRT). All pts received CNS-TKI. The 2-year rate of LR in the TKI group was 20% (95% CI, 0-38%) vs. 5% (0-15%) in the RT+TKI group (p=0.067). The 2-year rate of ICR was 60% (95% CI, 12-80%) vs. 31% (7-51%) without and with RT respectively (p=0.3). Median OS without and with RT was 41.9 (95% CI, 20.2-NA) and 61.5 months (34.9-NA) (p=0.3), respectively. One SRS pt developed radionecrosis. Of 5 pts with LR, 3 required repeat craniotomy and postop RT; 1 required HA-WBRT.
CONCLUSION
In this small retrospective cohort of pts with resected NSCLC BMs with TGAs, forgoing adjuvant RT for CNS-TKI alone was not associated with worse OS or ICR at 2 years but was associated with a trend towards increased LR. More data are needed to understand the risks of LR and salvage treatments when treating NSCLC pts with resected BMs with TGAs.

title: P11.19.B NASCENT CLINICAL EXPERIENCE WITH RADIOTHERAPEUTIC MANAGEMENT OF MELANOMA BRAIN METASTASES IN PATIENTS TREATED WITH TUMOR-INFILTRATING LYMPHOCYTE (TIL) THERAPY
authors: A Choudhury; D P Lawrence; M J Frigault; S Cohen; M J Mooradian; R J Sullivan; M J Khandekar; K S Oh; P Brastianos; H A Shih; A M Haugh; A E Marciscano
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy is an emerging treatment option for treatment-refractory melanoma, FDA-approved in 2024. TIL therapy involves tumor harvest, isolation and ex vivo expansion of TIL, followed by lymphodepletion prior to TIL infusion. Studies for TIL therapy approval excluded patients with uncontrolled melanoma brain metastases (MBMs). Given the timeline from TIL harvest to infusion and use of lymphodepletion there are concerns about intralesional hemorrhage, intracranial progression and radiation therapy (RT) toxicity. While RT remains a cornerstone in management of MBMs, there are limited data on management during the peri-TIL therapy window and the safety/efficacy of integrating RT. Herein we review our institutional experience on clinical outcomes and toxicity among patients undergoing RT for MBMs that underwent TIL harvest.
METHODS
We performed a retrospective analysis of patients with advanced melanoma that underwent TIL harvest at a single institution from May to December 2024. Patients with MBMs were stratified by receipt of RT and timing of development of MBMs in relation to date of TIL harvest. Medical records were reviewed with attention to clinical outcomes, RT parameters and adverse events (CTCAEv5.0) related to TIL therapy or RT.
RESULTS
A total of 9 patients with MBMs and undergoing TIL harvest were identified. Median age was 63.2 years, and 55% of patients harbored a BRAF V600E variant. Median time from TIL harvest to infusion was 2.1 months and median follow-up post-harvest was 4.4 (2.1-8.3) months. One patient did not undergo infusion due to TIL product not meeting specification. Two patients had known MBMs and underwent RT >3mo prior to TIL harvest. 55% (5 of 9) of patients developed new MBMs during the window from TIL harvest to infusion. 67% (6 of 9 patients) underwent brain-directed RT. 83% (5 of 6) were treated with focal stereotactic RT with 10 MBMs treated over 6 treatment courses. One patient underwent hippocampal-avoidant WBRT. Of note, 50% of patients that underwent RT had evidence of possible intralesional bleed noted on brain MRI prior to RT. RT-related toxicity was minimal with grade 1-2 fatigue, grade 1 headaches and no radiographic or symptomatic radiation necrosis. There were no intracranial bleeding events after TIL harvest. Neurotoxicity related to TIL therapy was observed including grade 2-3 encephalopathy, grade 3 fatigue, and grade 2 headaches. At last follow up, regional brain control was 67% and irradiated local control was 83%.
CONCLUSION
Our institutional experience suggests that treatment of MBMs with RT in patients undergoing TIL therapy is feasible and safe. Given the risk of intracranial progression or development of new MBMs between TIL harvest and infusion, RT is an option as a consolidative ‘bridging’ therapy for intracranial disease control.
