title: P14.21.B IMPACTS OF SEX AND RACE/ETHNICITY ON INCIDENCE OF VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA ACROSS THE LIFESPAN IN THE UNITED STATES
authors: M Price; K Parmar; K M Walsh; J Benedetti; C Kruchko; Q T Ostrom
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Vestibular schwannomas (VS) are benign tumors arising in the vestibulocochlear nerve. Previous research has identified sex and racial/ethnic differences in risk for these tumors with higher incidence occurring in female and older White populations, and poorer overall survival among Hispanic and Black populations. In this analysis, we aim to assess the joint effects of age, sex, and race and ethnicity on incidence of VS.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States (CBTRUS) is an aggregation of data from the CDC’s National Program of Cancer Registries and NCI’s Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results Program which, in combination, cover the entire US population. VS was defined using ICD-O-3 histology (9560/1) and topography (C72.4) codes for individuals diagnosed between 2004 and 2021, and excluded cases diagnosed by autopsy or death certificate only. We calculated average annual age-adjusted incidence rates, and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) by sex, race/ethnicity, and age at diagnosis. IRRs were considered statistically significant at a P-value<0.05. Statistical interaction was determined using Poisson models.
RESULTS
A total of 76,852 VS cases were diagnosed from 2004-2021 (53.0% female). Overall, 81.2% of cases were in non-Hispanic White persons, while 8.2% were in Hispanic persons (any race) and 4.9% were in non-Hispanic Black persons. Incidence of VS peaked in those 60-69 years. Incidence was significantly higher among females from 10-59 years, with peak female/male difference in ages 20-29 years (IRR=1.29, p-value<0.001). Non-Hispanic Black persons had significantly lower incidence compared to non-Hispanic White persons overall, within sexes, and when stratified by sex or age group. The magnitude of the observed difference by sex varied with race/ethnicity. There was a significant statistical interaction between racial ethnic group and sex (race/ethnicity*sex) for those 50-59 years and 70-79 years. This observation held when restricted to those diagnosed with radiographic confirmation only, but no significant interaction by race/ethnicity and sex occurred among those diagnosed with microscopic confirmation, suggesting it may result from varying diagnostic patterns or access to care.
CONCLUSION
This study identifies an elevated risk of VS in Non-Hispanic Whites individuals relative to both Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic individuals, beginning shortly after puberty and continuing to middle adulthood. Non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity conferred decreased risk of VS more significantly among men than among women. These results identify significant differences in the incidence of VS by race/ethnicity, sex, and age.

title: P14.22.A A NOVEL IMMUNOCOMPETENT ORTHOTOPIC MOUSE MODEL TO STUDY EMBRYONAL TUMORS WITH MULTILAYERED ROSETTES (ETMRS): DEVELOPMENT AND CHARACTERIZATION
authors: I Beasain; I Hervás; S Nuin; S Morales; D Palacios-Alonso; R Hernandez; J Marco; M González; M Zalacaín; D Largaespada; M Alonso
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Embryonal tumors with multilayered rosettes (ETMR) are rare and highly aggressive pediatric brain tumors, characterized by poor prognosis and a median survival below one year. Diagnostic markers include multilayered rosettes, amplification of the C19MC microRNA cluster, and elevated LIN28A expression. To improve understanding of ETMR pathogenesis and support the development of immunotherapies, immunocompetent preclinical models are urgently needed. However, such models remain scarce. This study aims to generate and characterize a novel orthotopic ETMR mouse model in an immunocompetent setting.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The murine primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) cell line DF1-MYC, engineered via a MYC-overexpressing RCAS system in a C57BL/6J background, was used for tumor induction. Cells and derived allografts were implanted orthotopically into the supratentorial region of four weeks old NSG (immunodeficient) and NTV-a p53^floxed (NP53) immunocompetent mice. Tumor development and survival were monitored, with survival curves calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded brain tissues were analyzed by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, as well as immunohistochemistry for Ki67, c-Myc and Lin28a. Transcriptomic profiling was performed by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq).
RESULTS
Direct implantation of DF1-MYC into NP53 mice resulted in low tumor incidence, with only one small tumor exhibiting multilayered rosettes. To improve model consistency, tumors established in NSG mice were subsequently allografted into NP53 hosts. The resulting model, termed MYC384, showed 70% tumor penetrance and a median survival of 36 days. Histopathological evaluation revealed features characteristic of human ETMR, including poorly differentiated, proliferative cells with multilayered rosettes. Further molecular refinement is underway via overexpression of LIN28A and c-Myc in the MYC384 model to enhance ETMR fidelity.
CONCLUSION
The MYC384 model constitutes a promising immunocompetent platform for ETMR research, reproducing key histological characteristics observed in human disease. It offers a valuable resource for studying tumor biology and evaluating novel therapeutic approaches.

title: P14.23.B CLINICAL ASPECTS AND MANAGEMENT OF CNS SOLITARY FIBROUS TUMORS: A CASE-BASED REVIEW
authors: D Antão; J Bandeira Costa; I Guimarães; N Ferreira; M Mafra; E Gouveia; J Marques; A Azevedo; I Costa
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Central nervous system (CNS) solitary fibrous tumors (SFT)/hemangiopericytoma is a relatively rare soft tissue vascular tumor. It is widely recognized as an aggressive disease with high recurrence rates. The best treatment approach is still debated, especially in recurrent disease, as well as the best protocol for systemic surveillance.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a single center retrospective study exploring demographics, treatment patterns, progression free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients (pts) diagnosed with CNS SFT/hemangiopericytomas in a portuguese oncological center. IBM SPSS Statistics version 23 was used for analyzing procedures.
RESULTS
Fourteen patients were diagnosed with SFT between September 2008 and October 2024. The median age was 59.5 years old, 57.1% (n=8) were female. Regarding the histological WHO tumor grading score, 50.0% were grade 2 (n=7), 35.7% were grade 3 (n=5) and 14.3% were grade 1 (n=2). The lesions were most commonly supratentorial - 9 pts (64.3%), followed by 4 (28.6%) in the posterior cranial fossa and 1 (7.1%) in the cervical spine. All patients were submitted to surgical resection - 64.3% (n=9) gross total resection (GTR) and 35.7% (n=5) partial resection. The majority, 85.7% (n=12), was submitted to adjuvant focal radiotherapy (RT) - 66.7% after the first resection (n=8) and 33.3% after surgical reintervention on disease recurrence (n=4). Of the patients who were not irradiated, one died shortly after diagnosis and the other has a grade 1 SFT with a short follow-up period. Disease relapse occurred in 57.1% (n=8) - 35.7% (n=5) locoregional recurrence and 35.7% (n=5) systemic disease; 2 pts had both. Among the patients who relapsed, 75% of pts had previous GTR (n=6). In the 6 pts without metastasis or recurrence, half had GTR and the other half had partial resection. Systemic disease occurred in 3 pts with GTR and in 2 pts partial resection. Palliative systemic therapy was administered to 4 patients with chemotherapy, tyrosine-kinase inhibitors and/or immunotherapy. Three of these patients had progressive therapeutic escalation that varied between dacarbazine (n=3), temozolamide and bevacizumab (n=2), pembrolizumab (n=2), doxorubicine (n=1) and trabectedine (n=1). The median follow-up time was 84.5 months (range 1-158 months). Currently, a total of 7 pts (50.0%) are still alive. The median PFS was 72 months (95% CI, 53-91 months) with a PFS rate at 24 months of 90.9%. The median OS was 109 months (95% CI 84-134 months), with an OS rate at 24 months of 92.9%.
CONCLUSION
CNS STFs manifest with heterogeneous behavior. As described in the literature, recurrent and metastatic lesions can occur despite gross total resection followed by radiotherapy. Further studies with bigger cohorts are needed to establish standardized treatment options specially for recurrent or systemic disease.

CONCLUSION
CNS STFs manifest with heterogeneous behavior. As described in the literature, recurrent and metastatic lesions can occur despite gross total resection followed by radiotherapy. Further studies with bigger cohorts are needed to establish standardized treatment options specially for recurrent or systemic disease.

title: P14.24.A CLINICAL, HISTOPATHOLOGICAL AND MOLECULAR FEATURES OF FOUR CASES OF MENINGEAL MELANOCYTOMA
authors: M Koblížek; J Soukup; P Kašparová; O Bradáč; D Šustrová; L Krsková; J Zámečník
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Meningeal melanocytoma is a rare primary melanocytic tumor of the central nervous system. Due to its low incidence, clinicopathological and molecular data remain limited. We present a series of four cases to highlight the spectrum of clinical and morphological features, the immunohistochemical profile with varying proliferative activity, and specific genetic alterations.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We retrospectively reviewed four cases of meningeal melanocytoma diagnosed at our institution over the past 10 years. Histological examination and immunohistochemistry were performed in all cases. In one recent case, DNA-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) was also conducted. Clinical follow-up data were obtained from the hospital records.
RESULTS
The patients ranged in age from 36 to 73 years and included two males and two females. Tumor locations were the thoracic spinal cord (n=1), pineal region (n=1), basal temporal region (n=1), and unspecified supratentorial meninges (n=1). The tumors were hypercellular, composed of oval to spindle-shaped or epithelioid cells. All tumors showed at least focal melanin pigmentation. Immunohistochemistry was positive for S100 and HMB45, and negative for EMA and cytokeratins in all cases. The Ki-67 proliferation index ranged from 1% to 15%. In the most recent case, occurring in a 73-year-old woman, NGS revealed a GNA11 p.Q209L mutation. Follow-up data were available in all cases, with durations ranging from 1 to 7 years. Local recurrence occurred in two of these cases, both three years after the initial therapy. None of the patients died of the disease during the follow-up period.
CONCLUSION
Our series illustrates the histological and immunophenotypic consistency of meningeal melanocytomas across a broad age spectrum and various CNS locations. The variability in proliferative activity and the occurrence of delayed local recurrence despite multimodal therapy highlight the tumor’s intermediate biological potential. Molecular testing may support the diagnosis and aid in excluding metastatic melanoma.

title: P14.25.B DECODING MORPHO-MOLECULAR DIVERSITY IN GLIOSARCOMA AND INSIGHTS INTO RESISTANCE USING SPATIAL TRANSCRIPTOMICS
authors: D Savran; N Schoebe; N Berghaus; D Reuss; M Ratliff; C Herold-Mende; S M Krieg; W Wick; A von Deimling; D Heiland; F Sahm; P Sievers
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Gliosarcoma, a rare and aggressive variant of IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, is characterized by striking intra-tumoral heterogeneity with alternating glial and mesenchymal differentiation. The mesenchymal component is often enriched at recurrence and associated with therapy resistance, suggesting treatment-driven clonal selection. Despite its poor prognosis and distinct histology, gliosarcoma remains underexplored at the molecular level, with no systematic profiling of its cellular or spatial architecture - limiting progress toward targeted therapies.
METHODS
Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was performed on eight FFPE gliosarcoma samples, complemented by spatial transcriptomic profiling (10X Visium) in four matched cases. Multimodal integration enabled high-resolution mapping of malignant and non-malignant compartments. To enhance spatial context extraction and to model tumor-microenvironment interactions, advanced computational approaches, including graph neural networks (GNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), are being developed.
RESULTS
Integration of snRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomic data revealed a distinct population of stromal-like malignant cells enriched for mesenchymal signatures. Compared to conventional glioblastoma, gliosarcoma samples exhibited a reduced presence of neural progenitor cell (NPC-like) and oligodendrocyte progenitor cell (OPC-like) states, suggesting early dominance or selective expansion of the mesenchymal compartment. Spatial annotation of the tumor microenvironment revealed immune-rich niches populated by disease-associated microglia (DIMs), damage-associated macrophages (DAMs), and macrophages (MACs). Preliminary spatial modeling indicates potential interactions between immune population and mesenchymal-like tumor cells that may support therapy-resistant niches.
CONCLUSION
This ongoing study integrates single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic profiling to characterize mesenchymal transition and resistance in gliosarcoma. Early findings highlight a distinct mesenchymal-like malignant population and associated immune environments that may drive resistance. Further computational modeling aims to uncover key cellular interactions and molecular programs, that could inform novel therapeutic strategies.

title: P14.26.A MEK INHIBITION IN ADULT PATIENTS WITH PILOCYTIC ASTROCYTOMAS HARBORING NF-1 MUTATIONS
authors: K Rounis; A Falk Delgado; C Illies; A Shamikh; T Wangerid; M Jensdottir; J Bartek; O Persson; A Hietala; S Friesland; H Carstens; G Stragliotto
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Pilocytic astrocytomas (PA) are rare primary brain tumors in adults and they demonstrate worse clinical outcomes compared with PAs in children. Surgery is the primary treatment option and radiation therapy (RT) is administered in the setting of symptomatic relapse after surgical excision. However, RT is associated with serious late side effects and an increased risk of malignant transformation and chemotherapy has demonstrated modest efficacy in adults with PAs.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Molecularly, PAs are characterized by the activation of the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway. Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) inhibitors have been effective in the treatment of PAs in children but data in adult patients are lacking. Five adult patients in our institution (age range: 30-79 years), four with PAs and one with pilocytic astrocytoma with anaplastic transformation, were administered trametinib, a MEK 1-2 inhibitor. All of the patients’ tumours harboured somatic NF-1 mutations and only one of the patients had a germline NF-1 mutation. Response to trametinib was assessed according to RANO 2.0 criteria.
RESULTS
Three out of five patients had partial response (PR) and two experienced stable disease (SD) as best response to treatment. Two out of five patients had substantial neurological benefit. The median Progression-Free Survival (PFS) was 16.65 months (95% CI: 7.81 - 25.49) in our cohort.
CONCLUSION
These data demonstrate that MEK inhibition is active in adult patients with PAs and it can provide prolonged disease control. Thus, it can be used either as a salvage therapy or as an earlier systemic treatment option in order to prolong RT administration.

title: P14.27.B LONG-TERM OUTCOMES AND MOLECULARLY-GUIDED MANAGEMENT OF ADULT MEDULLOBLASTOMA: DATA FROM A SINGLE-INSTITUTION EXPERIENCE
authors: A Bosio; M Maccari; M Padovan; M Caccese; M Bolshinsky; A Galiano; F Cavallin; L Bellu; F Pasqualetti; S Lonardi; G Lombardi
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Medulloblastoma(MB) is an exceedingly rare malignancy in adults, with limited prospective data guiding its management. Although multimodal treatment remains the standard, recent molecular profiling has enabled the introduction of targeted therapies, such as SMO-inhibitors for SHH-activated tumors. This study aims to describe clinical characteristics, treatments - including the use of targeted therapy - outcomes, and long-term sequelae in a monocentric cohort of adult MB pts, providing insights to optimize future therapeutic strategies.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We retrospectively analyzed adult MB pts treated at Veneto Institute of Oncology, Padua, Italy between November 2011 and February 2025. Clinical, molecular and treatment data, including extent of surgery and RT details were collected. Response was assessed using RANO criteria, treatment-related toxicity according to CTCAEv5.0. Survival outcomes were estimated using the K-M method.
RESULTS
We included 29 pts (median age 34ys, IQR 22-41; 44.5% males), with a median FU of 71ms (IQR 32-112). At diagnosis, 86% were symptomatic, 55% had an ECOG PS 0, and desmoplastic/nodular was the most frequent histology(48%). Molecular subgrouping was available in 45%, with SHH activation being the most common (31%). All pts received craniospinal-RT; 18 pts(62%) received adjuvant CT with cisplatin-etoposide±cyclophosphamide, 6(21%) cisplatin-lomustine±vincristine, 3(10%) an intensive pediatric regimen and 2(7%) did not received CT due to comorbidities. First-line CR was achieved in 65%. Overall, 38% experienced PD and 24% died. Three pts received vismodegib at recurrence: one (M0 stage, high-risk) received 3 cycles without toxicity, had PD at 3ms from vismodegib start and died at 30ms from diagnosis; one (M2 stage, high-risk) received 5 cycles without toxicity, had PD at 4ms and died at 64ms. One patient (M0 stage, high-risk) received 11 cycles, developed G1 toxicity and did not experience PD until now (11ms). Three patients received re-RT at PD. The 3-year PFS and OS rates were 78% and 92%, respectively. Stratified analyses suggested worse outcomes associated with high-risk class, subtotal resection, and lower baseline ECOG PS. Grade 3-4 toxicity occurred in 29%(7/24 evaluable). Long-term complications included neurocognitive impairment(21%) and RT-induced secondary malignancies (10%) at a median of 46ms.
CONCLUSION
Our findings confirm the clinical and biological heterogeneity of adult MB, highlighting the need for a multimodal approach. Long-term survivorship is often achievable, though late toxicities remain a concern. Vismodegib showed a significant impact on outcome. Future efforts should focus on integrating molecular profiling into routine practice to better stratify risk and personalize therapies, along with the adoption of treatment de-intensification strategies to mitigate long-term sequelae.

title: P14.28.A CLINICAL AND MOLECULAR CHARACTERIZATION OF ADULT-ONSET MEDULLOBLASTOMA: FIRST RESULTS FROM REAL WORLD DATA OF A MULTICENTER PROSPECTIVE COHORT IN LATIN AMERICA
authors: A González-Vázquez; M Serrano-Murillo; B Cacho-Díaz; A O Chavez-Martínez; B E Lazo Poveda; T Wegman-Ostrosky; D Dávila-Dupont; A Rodríguez-Camacho; F Maldonado-Magos; G A Gutiérrez-Aceves; S Moreno-Jiménez; L Hernández-Sánchez; J O Santellán-Hernández; D A Vega-Moreno; C H Caro-Sánchez; A M Cano Valdez; O Arrieta; E Caballe-Pérez
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Adult-onset medulloblastoma (aMB) represents less than 1% of adult brain malignancies. Adult treatment strategies remain poorly defined and are frequently extrapolated from pediatric protocols. This challenge is particularly pronounced in Latin America, where prospective data are lacking and access to diagnostics and treatment remains limited.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a prospective observational cohort study involving adult patients (≥16 years) with newly diagnosed aMB treated between May 2024 and March 2025 across a network of tertiary referral centers in Mexico, including the INCan and the INNN. Eligible patients were consecutively enrolled at diagnosis. This report presents the first 13 patients from this ongoing cohort.
RESULTS
Median age was 28 years (IQR 21-32), and 53.8% were male. Tumor locations included cerebral hemispheres (53.8%), vermis (38.5%), and fourth ventricle (7.7%). Presenting symptoms were headache (100%), nausea/vomiting (92.3%), ataxia or cerebellar signs (76.9%), and others such as visual disturbances, cranial nerve deficits, and sensory complaints (30.8% each). Hydrocephalus was present in 92.3%, all requiring shunt placement. Metastatic disease (M1-M4) was found in 46.2%, while 53.8% were M0. Per Packer’s criteria, 92.3% had high-risk disease. Histologic subtypes were desmoplastic/nodular (76.9%) and classic (23.1%). Of 11 patients with molecular subgrouping, 54.5% were SHH-activated TP53 wild-type, 18.2% SHH-activated TP53-mutated, and 18.2% non-SHH/non-WNT. Most patients (84.6%) underwent subtotal resection or biopsy; only 2 had gross total resection. Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) at 36 Gy was administered to 92.3%, with a median tumor bed boost of 55.8 Gy. One patient received a posterior fossa boost (54 Gy). The median interval from surgery to radiotherapy was 116.5 days (range 24-187), and the overall treatment time was 46 days (range 26-69). Concurrent vincristine chemotherapy was given to 83.3%. One patient had neoadjuvant chemotherapy; 61.5% received adjuvant chemotherapy. The most common regimen was cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine (46.2%), followed by temozolomide (15.4%). Adverse effects included gastrointestinal symptoms and anemia (23.1% each), neutropenia (15.4%), and ototoxicity and neuropathy (7.7% each).
CONCLUSION
This first prospective Latin American study on aMB highlights the predominance of SHH-activated subtypes, frequent presentation with advanced disease, and significant delays in initiating radiotherapy. Despite limited resources, most patients received multimodal treatment. These findings emphasize the urgent need for earlier diagnosis, faster treatment initiation, and standardized care pathways for aMB in low- and middle-income countries

title: P14.29.B QUANTITATIVE BRAIN MRI ANALYSIS IN NEURODEGENERATIVE LANGERHANS CELL HISTIOCYTOSIS
authors: C Baek; L Rincon de la Rosa; I Aliouat; L Guichard; E Pappa; L Leguennec; L Nichelli; A Sangare; M Habert; E Bayen; A Del Cul; K Mokhtari; F Cohen; J Haroche; S Héritier; J Donadieu; K Hoang-Xuan; A Alentorn; A Idbaih
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Neurodegenerative Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (ND-LCH) is a severe central nervous system involvement complicating LCH. ND-LCH is characterized by a cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal signs, pseudobulbar palsy, cognitive impairment, and behavioral disturbances. Cerebellar atrophy, the most common MRI finding, has been widely described in the literature. However, the natural history of volumetric changes in the cerebellum has never been examined. In this study, we aim to perform a quantitative analysis of the cerebellar atrophy in ND-LCH patients compared to a control cohort.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
MRI of patients with ND-LCH were compared to those of controls. An automated cerebellum analysis was performed using the Volbrain software (CERES) and a linear regression analysis was used to score the severity of cerebellar atrophy over time.
RESULTS
We retrospectively analyzed follow-up MRI of 16 adult patients with ND-LCH compared to those of 22 control patients. We examined an average of four MRIs per patient over a median follow-up period of six years. All patients with ND-LCH exhibit global and cortical cerebellar atrophy over time. The average atrophy rate is -1.86 cm³/year (range -5.90 to 0.34) and is heterogeneous between patients. All cerebellar lobules are affected by atrophy.
CONCLUSION
Longitudinal quantitative MRI analysis of the cerebellum in ND-LCH: (i) is feasible, (ii) confirms significant global and cortical cerebellar atrophy in patients with ND-LCH over time, (iii) estimates the rate of cerebellar atrophy, and (iv) could be useful as a therapeutic endpoint in a clinically slow-progressing disease. Further studies are needed to validate our findings.

title: P15.01.A END-OF-LIFE CARE EXPERIENCES AND LONG-TERM OUTCOMES OF BEREAVED NEURO-ONCOLOGY CAREGIVERS: “IT’S A CLUB NOBODY WANTED TO JOIN, BUT WE’RE THERE”
authors: S Meer; R Miller; P Buckle; L Murray; C Lewis-Smith; L Ziegler; K Piil; F W Boele
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Even years post-bereavement, neuro-oncology caregivers are known to suffer serious and long-lasting adverse outcomes. To identify opportunities to enhance support, we investigated caregiver experiences during the patient’s end-of-life (EoL) phase and the dying process, related to their post-bereavement outcomes.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
In a sequential mixed-methods study, caregivers who were ≥6 months post-bereavement completed a quantitative survey (reported separately). A nested sample of caregivers were invited to take part in online focus groups covering the EoL phase, the period surrounding the patient’s death, and their post-bereavement outcomes. Following audio transcription, data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The study was co-designed by bereaved caregivers, who also co-facilitated the groups and contributed to data analysis.
RESULTS
Three groups with, in total, 11 caregivers (64% women, 55% partners of patients) of deceased patients diagnosed with glioblastoma were held. Themes covered 1) care experiences in the EoL phase (covering communication, information, support needs, and balancing family dynamics), 2) caregiver experiences surrounding patient death, and 3) immediate and longer-term post-bereavement outcomes (covering complex and conflicting emotional responses, expectations and strategies to cope with grief, and the value of formal and informal support).
CONCLUSION
Findings highlight ongoing significant and unmet emotional support needs of bereaved neuro-oncology caregivers. Caregivers want and deserve to be proactively offered adequate and timely support which could limit the long-lasting adverse impact of providing care.

Findings highlight ongoing significant and unmet emotional support needs of bereaved neuro-oncology caregivers. Caregivers want and deserve to be proactively offered adequate and timely support which could limit the long-lasting adverse impact of providing care.

title: P15.02.B THE EXPERIENCES OF PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT HIGH-GRADE GLIOMAS USING A PATIENT DECISION AID DURING NEUROSURGICAL CONSULTATIONS
authors: H Sørensen von Essen; M Heintz Sparrebro; L Bjerregaard
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Despite intensive surgical and oncological treatment, patients with a high-grade glioma (HGG) face an average survival time of less than two years from diagnosis, and all patients will inevitably experience a tumor recurrence during their disease trajectory. When the recurrence is diagnosed, a decision about treatment and care needs to be made. Previous studies show that patients with HGG prefer to be involved in shared decision making (SDM) and want their family members to be involved. To increase patient and family involvement and support SDM, we developed and implemented a patient decision aid, the Decision Helper, in neurosurgical consultations with patients with recurrent HGG. The Decision Helper is a paper-based tool that helps structure the consultation and decision making, emphasizing the available treatment options and patient preferences. The objective of the present study was to explore how patients and family members experience using the Decision Helper.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Semi-structured interviews were conducted with patients and their family members immediately after the neurosurgical consultation. The interviews were transcribed and analyzed using a reflexive thematic analysis approach.
RESULTS
Fourteen patients and 14 family members were interviewed. Most of the family members were the patients’ primary caregivers. The analysis generated four overall and overlapping themes: Theme I: The Decision Helper’s impact on the consultation, focusing on the clinicians’ use of the Decision Helper. Theme II: The Decision Helper’s effect on the decision, emphasizing decisional conflict and the actual treatment decision. Theme III: The Decision Helper’s impact on patient involvement, describing the patients’ and families’ experiences of decision involvement and decision support. Theme IV: The acceptability of the Decision Helper concerning the layout and use of the Decision Helper during the consultation.
CONCLUSION
Patients with recurrent HGG and their family members highlighted the Decision Helper as increasing their level of involvement and understanding of the clinician’s information. The Decision Helper made differentiating between the available options easier, and patients and family members appreciated the tangible paper-based format. Even in cases where the patients had a clear decision preference before the consultation, they were positive towards using the Decision Helper and expressed that it helped decrease their decisional conflict. The use of patient decision aids in neurosurgery is relatively new. However, the findings from the present study indicate the positive potential of implementing SDM and patient decision aids for this patient population.

title: P15.03.A SUPPORTIVE CARE FOR PATIENTS WITH PRIMARY HIGH-GRADE BRAIN TUMOURS AND THEIR RELATIVES: A SCOPING REVIEW
authors: P Ståhl; I Henoch; R Schenell; B Rydenhag; A Smits; A Ozanne
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Patients diagnosed with high-grade brain tumours and their relatives face significant challenges, necessitating the identification and development of effective support interventions. This scoping review aimed to systematically map existing support interventions for patients with glioblastoma or other primary high-grade brain tumours and their relatives.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A scoping review was conducted, including studies published between 2013 and 2025, yielding 3,749 records from PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science. The PRISMA-ScR guidelines guided the methodology. After screening, 34 articles were included and data was organised, summarised, and synthesised.
RESULTS
Various types of support interventions were identified, including individualised support (n=10) and multi-component support program, support and assistance in care planning and preparedness (n=7), individual and multidisciplinary rehabilitation (n=6), psychotherapy, yoga and mindfulness (n=6), as well as different types of learning and educational program (n=5). Positive outcomes were observed across multiple domains, including quality of life, symptom relief, motor function, communication, psycho social well-being, hope, preparedness, and reduced hospital re-admissions. Additionally, interventions were associated with a reduction in symptom of depression and anxiety. However, many interventions were still in their early stages of development and required further evaluation.
CONCLUSION
The identification of a broad range of support interventions and their promising results for both patients and their relatives is encouraging. However, further research is needed to refine these interventions and ensure their effectiveness in clinical practice.

title: P15.04.B TELE-COGNITIVE REHABILITATION FOR ADULT LOWER GRADE GLIOMA: A PROSPECTIVE FEASIBILITY STUDY
authors: C Weyer Jamora; M Brie; P Bracci; E Smith; T Luks; S Phan; S Braunstein; N A Oberheim-Bush; N Butowski; J Clarke; J de Groot; J Barreiro-Rosado; R Almonen; S Chang; S Hervey-Jumper; J W Taylor
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Cognitive impairments are common in patients with lower-grade gliomas (LrGG, grades 1-3), yet evidence-based interventions are limited. Tele-health cognitive rehabilitation offers a potential solution. We conducted a pilot study investigating the adherence, satisfaction, and preliminary efficacy of tele-cognitive rehabilitation in adults with LrGG.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Eligible participants were adults with stable LrGG (≥ 6 months post-treatment) reporting subjective and objective cognitive impairments (>1 SD below average in ≥2 domains). Patients received three months of individual cognitive rehabilitation Goal Management Training (GMT) via telehealth which is a behavioral treatment designed to address cognitive impairments. Cognitive assessments and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) were collected at baseline (T1), post-intervention (T2), and 9 months post-baseline (T3). Adequate adherence required ≥80% of participants completing ≥80% of sessions. Adequate satisfaction was defined as a score ≥6/7 on a post-T2 survey. Preliminary efficacy was assessed using repeated measures t-tests, effect sizes, and reliable change indices (RCI) for within-group changes (T1-T2, T1-T3).
RESULTS
Thirty-two patients (median age 48 years; median 61 months post-diagnosis; 46% astrocytoma and 46% oligodendroglioma; 82% IDH mutant; 39% grade 2 and 61% grade 3; 64% prior radiotherapy) were prospectively enrolled between May 2019 and September 2023. GMT adherence was high at 88%. Significant improvements were observed in the WAIS-IV Working Memory Index from T1 (mean z=-0.12, SD 1.13) to T2 (mean z=0.06, SD 1.09; p=0.03, eta²=0.18), with 25% demonstrating reliable improvement. PROs also improved: Fatigue Symptom Inventory Interference Index decreased significantly from T1 (mean=3.37, SD 2.48) to T3 (mean=2.55, SD 2.42; p=0.04, eta²=0.18). Clinically evident fatigue (FSI >3) decreased from 50% at T1 to 25% at T3. The Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI)-Somatic subscale improved significantly both from T1 (mean=0.06, SD 0.84) to T2 (mean=-0.38, SD 0.60; p=0.001, eta²=0.33) and T1-T3 (mean=-0.34, SD 0.76; p=0.01, eta²=0.28). Overall satisfaction with GMT was excellent (mean=6.87/7, SD 0.35).
CONCLUSION
Tele-cognitive rehabilitation using individual GMT is feasible for adults with stable LrGG, demonstrating good adherence and high patient satisfaction. Preliminary results show promising improvements in working memory, fatigue interference, and somatic distress, with some effects sustained 6 months post-intervention. Further research is warranted to confirm efficacy and explore mechanisms of action.

title: P15.05.A EXPLORING THE IMPACT OF BRAIN TUMOR-RELATED VIOLENT BEHAVIOR ON NEXT-OF-KIN: A QUALITATIVE STUDY
authors: A Guenna Holmgren; A Malmström; J Simmons; E Degsell; L Kastbom
abstract:
BACKGROUND
There is a significant knowledge gap regarding violence associated with somatic illnesses, such as brain tumors. While rare case reports exist in the literature, numerous testimonies from members of the Swedish Brain Tumor Association describe cases where next-of-kin have been subjected to severe violence by individuals with brain tumors. Both in Sweden and internationally, research is scarce on how next-of-kin experience and are affected by violence when the perpetrator is suffering from a brain tumor. Moreover, there are no established guidelines for how support should be provided to this group of victims, whose circumstances often fall outside the traditional frameworks of the legal system, social services, and healthcare.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The Swedish national project BRAVE: Brain Tumor Related Aggression and Violence Exposure comprises qualitative studies, the first aimed to explore the experiences and support needs of next-of-kin who have been exposed to violence by a person suffering from glioma. Twenty-five semi-structured interviews were conducted. The participants were asked to share their experiences and to describe what support they had received and/or would have needed from healthcare services, social services, authorities, and third parties. The interviews were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.
RESULTS
The analysis highlights the importance of healthcare providers understanding patients within their broader social and relational contexts, as well as the significance of continuity of care, which was highly valued by the participants. They also pointed out that the patients’ autonomy was often prioritized over the next-of-kin’s safety and well-being. While respecting confidentiality, they noted that healthcare’s sometimes rigid interpretations of these rules prevented them from sharing their experiences and potentially receiving support. Their support needs varied and evolved over time, highlighting the importance of customized information, practical assistance, and peer support.
CONCLUSION
This study provides insights into how support can be tailored for both patients and next-of-kin when personality changes caused by a brain tumor lead to violent situations. The results point to an urgent need for better support, tailored to the individual and their context.

title: P15.06.B BREAKING BAD NEWS IN NEURO-ONCOLOGY: A QUALITATIVE STUDY INTO THE EXPERIENCES AND NEEDS OF PATIENTS WITH GLIOMAS AND THEIR RELATIVES
authors: A de Boer; M Wagemakers; S A Kuipers; S Bunskoek; A M Buunk
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Healthcare professionals working with patients with gliomas face the challenge of navigating difficult conversations. After surgery the neurosurgeon discusses the diagnosis with the patient and their relatives. Tailored communication in this bad news conversation is essential, especially given the frequent cognitive impairments in this population. However, the specific needs of patients and relatives remain insufficiently understood and existing guidelines for breaking bad news have not been validated for this group. We aimed to explore the experiences and needs of patients and their relatives during bad news conversations, examine current practices, and assess how well current communication practices align with these needs.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a single-center qualitative case study in the Netherlands. First, five bad news conversations were recorded and observed using a literature-based observation guide to assess the current situation and evaluate adherence to existing guidelines. Next, we conducted five additional dyadic interviews with patients and relatives. Descriptive statistics were applied on outcomes of the observations. Thematic analysis was used to analyse the interviews.
RESULTS
While the conversations each followed a certain structure, they varied in approach and did not fully adhere to existing general guidelines. Interview analysis revealed four main themes: communication about the diagnosis, social dynamics and support, information processing, and expectations and reactions. Participants valued direct, honest communication with room for questions. Although the diagnosis was often anticipated hope remained central. An empathic personal approach was appreciated, though extensive emotional support from the neurosurgeon was not expected. Patients were emotionally reserved while relatives responded more visibly. After the conversation many expressed a desire for written summaries. Communication largely aligned with participants’ needs.
CONCLUSION
This study provides insights into the experiences and needs of patients with gliomas and their relatives during bad news conversations. Clear, empathic communication with room for questions was valued with a focus on transparency and hope. Communication practices in this center met the needs of patients and relatives, although they did not fully adhere to existing general guidelines. This suggests the potential value of developing tailored guidelines for this specific population. Future research should explore how cognitive functioning affects emotional processing during bad news conversations and the role of emotional support in refining communication strategies for glioma care.

title: P15.07.A PATIENT’S SUBJECTIVE ASSESSMENT OF COMFORT WITH TREATMENT OF BRAIN METASTASES WITH STEREOTACTIC RADIOTHERAPY
authors: M Rucinska; K Osowiecka; J Bordakiewicz; D Pokorska; D Cieniawa; S Nawrocki
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Local treatment of metastatic lesions in the central nervous system is currently the treatment of choice. Stereotactic radiotherapy is the preferred method for some patients due to its low invasiveness. The purpose of this study was to assess perceptions of the inconvenience and comfort of stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastases.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
The study included 16 patients (37-83 years, mean age 61 years) undergoing stereotactic irradiation for brain metastases using a Cyber Knife or ZAP-X. A specially created for this study questionnaire of 20 close-ended questions with an opportunity to explain the reason for the answer was used. The study was approved by the Bioethics Committee at the University of Warmia and Mazury w Olsztynie.
RESULTS
Nearly half of the patients (46%) surveyed felt nervous while waiting for treatment, more female than male (p=0.04). In contrast, irradiation itself was a cause of stress for only one responder (6%). The vast majority of patients reported no problems or difficulties related to the mask used, head support, maintaining body position during treatment, duration of treatment, etc. Women were significantly more likely than men to complain about the inconvenience of immobilizing their heads with a mask (p=0.04). No differences were observed depending on the age of the patients or the radiotherapy device used. All but one patient reported that they would agree to repeat stereotactic brain radiotherapy if necessary.
CONCLUSION
Stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastases using Cyber Knife and ZAP-X is subjectively well tolerated by patients.

title: P15.08.B PILOTTESTING OF A PROBLEM LIST FOR CAREGIVERS OF ADULT NEUROONCOLOGICALPPATIENTS: IDENTIFYING UNMET NEEDS AND RELEVANT CHALLENGES
authors: D Lindner; M Spieker; L Grosse; D Rieger; M Tatagiba; G Tabatabai; M Renovanz
abstract:
BACKGROUND
The diagnosis of a brain tumor represents a significant psychosocial burden for patients’ caregivers. Despite this, there is a lack of psychosocial screening tools specifically adapted to the needs of caregivers in neuro-oncology. The aim of this study was to pilot test a problem list designed as a holistic needs assessment tool tailored to the specific unmet needs of caregivers, to be used alongside with the Distress Thermometer scale.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We tested a self-developed preliminary problem list with caregivers of neuro-oncology patients and conducted qualitative interviews to assess its relevance and applicability. The list comprised 38 items across six domains: physical, emotional, social, practical, daily life challenges, and issues arising from the patient’s impairment. Free-text responses were allowed to identify additional needs. Inclusion criteria included being a primary caregiver, providing informed consent, and sufficient German language skills. Sample size was guided by data saturation, and interviews were analyzed using MAXQDA.
RESULTS
The semi-structured interviews included eight core questions addressing aspects such as the length and clarity of the problem list, emotional responses during completion, practical utility, and any missing content. A total of 24 caregivers participated (n = 13 male, n = 11 female), most being partners of the patients. The average interview duration was 15 minutes. Caregivers most frequently endorsed physical and emotional concerns, particularly “depressed mood” (15/24; 63%), “fatigue” (13/24; 54%), and “sleep problems” (13/24; 54%). Most participants (n = 15) reported no difficulties understanding the items. However, 12.5% (n = 3) found the item “changes in emotional behavior of the affected person” unclear. This item was removed, as a related and well-understood item —“changes in personality”— coveres similar content. Additional unmet needs identified included “planning of everyday life,” “loss of autonomy,” “fear of dying,” and “feeling abandoned to cope alone.”
CONCLUSION
The pilot study supports the feasibility and acceptability of the problem list as a caregiver-focused assessment tool. It appears to adequately capture the unmet psychosocial needs of caregivers of brain tumor patients and may enhance targeted assessment and support in clinical practice.

title: P15.09.A EVALUATION OF AN ART-BASED INTERVENTION IN NEURO-ONCOLOGICAL PATIENTS - A PILOT STUDY
authors: M Renovanz; M D Ziegler; G Tabatabai; M Tatagiba; M Nadji-Ohl
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Brain tumor diagnoses often cause significant psychological distress in patients and their caregivers, frequently accompanied by neurocognitive deficits and personality changes. Art observation has been shown to positively affect neurocognition and activate brain regions involved in reflective processing, such as the Default Mode Network. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and psychosocial impact of a structured art-based intervention.
METHODS
In this single-center study, brain tumor patients and their relatives participated in guided art tours at a local museum. Each session centered around three themes grounded in the principles of neuroaesthetics. During the 60-minute tours, selected artworks were discussed from both a neuroscientific perspective by a neurosurgeon and an artistic perspective by an art historian. The experience was complemented by carefully chosen music that matched the themes. Vital signs were recorded before and after each session. Participants also completed a study-specific questionnaire assessing the perceived emotional and cognitive effects of the intervention, using a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree). Additionally, validated instruments were used to measure psychological distress and health-related quality of life. The primary outcomes included feasibility, emotional responses based on questionnaire data, and changes in vital signs.
RESULTS
A total of 16 patients (7 male, 9 female patients) and 11 caregivers attended eight sessions between August 2023 and July 2024; additional sessions followed from March to May 2025. Overall, 25 of 27 participants (14 patients, 11 caregivers) completed the evaluation. Most reported positive experiences: 21 participants (12 patients, 9 caregivers) felt emotionally relieved; 17 (11 patients, 6 caregivers) experienced cognitive stimulation; 20 (11 patients, 9 caregivers) reported increased curiosity; and 20 (12 patients, 8 caregivers) described a positive impact on daily life. Negative responses were rare, with only 4 participants disagreeing or strongly disagreeing with feeling emotionally relieved. No adverse events occurred, and vital signs remained stable, in patients and caregivers.
CONCLUSION
This pilot study demonstrates that the art-based intervention is feasible and well accepted by both neuro-oncology patients and their caregivers. Preliminary results support further investigation of art observation as a complementary therapeutic approach.

In this single-center study, brain tumor patients and their relatives participated in guided art tours at a local museum. Each session centered around three themes grounded in the principles of neuroaesthetics. During the 60-minute tours, selected artworks were discussed from both a neuroscientific perspective by a neurosurgeon and an artistic perspective by an art historian. The experience was complemented by carefully chosen music that matched the themes. Vital signs were recorded before and after each session. Participants also completed a study-specific questionnaire assessing the perceived emotional and cognitive effects of the intervention, using a 4-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree). Additionally, validated instruments were used to measure psychological distress and health-related quality of life. The primary outcomes included feasibility, emotional responses based on questionnaire data, and changes in vital signs.
RESULTS
A total of 16 patients (7 male, 9 female patients) and 11 caregivers attended eight sessions between August 2023 and July 2024; additional sessions followed from March to May 2025. No adverse events occurred, and vital signs remained stable, in patients and caregivers.
CONCLUSION
This pilot study demonstrates that the art-based intervention is feasible and well accepted by both neuro-oncology patients and their caregivers. Preliminary results support further investigation of art observation as a complementary therapeutic approach.

title: P15.10.B TOWARDS EARLY INTEGRATION OF PALLIATIVE CARE IN GLIOBLASTOMA PATIENTS: CO-DESIGN OF AN INTEGRATED CARE PATHWAY AND ALTERNATIVE PAYMENT MODEL
authors: E K van der Poort; M C Baas-Thijssen; M Oomes; M J Vos; R M Pieterman; E F de Vries; Y M van der Linden; J F Koekkoek
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Despite the significant symptom burden and incurable nature of glioblastoma, palliative care is often introduced late and is not consistently part of routine practice. Care delivery remains fragmented, with limited coordination between providers, resulting in suboptimal advance care planning (ACP), inadequate symptom management and insufficient psychosocial support. Early integration of palliative care can better address the needs of patients and caregivers, improve quality of life, and reduce unnecessary care in the end of life phase. Consequently, there is a critical need to systematically integrate palliative care into routine neuro-oncological care. Alternative payment models (APM) can incentivize timely and integrated palliative care by aligning reimbursement with high-quality and coordinated care instead of rewarding the volume of services. This study aims to design an integrated care pathway and APM to support the early integration of palliative care for patients with glioblastoma.
METHODS
We used participatory design research, engaging stakeholders from neuro-oncology, specialty palliative care, primary care, district nursing, healthcare administration, health insurance, health economics, and patient advocacy. The design process consisted of three phases and involved 13 informal interviews (with healthcare professionals (HCPs), patients or caregivers), six expert meetings and two co-design workshops.
RESULTS
In phase 1, we mapped the current care pathway and identified barriers to early palliative care integration. Major barriers included: 1) variation in timing and need of ACP, 2) HCP hesitation in initiating ACP, 3) unclear referral triggers for specialist palliative care, 4) inadequate coordination between primary and secondary care, 5) limited experience with glioblastoma in primary care due to low prevalence. In phase 2, iterative prototyping was used to design a care pathway, including a protocol with referral triggers. Key components include: initiation of ACP by neuro-oncologist within six weeks after diagnosis, transmural multidisciplinary team meeting before treatment in complex cases, ongoing transmural coordination, referral to specialist palliative care, and caregiver aftercare. Phase 3 is currently ongoing, during which we develop and evaluate scenarios for an APM. The APM should minimize administrative burden given the small patient population and be scalable to other oncological conditions.
CONCLUSION
The co-designed integrated care pathway offers a feasible and scalable framework for systematically integrating early palliative care for patients with glioblastoma. Next steps include establishing contractual agreements, implementing the pathway and APM, and evaluating patient, clinical and system-level outcomes.

title: P15.11.A ENHANCING COGNITIVE ACCESSIBILITY IN PSYCHOTHERAPY FOR ADULTS WITH BRAIN TUMORS: A PATIENT-INFORMED APPROACH TO INTERVENTION ADAPTATION
authors: A R Loughan; A Lanoye; G Zarrella; A Fox; C Kleva
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Many adults with brain tumors experience double vulnerability—significant emotional distress alongside cognitive decline. These cognitive changes often prohibit their inclusion in psychotherapeutic intervention research due to restrictive eligibility criteria; however, small adaptations may support cognitive accessibility and enable engagement in interventions that promote wellbeing. This analysis aimed to identify and evaluate strategies to accommodate the neurocognitive needs of patients with brain tumors to enhance their engagement in psychotherapeutic interventions.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We conducted a series of feasibility studies of Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully (CALM), a 6-session psychotherapeutic intervention, in adults with primary and secondary brain tumors. First, in a single-arm pilot trial, 18 participants rated which evidence-informed accommodations would support their cognitive limitations and enhance engagement in future trials during exit interviews. Recommendations proposed by >60% were integrated into the subsequent randomized pilot trial, in which 28 participants reported by dichotomous scale (yes/no) whether these cognitive accommodations were beneficial during the CALM intervention.
RESULTS
Participants in the single-arm pilot trial (N=18) recommended appointment reminders (100%), CALM topic refreshers (94%), prior session summaries (88%), CALM visual handouts (82%), time in-session for content consolidation (71%), and notepads (65%). These accommodations were incorporated into the subsequent randomized pilot trial, of which participants (N=28) reported the following as beneficial: appointment reminders (96%), prior session summaries (96%), CALM topic refreshers (88%), time in-session for content consolidation (89%), CALM visual handouts (69%), and notepads (48%).
CONCLUSION
Participants with primary and secondary brain tumors most recommended evidence-informed cognitive accommodations included: 1) appointment reminders to support session attendance, 2) CALM topic refreshers and prior session summaries to support memory, and 3) additional time to assist with slower processing and support comprehension during conversation. Notepads were highly recommended in the single-arm pilot, but were considered less beneficial in the randomized pilot trial. Targeted adaptations, such as providing an interactive participant workbook rather than a blank notepad, may bolster the benefit for participants. Implementing supportive cognitive strategies is vital to promoting neuro-oncology inclusion in psychotherapeutic interventions and meeting the needs of this underserved population.

title: P15.12.B A STEP TOWARDS SHARED DECISION-MAKING: SHARING GOALS VIA AN APP PROMOTES PATIENT GOAL COMMUNICATION WITH BRAIN TUMOR PATIENTS IN NEUROSURGICAL CONSULTATIONS
authors: I J Bras; G J Rutten; P Lodder; M M Sitskoorn; P Hoogendoorn; K Gehring
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Shared decision-making (SDM) aims to combine medical expertise with patient preferences and values. SDM literature and implementation have mostly focused on medically informing patients, whereas a recent model of SDM emphasizes the importance of explicitly discussing patients’ goals. This study assesses the impact of sharing patient goals via an app on how often goals are mentioned and on the level of observed SDM in neurosurgical consultations.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Participants were untreated adult patients with a presumed diagnosis of glioma or meningioma. Data were collected for two groups: an observational group and an intervention group, who used the Goings-On app®. This smartphone app allows patients to enter their goals with personal photos and log within a minute a day on a 5-point Likert scale the attainment of these goals, as well as symptom burden. This information is available to the neurosurgeon in the electronic patient file for use during the consultation. Consultations were audio-recorded and patient goals were counted if they were explicitly framed as goals in the consultation or identified as goals through the Goings-On app®. The OPTION-MCC, an observer-based coding scheme, was used to rate SDM behaviors of the neurosurgeons (scale 0-100, with higher scores representing more SDM), such as eliciting patient goals, providing information about options, eliciting and integrating preferences, and evaluating the decision. Differences between groups in the number of goals mentioned and observed SDM were assessed using generalized linear mixed models with different target distributions and link functions depending on the type of outcome.
RESULTS
The intervention group (n=49) registered 237 goals (range 1-9) in the Goings-On app®. During consultations, at least one goal was mentioned in 42% of the observational group (n=66) compared to 88% in the intervention group. A significant difference was observed for the total number of goals mentioned, where 41 goals were mentioned in the observational group vs. 135 in the intervention group (F=44.052, p=0.012). OPTION-MCC scores did not differ significantly between groups, with a mean of 43.2 ± SD15.8 (range 14.3-85.7) for the observational group and 50.1± SD18.5 (range 10.7-89.3) for the intervention group (F=1.062, p=0.439).
CONCLUSION
The app successfully facilitated bringing patient goals into the conversation about neurosurgical care, although this did not translate into a higher level of observed SDM. Future research should explore what neurosurgeons need to better integrate goals into SDM to ultimately achieve care that is aligned with what matters most to patients.

title: P15.13.A DESIGNING A NOVEL NEURO-ONCOLOGY SURVIVORSHIP SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT PROGRAM FOR BRAIN TUMOR SURVIVORS: DISCUSSIONS WITH CLINICAL TEAM MEMBERS, PATIENTS, AND CAREGIVERS
authors: K F Figuracion; A Appleby; F M Lewis; D P Sheppard; M Pacheco; A Smith; H Donovan; K D Johnson; K Sofie; W Jung; J Graber; L M Halasz; S Fogh; L P Taylor; H Greenlee; S J Hardy
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Isocitrate dehydrogenase mutant glioma brain tumor (IDHmBT) commonly affects adults with a mean age at diagnosis of 41 years old. Advances in surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation (RT) have extended the overall median survival of IDHmBT survivors. Unfortunately, up to 75% of IDHmBT survivors experience neurological symptoms that significantly impact their overall quality of life (QoL). Nurse-led symptom management interventions to increase self-efficacy, the belief in one’s ability to cope to achieve a desired outcome, have been shown to reduce symptom burden among cancer survivors. However, these studies often excluded patients with BT. Currently, limited interventions have been developed to increase self-efficacy to reduce symptom burden and improve QoL among BT survivors. This abstract aims to present the development of our novel neuro-oncology survivorship curriculum called Symptom management Education to Living Fully (SELF).
METHODS
Using the National Institute of Health (NIH) Stage Model for Behavioral Intervention Development, we reviewed qualitative and quantitative studies. We collaborated with subject matter experts (neuropsychologists, nurses, neuro-oncologists, radiation oncologists, behavioral scientists, theorists) and a patient advocate, to initially inform the content of the SELF intervention (Stage 0 of the NIH Stage Model). Social Learning Theory was used to design the curriculum. In Stage Ia, we conducted an in-person focus group with clinicians to receive feedback on curriculum, content, and delivery. Virtual 1: 1 interviews with stakeholders (patients and caregivers) are underway to refine and modify the SELF curriculum. Deductive coding will be used to analyze the interviews.
RESULTS
The SELF intervention is a 5-30 minute patient education curriculum to be delivered virtually every 2 weeks by a nurse interventionist. Patient education includes skill building for monitoring symptoms, understanding brain tumor and brain injury, and promoting healthy behaviors for brain health. To increase accessibility, SELF will be delivered both virtually or in-person per patient preference. The focus group of clinicians (nurses [n=4], social worker [n=1], and neuropsychologist [n=1]) suggested modification to include the language to present brain injury education, integration of a survivorship care plan, and prioritizing patients at least 6 months after BT diagnosis or treatment initiation. Interviews with stakeholders are expected to conclude in July 2025.
CONCLUSION
To our knowledge, SELF is the only nurse-led symptom management intervention for IDHmBT survivors designed to increase self-efficacy, reduce symptom burden, and improve QoL. Symptom management interventions are necessary to support patients and their caregivers after treatment. SELF will be modified prior to conducting a pilot/feasibility trial (NIH Stage Ib).

title: P15.14.B NURSE-LED SUPPORT PROGRAM FOR NEURO-ONCOLOGY PATIENTS AND THEIR FAMILIES
authors: L Kauffmann; R Schmeer-Oetjen; M Polemikos; J Krauss
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Patients with brain tumors and their family members are confronted with multiple challenges. In addition to the established therapeutic management, there is a need for the integration of supportive care in those patients. The aim of this study was to quantify the effect of a nurse-led support program in neurooncology patients
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A specialist nurse-led support program for neurooncology patients was implemented in 2018. Prior to (2017) and after the implementation (2018-2021), we used an anonymous validated questionnaire to assess patients’ satisfaction level regarding following items: general satisfaction, consideration of personal wishes, worries and fears, nursing care, nursing information, counseling and guidance and discharge planning
RESULTS
A total of 62 patients participated in the study. Before implantation of the specialist nurse-led support program, the majority of patients were already satisfied with the items general satisfaction; consideration of personal wishes, consideration of worries and fears; and nursing care in general; while less patients were satisfied with the remaining items. After implantation of the program, the proportion of patients who were satisfied with the first four items was slightly higher, but a marked improvement was found for information, counseling and guidance (p=0.003), and discharge planning (p=0.005).
CONCLUSION
A specialist nurse-led support program leads to significant improvement in patient care and help to cope with the multidimensional challenges in neurooncology

title: P15.15.A HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS’ PERSPECTIVES ON DELIVERING REHABILITATION TO ADULTS WITH HIGH GRADE GLIOMA
authors: A Zanotto; R N Glover; K Hansen; F W Boele
abstract:
BACKGROUND
While rehabilitation therapy can improve functional outcomes and quality of life of patients with high grade glioma, there is minimal literature available to guide recommendations when working with this group of patients in a rehabilitation setting. The aim of this study was to understand the challenges and opportunities that healthcare professionals report about delivering rehabilitation to patients with glioblastoma.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
To meet study aims, we performed focus groups with healthcare professionals in an outpatient community-based rehabilitation setting in the Midwest region of the United States. Healthcare professionals with and without experience working with patients with high-grade glioma were recruited. Focus groups were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.
RESULTS
Eight focus groups with a total of 29 healthcare professionals were conducted. Six focus groups (n = 21) were conducted with healthcare professionals who self-identified as having experience working with patients with high grade glioma, while the remaining two focus groups (n = 8) were conducted with healthcare professionals who identified as not experienced with this patient group. Ten participants were occupational therapists, ten were physical therapists, six were speech and language pathologists, three were other healthcare professionals. Mean age was 35.3 years (age range 24-61 years). Five participants were male (17.2%). The overarching notion resulting from the analysis was outlining Factors influencing therapy process. Within that six themes were identified: (1) Unique challenges in the context of high-grade brain tumor, (2) Awareness of prognosis, (3) Communication with oncology team, (4) Role of rehabilitation during end-of-life, (5) Impact on therapists, and (6) Role of family.
CONCLUSION
Healthcare professionals outlined the emotional and professional impact and challenges related to working with patients with high grade glioma. Since healthcare professionals who participated in this study were not based in a neuro-oncology setting, they were able to compare their experience of working with patients with high grade glioma with that of delivering rehabilitation to patients with other conditions, such as stroke or traumatic brain injury. The study brings insight into the role of rehabilitation therapy from the clinicians’ perspective and the findings will help with the development of rehabilitation guidelines.

title: P15.16.B ASSESSING THE RELATIONSHIP OF PATIENT CHARACTERISTICS, SYMPTOM BURDEN, PLACE OF DEATH, AND THEIR IMPLICATIONS FOR END-OF-LIFE CARE IN PATIENTS WITH GLIOMAS: A SINGLE-CENTER OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
authors: S M Christ; C J Reynolds; A Veuve; P Heesen; E Le Rhun; M Guckenberger; D Blum; M Weller; C Hertler
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Patients with gliomas, particularly those of higher grades, experience a high symptom burden and have amongst the poorest survival rates in oncology. Neurological deterioration profoundly affects quality of life, especially during the end-of-life (EOL) phase. Understanding the relationship between patient characteristics, symptom burden and place of death offers opportunities to optimize palliative care provision.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
This retrospective, single-center observational study analyzed 394 patients with gliomas treated at the Comprehensive Cancer Centre Zurich (CCCZ) between 2015 and 2023. Data were extracted from medical records, focusing on demographics, disease characteristics, symptoms in the final three months of life, cause and place of death. Statistical analysis, including cross-tabulation, was used to assess associations between variables.
RESULTS
The median age at diagnosis was 60 years (interquartile range (IQR), 50-69) and the median age at death was 62 (IQR, 52-70) years. The median overall survival was 1.49 (IQR, 0.97-2.46) years. The majority of patients (n=347; 88%) had WHO grade 4 gliomas, predominantly glioblastomas. Symptom burden in the last three months of life was high, with 261 patients (66%) experiencing motor dysfunction, 190 (48%) neurocognitive decline, 164 (42%) vision impairment, and 155 (39%) speech difficulties, respectively. Seizures were reported in 77 patients (20%). Symptom co-occurrence was significant, particularly between motor dysfunction and neurocognitive impairment. 180 patients (46%) had a burden of four or more recorded symptoms. Place of death was identified in 179 patients (45%). Among these, 58 patients (32%) died in inpatient palliative care, 46 patients (26%) at home, 28 patients (16%) on other inpatient wards, and 28 patients (16%) in hospice. WHO grade 4 tumors and a higher symptom burden were both independently associated with inpatient death (p<0.05). While the majority of patients (n=185; 67.5%) received specialist care, referral to palliative care services occurred late in the disease trajectory for most patients, typically within 90 days before death. Advance care planning (ACP) was rarely available (4.9%), and EoL decision-making documents were generally lacking.
CONCLUSION
This study highlights the urgent need for earlier palliative care integration into routine neurological and radio-oncological clinical care of patients with gliomas with high symptom burden at EoL. Facilitating ACP and enabling home deaths may help align care with patient preferences, while recognizing that those with high-grade disease and severe symptom load remain at greater risk of institutional EoL care and place of death.

Advance care planning (ACP) was rarely available (4.9%), and EoL decision-making documents were generally lacking.
CONCLUSION
This study highlights the urgent need for earlier palliative care integration into routine neurological and radio-oncological clinical care of patients with gliomas with high symptom burden at EoL. Facilitating ACP and enabling home deaths may help align care with patient preferences, while recognizing that those with high-grade disease and severe symptom load remain at greater risk of institutional EoL care and place of death.

title: P15.17.A END-OF-LIFE CHALLENGES IN NEURO-ONCOLOGICAL PATIENT CARE: A YOUNGNOA SURVEY
authors: L Lazaridis; N B Pepper; P Klein; C Oster; S Agkatsev; I Mildenberger; R Berg; S Seidel; S Sharma; R Bodensohn; P Hau; G Tabatabai; P Roser; B Mallmann; C Kleinschnitz; U Sure; C Seliger; M Glas; M Platten; S Combs; M Müther; S Kebir
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Malignant brain tumors inevitably recur, leading to progressive neurological decline. Palliative care is essential for optimizing patient outcomes, yet its integration into neuro-oncology remains inconsistent. We conducted a nationwide survey to evaluate palliative care practices among German neuro-oncologists and assessed the impact of physicians’ comfort on end-of-life discussions in patient care.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
A nationwide, anonymous survey was distributed to 481 neuro-oncologists who are members of the Neuro-oncology Working Group of the German Cancer Society. The questionnaire, developed in collaboration with board-certified palliative care specialists, evaluated physicians’ demographic characteristics, palliative care knowledge, and access to palliative care resources.
RESULTS
Of 92 respondents, 81 (88%) reported comfort in discussing end-of-life issues, while 11 (12%) expressed discomfort. Physicians comfortable with these discussions more frequently addressed withholding of life-sustaining interventions (88% versus 55%, p=0.011), arranged home care (81% versus 64%, p=0.019), and facilitated hospice placement (68% versus 36%, p=0.021). They also initiated these conversations earlier and observed greater patient receptivity to palliative care (p=0.049). These associations remained significant in multivariable logistic regression.
CONCLUSION
While most neuro-oncologists report comfort with end-of-life discussions, this comfort strongly influences timing and extent of palliative care integration. Our findings highlight the need for structured palliative care training to ensure timely and effective discussions, ultimately improving care for neuro-oncological patients.

title: P15.18.B RETURN TO WORK, SOCIAL, AND LEISURE ACTIVITIES AFTER AWAKE SURGERY FOR GLIOMAS
authors: A M Buunk; J M Spikman; F F Siebenga; H Jeltema; M Wagemakers; A Rofes
abstract:
BACKGROUND
To measure outcome after awake craniotomy for gliomas, attention has shifted from purely oncological outcomes to long-term quality of life and functional recovery. One important yet underexplored dimension of recovery is the resumption of everyday roles—not only employment, but also resuming social activities and participation in leisure activities. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate role resumption in the long-term after awake surgery, and explore possible related demographic and disease-related factors.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Patients with gliomas who underwent awake surgery between 2018-2022 were asked to participate, at least 6 months post-surgery. Resumption of work, social activities and leisure activities was investigated with the Role Resumption List (RRL), which was sent to patients. The RRL includes questions about changes in amount and quality of activities compared with pre-morbid levels, dichotomized in ‘complete resumption’ and ‘incomplete resumption’. Relationships with time since surgery, WHO grades, age, sex, and educational level were calculated using Spearman correlations, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Chi-square tests.
RESULTS
25 patients completed the questionnaire and were included (M age = 47.6, range 17-69, M months since surgery = 19.6, WHO grades 2-4). Before surgery, 22 patients (88%) were employed. After surgery, 40.9% fully resumed their previous occupation. In the group of patients who did not return to work, age and WHO grade were significantly higher. Additionally, 60% reported changes in leisure activities after surgery (partial resumption of leisure activities or no activities at all). Significant associations were found with age and time since surgery: older patients and those at a shorter interval post-surgery reported more problems in leisure resumption. For social roles, 36.4% of patients reported changes (spending less time with family and friends and/or loss of quality of social relationships). No significant associations with demographic or disease-related variables were found for social role resumption.
CONCLUSION
After awake surgery for gliomas, work, leisure and social activities resumption can be affected. Disease severity (i.e. WHO grade) appears to be important in resuming work, but not for leisure and social activities. Additionally, older patients tend to report more problems in resumption of leisure and work activities. Importantly, this study was conducted within the context of clinical care and involved a relatively small patient group, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. A further understanding of patterns and predictors of role resumption following awake surgery, also in comparison to non-awake surgery, is essential to optimize patient-tailored guidance.

title: P15.19.A DUTCH HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS’ EXPERIENCES, PERSPECTIVES, AND BARRIERS TOWARDS PHYSICAL ACTIVITY PROMOTION IN GLIOMA PATIENTS
authors: M E Blom; M Klein; M Gorter; P C de Witt Hamer; J M Niers; J G Jelsma; L Douw
abstract:
BACKGROUND
To bridge the gap between well-recognized benefits of physical activity (PA) and its practical implementation for glioma patients specifically, we investigated healthcare professionals’ experiences, perspectives, and barriers in promoting PA for this patient group.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We developed an online survey consisting of 25 questions for healthcare professionals involved in the care of glioma patients in the Netherlands. The survey included open- and closed-ended questions, the latter of which were based on Likert scales (1-5). The survey was initially distributed via email by the Dutch Neuro-Oncological Society (LWNO), and later distributed by individual healthcare professionals. Participants provided online informed consent.
RESULTS
A total of 55 healthcare professionals from 20 different centers completed the survey, with neurology and nursing being the most represented specialties. The majority of professionals (58%) indicated that they often or very often receive questions about PA throughout all stages of the disease. These questions mainly focused on whether PA was allowed and what types of activities were appropriate. In addition to responding to patient inquiries, 76% of professionals reported that they often or very often proactively provide PA advice. This advice typically involved low-intensity activities, such as daily walking, but did not refer to any established PA guidelines. In addition to this advice, professionals often highlighted the benefits of PA, including improved quality of life, reduced symptoms, and better treatment adherence. Nonetheless, opinions on the strength of evidence supporting the effectiveness of PA were mixed, with 62% of the professionals remaining neutral. Commonly reported drawbacks of PA in glioma patients included concerns about overexertion and potential feelings of inadequacy among patients who are unable to follow advice. Despite these concerns, PA was generally considered safe when tailored to patients’ abilities. Frequently reported barriers to promoting PA included a lack of information materials (37%), limited knowledge among professionals (33%), and limited referral opportunities (27%). Importantly, 89% of the professionals supported the integration of PA into glioma care and 56% expressed a need for specific guidelines to help facilitate its implementation.
CONCLUSION
PA is a frequent topic of discussion between patients and healthcare professionals, but the advice provided could improve. Developing specific guidelines for glioma patients may help address common barriers to promoting PA and support professionals in providing more tailored advice. As a crucial first step toward developing such guidelines, future research should focus on evaluating targeted PA interventions.

title: P15.20.B CALM IN THE FACE OF BRAIN CANCER: INTERIM ANALYSIS OF A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED FEASIBILITY TRIAL FOR NEURO-ONCOLOGY PATIENTS WITH ELEVATED PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS
authors: A Loughan; A Lanoye; G Zarrella; A Fox; A Davies; C Kleva
abstract:
BACKGROUND
Both patients with primary and secondary brain tumors experience substantial psychological distress but have historically been excluded from psychological research. Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully (CALM), a supportive-expressive psychotherapy, has proven to reduce depression and death anxiety in advanced cancer patients, but trials in neuro-oncology have been limited. Due to potential concerns regarding recruitment and retention among this unique population, we conducted a randomized feasibility pilot trial. This report describes interim feasibility and acceptability analyses of the first pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) of CALM in neuro-oncology.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
In this ongoing NIH ORBIT model Phase IIc pilot RCT, 60 adults with primary or secondary malignant brain tumors and elevated distress (depression and/or death anxiety) are randomized (2: 1) to a six-session CALM intervention or usual care (UC; i.e., referrals to local/national resources). Online survey data were collected at baseline, 3 months (post), and 6 months (follow-up) across both arms. A priori benchmarks were set to assess feasibility and acceptability: rates of enrollment (>30%), assessment completion (post=>70%, follow-up=>60%), perceived benefit (>4/5), and recommendation of CALM (>75%).
RESULTS
A multimodal national recruitment model has screened 105 patients, of which 69 were eligible and 60 enrolled (87% enrollment rate; 67% female; 88% White; Mage=52). Current overall assessment completion rates are 77% at post (n=40/52; 77% CALM, 76% UC) and 69% at follow-up (n=33/48; 67% CALM, 69% UC), with 8 participants still undergoing study procedures. For those randomized to CALM (n=39), perceived benefit appears high (M=4/5 rating), and all CALM participants (100%) report they would recommend the intervention to others with malignant brain tumor.
CONCLUSION
We far surpassed our benchmark enrollment rate and achieved our target sample size, reflecting feasibility of our multimodal national recruitment approach spanning local efforts, outreach to neuro-oncology providers, and social media and patient advocacy groups. Though we have yet to complete our data collection period for 3- and 6-months, interim metrics are above target retention benchmarks across both arms. Intervention acceptability among those randomized to CALM is high. The secondary aim of this trial is to examine rates of clinically significant change with respect to depression and death anxiety; in combination with our feasibility and acceptability data, this will inform our planned randomized effectiveness trial of CALM in neuro-oncology.
